items.body: 33 takes the traditional age of Christ at his death as the axis of a twelve-part electroacoustic cycle concerned with creation, incarnation, suffering, death and renewal. Yara Mekawei and Amir Rezk draw on biblical passages, Coptic Orthodox liturgy and Arabic recitation, but rarely allow the texts to remain intact: voices are repeated, stretched and submerged until scripture begins to function as rhythm and texture. Dense drones, fractured percussion, recitation and sudden clearings give the record a ceremonial character without turning it into devotional music. Its structure is particularly effective. “LOGOS” begins with John’s “In the beginning was the Word”; by “New Creation,” Revelation has replaced Genesis, with the first heaven and earth passing away and death itself disappearing. Between them, “Mysterion,” “33,” “Harrowing of Hades” and “Sackcloth Love” trace a passage through Eucharist, Crucifixion, descent and mourning. Musically, 33 sits between electroacoustic composition, dark ambient, and industrial electronics with a hint of prog rock, although none of those descriptions quite accounts for its restless construction. Mekawei and Rezk work with low drones, distorted orchestral sonorities, spoken voices, granular processing and percussion that repeatedly breaks apart just as it appears to settle into a pattern. The music can be oppressively dense, then abruptly hollowed out to expose a voice or a thin electronic residue. Rather than using electronics as accompaniment to the religious texts, the pair subject voice and instrumental material to the same processes: syllables become pulses, recitation turns into noise, and acoustic sounds lose their identifiable origins. This constant movement between intelligibility and abstraction gives the album much of its tension. What begins with a private anxiety surrounding the age of 33 expands into a work about mortality and transformation, with ancient texts treated not as historical artefacts but as material that can still be sounded, fractured and inhabited. To help us further navigate the album, we reached out directly to Yara Mekawei and Amir Rezk. 33 seems to follow an unusually coherent spiritual trajectory: from the Logos and creation in “LOGOS” and “Genesis,” through embodiment, suffering and death, to resurrection and finally the New Jerusalem in “New Creation.” Yet the album never feels like a straightforward retelling of scripture; texts are fragmented, repeated, obscured and absorbed into the electronics. Did you conceive the twelve tracks as a narrative or liturgical cycle from the outset, and how important was it that this progression could be felt without necessarily being understood literally? From the very beginning, we did not set out to create a straightforward textual retelling or a literal recitation of scripture. For us, the sacred texts are not static history; they are a living, sonic score. The progression across the twelve tracks was essential because we recognized that the trajectory of Christ’s life, from incarnation and embodiment, through suffering, descent, and ultimate renewal, is not merely a historical or theological timeline. It is a universal, spiritual archetype. It is a pattern that exists in the world and plays out in our own lives, in human endurance, migration, grief, and rebirth, whether we consciously recognize it or not. By weaving Yara’s personal story, her family inheritance, her grandmother’s warning, her lived experience of displacement and transformation, into this grander framework, the album becomes a dual narrative. The fragmentation, repetition, and electronic processing of the texts reflect how personal memory and sacred history actually operate in human consciousness: rarely as a clean, linear text, but as lingering textures, echoes, and internal pictures. It was crucial that a listener could feel this emotional and spiritual weight instinctively without needing to decipher every word literally, because the underlying trajectory of endurance and transformation is something universally felt in the human spirit. The number 33 begins from something intensely personal — a maternal warning about the thirty-third year of life — but the album gradually connects that age to Christ’s suffering, death and resurrection. In the title track especially, the language of Isaiah’s suffering servant and the Crucifixion seems to make personal vulnerability and sacred history overlap. How did that private association with the age of 33 become the organising principle of the record, and did making the album change what that number meant to you? The connection became obvious the moment we realized that 33 was not just a personal chronological marker, but the darkest point in Christ’s earthly life, the threshold of Gethsemane and the Cross, where He faced an unrepeatable cup of unknown suffering and abandonment. In our own human lives, those rock-bottom moments, where we carry an unbearable personal weight or face severe displacement, often become the precise pivots for profound transformation. The warning Yara inherited about the thirty-third year was essentially pointing toward this exact kind of personal Gethsemane: a room where you are tested to your limits, forcing a parallel between our lived vulnerability and what Christ endured. Creating 33 completely changed what that number means to us. Through the process of writing and immersing ourselves in these detailed sonic patterns and raw emotions, 33 transformed from an ominous, looming warning into a symbol of profound solidarity. It fixed a truth in our minds: our suffering in this life is never meaningless, nor is it carried in isolation. The Divine chose to step into human history and share directly in our exact grief, exile, and pain. Through making this record, the thirty-third year ceased to be a room of fear, becoming instead a reminder that we are never truly alone in the dark. Sacred language in 33 occupies a strange position between meaning and sound. Biblical passages, Coptic Orthodox material, Arabic and other vocal fragments can initially be intelligible, but repetition and electronic processing often push them toward rhythm, texture or something resembling incantation. Yara, your previous work has already explored ways of translating sacred texts into sonic structures; how did the two of you approach the voice here? Were you interested in preserving the theological meaning of these texts, or in reaching a point where the sound of devotion itself becomes the compositional material? For us, it was never a choice between preserving theological meaning or turning the text into pure abstraction, we wanted both. We approached the sacred texts as both a coherent narrative framework and a stream of subconscious thought, treating the voice as a primary musical texture. We deeply respect the inherent power of music to imprint a specific fingerprint upon the mind and the soul. However, we wouldn’t use the word “incantation” to describe this process. Instead, we see the voice and its electronic transformations as a sonic blessing carried through the physical sound waves themselves. We knew that many people listening across the world wouldn’t understand Arabic or Coptic, but we believed that sound itself can transcend language barriers. By layering, repeating, and processing these sacred fragments, we wanted to carry the spiritual energy and raw devotion directly to the listener’s intuition. The theological meaning grounds the structure, while the sonic vibration allows the blessing to reach anyone who listens, regardless of whether they can translate the words. There is a striking circularity between the beginning and end of the album. “LOGOS” opens with John’s “In the beginning was the Word,” while “New Creation” ultimately arrives at Revelation’s vision of the first heaven and earth passing away, God wiping away every tear, and death ceasing to exist. Between those points, the music moves through creation, the body, Eucharist, suffering, mourning and resurrection. Do you think of 33 as moving from one creation to another — and, if so, is “new creation” primarily a Christian theological idea for you, or does it also describe a personal process of destruction and transformation that took place while making the record? It is deeply both: a personal process of transformation and a theological truth made manifest. On a personal and artistic level, 33 is our very first collaboration together, so the album itself is literally a “new creation” born from our two individual musical worlds. We share the belief that marrying the arts with the sacred is like bringing heaven and earth together, much like the Incarnation of the Divine Logos coming down to breathe new life into His creation and bloom into a new Tree of Life. J.R.R. Tolkien spoke of artists as “sub-creators” or co-creators alongside the Great Creator. By deliberately inviting the Divine into our sound, making a “new creation” was never about trying to invent a new genre of music; it was about marrying the eternal with the earthly, which makes the work spiritual and new at its core. Making this album was an essential process of bringing light directly into the desolation of our own personal suffering and “stations” of life. It was a way to ground those difficult experiences in hope and meaning, not just for ourselves, but hopefully for anyone who listens to the record. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items.body: The Getaway could easily have stood on its own, but the remix sequence expands its central idea: fractured industrial sound behaving almost like an alien transmission, constantly mutating through minute edits, glitches, and rhythmic interference. Chiseled from front to back with remarkable precision The Getaway by Unterm Rad   Mike Slansky, operating as Unterm Rad, continues his run of punishing industrial IDM with The Getaway for the ever-consistent Bulgaria-based Mahorka imprint. With a background spanning audio engineering, expansive sound design, and graphic work reaching back to the Tympanik Audio era, Slansky was also a key component of the now-shuttered Point Source Electronic Arts collective. His work has long occupied darker electronic spaces, and The Getaway pushes further into that territory through an unusually constrained process: the album was composed entirely from short instrument clips and sounds supplied through Point Source’s Genome sample kits, each fragment carefully edited, processed, and sequenced until it evolved into something entirely new. No synthesizers, AI, or outside sound sources were used, adhering to the open-source spirit of the Genome project. Seven original pieces emerge as dark-grey slabs of machinery, where microscopic edits and fractured rhythms give each track a strangely extraterrestrial charge. Up front, “Hang Me Out To Dry” drives through minimal industrial fissures with a beat-heavy barrage of rugged technoid tones, metallic grit, and tightly controlled distortion. “They’re On To Us” narrows the focus further, exposing Slansky’s precision-built rhythmic glitches as tiny mechanical movements seem to twitch beneath the surface, while “Cornered” opens into broken beats and cavernous echoes, giving the record a sense of mechanical engineer​ing operating somewhere far beyond human reach. Transparent details become increasingly exposed :: The final six pieces hand Slansky’s material over to Access to Arasaka, Evaluation Copy, Vaag, Feederwire, Hexalyne, and Cole, each pulling the source tracks into a distinct interpretation. Rather than simply extending the album, these remixes reveal just how much microscopic movement exists inside Slansky’s sound structures. Access to Arasaka and Hexalyne sharpen the material into brisk, erratic sci-fi electro-nics; Evaluation Copy scorches through beats and bass; Vaag bends the rhythms into flexible broken beat contortions; and Feederwire drags everything through piercing industrial low-end vibrations. Cole’s closing interpretation is perhaps the most surreal, stripping the machinery back until its strange, transparent details become increasingly exposed. The Getaway could easily have stood on its own, but the remix sequence expands its central idea: fractured industrial sound behaving almost like an alien transmission, constantly mutating through minute edits, glitches, and rhythmic interference. Closing with “The Walls Are Closing In,” before the remixes kick in, Slansky lets pressure evaporate into sparse technoid shifts, leaving behind an album that feels both rigorously engineered and strangely alive. By opening his source material to collaborators, he turns a tightly controlled sonic experiment into a broader study of industrial texture, glitch mechanics, and extraterrestrial electronics—chiseled from front to back with remarkable precision. The Getaway is available on Mahorka. [Bandcamp] The Getaway by Unterm RadThe post Unterm Rad :: The Getaway (Mahorka) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items.body: “The devil is busy” is what churchgoers say when trouble arrives, and Seun Kuti & Egypt 80 take the phrase, as “Devil Just Busy”, and point it at the darkness closing over contemporary society. Seun turns the preachers’ own words back on them: on the title track and first single of his upcoming album Na Dem, he already listed reverends, bishops, pastors and imams among the “winch men” he wants saving from, and his father Fela Kuti went after the same pulpits on “Shuffering and Shmiling” in 1978. “DJB” gives the phrase seven minutes of dark, mid-tempo afrobeat, laid down by two drummers, Mario Orsinet and Femi Koleoso, and two bassists, Kunle Justice and Gbeke Ojutiku. Seun sings and plays saxophone on top, with two trumpets and four more saxophones building the horn arrangements around him. Koleoso, who leads Ezra Collective, also produced the track, as he did the whole of Na Dem. Na Dem arrives on 6 November via Django Music, eight days before Fela becomes the first African solo artist inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame. Seun, who inherited Egypt 80 at 14 when his father died in 1997, will be in Los Angeles to represent him at the ceremony, five weeks after the band play the city’s Regent Theater on 9 October. That date sits in a US run that also takes in Belly Up Tavern in Solana Beach on 7 October, FORM Arcosanti in Arizona and Webster Hall in New York on 14 October. Listen to “DJB” HERE The post Daily Discovery: Seun Kuti & Egypt80 – DJB appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: Review by brainsuccasurgery — The Science of the Seasons in 4 Points. Before discussing *La Scienza delle Stagioni*, Andrea Orlando's second album, it might be helpful to review the following preliminary points:1. The Bands. Andrea Orlando is the drummer on all four albums by La Coscienza Di Cena, an RPI band founded in Genoa in 2007, which released a superb self-titled debut album in 2011 and three other highly recommended albums between 2013 and 2018. Is it worth noting here that Genoa (Genova) is the birthplace of the illustrious PFM, one of the founding fathers of Italian progressive rock (RPI)?Before the formation of La Coscienza Di Cena, Andrea Orlando had already gained some recognition in this microcosm as a member of what it's fair to call the "Zuffanti nebula"?a transalpine prog music collective that began to coalesce around the Genoese bassist Fabio Zuffanti in the early '90s and gained greater visibility with Finisterre's debut album (1995).2. The Artist. Andrea Orlando joined Finisterre as early as 1997 on their *Live at Progday* and then on the fabulous *In Ogni Luogo* (1999), before returning for the 2019 comeback album. Orlando also played drums on *Mirrogames* (1998) by H�stsonaten, Zuffanti's other major band. In both cases, Orlando replaced Marco Cavani. To round out this overview, it's worth noting that drummer Andrea Orlando also contributed to the album by La Curva di Lesmo (2015), a duo that Zuffanti formed with Stefano Agnini, one of the two keyboardists on La Coscienza. And that brings us partially full circle.Let's now turn to the album itself by going over the other two points:3. The musicians. Since Andrea Orlando is one of the stalwarts of this famous Genoese music scene, it's no surprise that for his two solo albums, he called on other members of that same scene. For example, to give credit where credit is due, Zuffanti himself plays bass on one track from *La Scienza delle Stagioni*, and Boris Valle (Finisterre's longtime keyboardist) plays piano on another. Orlando, an accomplished drummer but also a capable keyboardist (with a predilection for the mellotron and organ), here cedes the piano parts?in addition to Valle?to Luca Scherani (H�stsonaten, La Coscienza di Zeno, La Curva di Lesmo) and to Agostino Marco (Finisterre, La Maschera, Zaal) for the Moog solos.On *Dalla Vita Autentica*, Andrea Orlando's previous solo album, the majority of the electric guitar parts were performed by two highly talented musicians: Marcella Arganese?who can be found in Ubi Maior and who regularly dazzles us with *Samura� of Prog*?and Laura Marsano, whom we've seen on Zuffanti's solo albums and those of drummer Maurizio Di Tollo. Two women on guitar?and not just any women?is rare enough to be worth noting, whatever the critics of "wokism" may say. On *La Scienza delle Stagioni*, Marcella has been replaced by Stefano Marelli, but Laura Marsano is always there to treat us to her poignant solos (the slow "Stagione Lontana"). The young singer Meghi Moschino contributes her calm, medium-toned voice to five of the seven tracks?a voice that reminds me a bit of Laura Mombrini's (Prowlers). On *Dalla Vita Autentica*, the robust vocals of Alessandro Corvaglia (another essential, ubiquitous figure on the RPI scene for several years), paired with those of Simona Angioloni (remember *Aries*, the band formed in the 2000s with? Zuffanti, him again), gave the whole a more robust feel. A matter of taste.4. The music. *La Scienza delle Stagioni* alternates between dynamic, vibrant tracks rooted in PFM's sun-drenched RPI, and tenderly romantic moments that unfold into expansive, emotionally charged symphonic prog, closer in style to *Hostsonaten*. By elegantly blending these two styles, the diptych "Il Sogno di Anastasia" (12:12) stands out as one of the album's most compelling tracks. In addition to "Il Sogno di Anastasia ? Parte Seconda," a lovely musical reverie with enchanting undertones, the album includes another instrumental, "City 40" (6:36), a sort of high-energy Latin version of "Samurai of Prog."The influence of Camel, noticeable from the very start of the previous album ("Le Forme Della Distanza"), is less pronounced throughout *La Scienza delle Stagioni*, giving way to more personal ideas, resulting in a kind of symphonic neo-prog with strong RPI influences. On the other hand, the extensive and frequent use of the mellotron (the long intro to "Stagione Lontana" with its celestial tones, or that of "La Strada del Ritorno," among others) draws the most serene moments toward the most ethereal Scandinavian prog.Of roughly similar length, the epic closing track, the highly symphonic "La Strada del Ritorno" (15:01), can be compared to the thrilling "Dalla Vita Autentica" (16:52), which closed the 2017 album of the same name, illuminated by an unforgettable solo by Marcella Arganese. But despite some structural and musical similarities, the comparison ultimately favors the latter, which is more ambitious and features more inspired melodies. Yet the melancholy that envelops the final section of "La Strada del Ritorno"?enhanced by Meghi's angelic voice and the serene appearance of the English and French horns?ultimately moves us, giving us the impression that a pale winter sun has come to breathe its loving breath upon us.At first glance, *La Scienza delle Stagioni* seems a little less striking than its predecessor, *Dalla Vita Autentica*. At the very least, it builds on its predecessor's strengths while retaining all its qualities, though without reaching quite the same heights. But let's not be fooled by first impressions. There are prog albums that possess a kind of natural clarity, made up of music whose beauty is immediately apparent; and others, like *La Scienza delle Stagioni*, that save their magic for a little later, revealing it just after we've finished listening, when we think we've moved on to something else. But that is the secret art of these mysterious works: to prepare for us an immediate future more beautiful than expected. *La Scienza delle Stagioni* possesses that special magic that fairies bestow as they lean over the cradle of certain works?a magic that stays with you and illuminates your path long after the notes have faded away.

items.body: Review by greenpete — They made a startlingly confident beginning with their exuberant, minor-label debut, An Evening With Dando Shaft (no, not a live album). But Dando Shaft's high-water mark arrived with this, their sophomore LP (often called the "Carousel" album, and released on RCA's short-lived Neon label, which only issued 11 albums total). This record dispenses entirely with drums, plunging deeper into varied, lyrical progressive folk. Singer Polly Bolton, from the wonderfully named village of Leamington Spa, joined the boys to bolster their string intricacies with her breathy, Sandy Denny-esque voice. The debut was marred only by the awkward "The Cat Song," but on the Carousel album, there's really not a bad cut. The Bulgarian-rhythmic songs of dual guitarists Dave Cooper and Kevin Dempsey, and mega-instrumentalist Martin Jenkins, are consistently strong, with Jenkins' mandolin, flute, and fiddle shining here. His tune "Whispering Ned," about a gent who enjoys indulging in sugar cubes (and whom the band evidently knew) adds an imaginative twist to the canon of drug songs. The upbeat "Pass it On" is notable for its exuberant chorus about values that have, sadly, since gone out of style. But the real highlights are "Till the Morning Comes" and "River Boat." Both feature Bolton's angelic vocals, the former a wispy duet with Cooper graced by luscious, gently psychedelic flute (Jenkins) and tablas (Ted Kay); and the latter an utterly breathtaking, pastoral delight that conjures green, rural England in poem-song.Bolton would stick around for Lantaloon, a good but inessential album, then depart after tiring of feeling like a "guest" vocalist. So if you plan to only get one album by this highly underappreciated psych-folk band...take a ride on the Carousel.- greenpete

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — A reunion, of sorts, in effect as all participants in this studio product had played with Jack in former bands; The Graham Bond Quartet (Bruce & McLaughlin), The Graham Bond Organization (Bruce & Heckstall-Smith), and Jack's previous album, Songs for a Tailor (with Hiseman). (Hiseman and Heckstall-Smith had, of course, been playing for a couple years together in David Greenslade's Colosseum--three albums worth.)1. "Over The Cliff" (2:56) a quick riff from Dick Heckstall-Smith's tenor sax launches bassist Jack Bruce and drummer Jon Hiseman into a rapid-paced expression of fairly straightforward Hard Bop Jazz. There is little to no input from John McLaughlin's guitar but Dick, Jack, and Jon are more than up for the trio presentation. Interesting and respected but this is not really my preferred type of music. (8.875/10)2. "Statues" (7:35) more blues-based Hard Bop Jazz from Dick, Jack, and Jon in which the trio dance around one another in tight and attentive circles, each playing their own consistent melody lines--Dick even going for the two-saxes in the mouth at the same time trick a couple times. In the fifth minute there is a cease and desist order so that Jack can bow his bass a bit, but then Jon rejoins with meagre little input from Dick (and, interestingly, none from John McLaughlin) before Jack steps back to let Jon have the spotlight a couple of times before the recapitulation of the opening themes over the final 35 seconds. Fine musicianship. (13.5/15)3. "Sam Enchanted Dick" - medley (7:28) bass and electric guitar recite the song's main melodies over Jon's drums for the first 30+ seconds before John is loosed with his distorted tone to solo for about a minute. Then it's Jack's turn in the third minute. John's chord accents are all I can pay attention to (for I am a HUGE fan of John's fascinating "rhythm guitar" choices). At 3:37 we hear the first squirts of Dick's, tenor sax--which leads, of course, to an extended solo for him (and yet my ears still find themselves paying attention to John's caustic chord interjections). Double saxes for a bit in the seventh minute before Dick's play on "Sweet Georgia Brown" lead to the song's finish. (13.5/15) a. "Sam Sack" b. "Rill's Thrills"4. "Born To Be Blue" (4:26) a gorgeous ballad with very sensitive performances from all four players. There is enough space in the soundscape of this song that I can very much appreciate the skills and creativity of each individual musician--which I need from time to time in order to better understand and value the musics I'm being exposed to. (9/10)5. "HCKHH Blues" (8:59) there is an auspicious threat of power and havoc in this song's music from its very opening. Despite Jack and John's pulling tendency to want to drift over into the Louisiana Bayous, Dick and Jon do a great job in keeping the spirit firmly anchored in less Southern traditions, more in the urban forms of expression. Finally pusuaded, John and Jack swing over to join Dick and John in their Coltrane-like explorations. (18.125/20)6. "Ballad For Arthur" (7:42) pensive bass notes are embellished by delicate cymbal and snare play while Dick explores his own melody ideas. There is enough focus in Dick's playing that Jack and Jon both feel empowered to let their own playing go a bit into the realms of improvisational freedom--until, that is, John feels inspired to join in (around 1:50). Thereafter John's "commanding presence" effects a stoppage from Jon (no drums or cymbal sound for over a minute!) while Dick tries to figure out how to play background accompanist role to John's spacial musings. With Jon's boisterous Jack DeJohnette-like return in the fifth minute, we find the other three suddenly inspired to become quite a bit more dynamic: each flying off in their own directions while somehow it all still manages to make sense from a collective view. With a minute left to go there is a sudden buildup and burst into controlled chaos before everybody backs out, spent. While I still don't "like" this kind of music, I understand anad appreciate the discipline and skill required to make it happen--to make it work. (13.5/15)7. "Things We Like" (3:38) another this time more targeted and speedy foray into the reactive/responsive side of Jazz' free jazz movement. There is a playfulness to this one that makes it a bit more amusing and, thus, enjoyable. (8.875/10)Total Time 48:04Despite the presence (and influence) of metamorphosizing guitarist John McLaughlin on four of the album's seven songs, the rest of the band on this album (Bruce, Hiseman, and Heckstall-Smith) are all playing Jazz, standard, blues-based Jazz albeit at times what we've come to call their own versions of "free jazz." John is the only one pushing boundaries, injecting non-standard sounds, riffs, and epithets. One might also argue that Dick Heckstall-Smith is pushing for more free jazz representation. Were I more of fan of straight Jazz (I'm trying, folks!) I might like this album more. As it stands, I feel hard-pressed to even consider this "Jazz-Rock Fusion" much less call it such.B+/4.5 stars; while Jazz afficionadoes might consider this a minor masterpiece of Jazz (or even Jazz-Rock Fusion), would call this a near-masterpiece and not a true representative of Jazz-Rock Fusion; to my mind Things We Like has got far more of the fire and focus of pure Jazz than it does of Fusion or progressive rock.

items.body: Review by Matti — Today is the official release date of the third album by Confusion Field, the Finnish heavy prog act sovereignly led by multi-instrumentalist, vocalist, composer and producer Tomi Kankainen. This time he plays himself all of the guitars as well, and the drums are now played by an Italian session drummer, Martino Malacrida. I have reviewed both of the earlier albums (dating from 2021 and 2023), and, given that I'm not an active listener or connoisseur of the heavier genres, I struggle a bit to find something new to say. But I certainly still feel Confusion Field makes "modern Finnish heavy prog at its best". If you have enjoyed CF before, you will have a great listening with this one too, or if you're new to the band, let's say that if you are into contemporary heavy/metal prog and bands such as Riverside and Porcupine Tree, you may be happily surprised. The moods are rather dark but not too depressive. The sound is very well produced and balanced. The guitars have the metallic bite but they don't go TOO far into aggressiveness for me to digest. The synths are incorporated into the meaty but clear texture, even though there may be slightly more of them than before. Malacrida is an excellent metal oriented drummer. No gun machine attacks but an intelligent sense of the whole. And what's best, Kankainen has an excellent voice quite comparable to Mariusz Duda of Riverside. This is something I cannot say very often within heavier end of prog. He never growls or yells at the top of his lungs and yet he has no difficulties whatsoever to convince the listener.The songs feel pretty tight at the average five minute length. All compositions sound fine and well crafted. Perhaps they aren't very distinctive from each other, in the progressive sense, but I don't get the feeling of tiresome sameness. The closing piece is the longest (7:16) and especially here the synths, a bit reminiscent of the mid-80's Simple Minds (Sparkle in the Rain, New Gold Dream), really make a nice extra dimension to the powerful soundscape. An album well worth checking out!

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — Early (First Wave) Jazz-Rock from Poland. This band's debut, we find them experimenting with blending several styles including Blues-Rock, Psychedelia, Procol Harum-like prog, orchestra-enriched lounge music, and more. The album was released in 1971 by Polskie Nagrania Muza.1. "Sen (A Dream)" (3:17) what feels like an ANTHONY PHILLIPS guitar piece opens this for the first 1:07 before a pause unleashes a bouncing organ chord, funky bass line, and Michael Giles-like drumming with simplistic guitar riffs over the top to announce the presence of melody. In the final 30 seconds there is this all out burst of WHO-like energy being expressed/expelled by all of the band members--which then seems to bleed/lead into the SANTANA-like frenzy that is the next song. A three-part suite in three minutes! Wow! (9.333/10)2. "Kuszenie (Temptation)" (3:29) the SANTANA-like percussion-driven full-band jam that features everybody flying at full speed. Maciej Gluszkiewicz' organ impresses as do the performances of all of the quartet members. (9.25/10)3. "Nerwy Miasta (The Nerves Of Cities)" (3:31) a slowed down PROCOL HARUM-like sound palette that comes off sounding like something from a Blues-Rock band like anything lead by vocalist ALEX LIGERTWOOD, Billy Gibbons, or 21st Century Polish band LIZARD. At the very end the band do a quick shift into high gear for minute of rousing organ-led instrumental fun to finish things off. (8.875/10)4. "Senne Wędr'wki (Wandering Dreams)" (3:52) orchestra-supported blues rock! Interesting! Quite like the sound of PROCOL HARUM. Nice imagination! (9/10)5. "Taniec Wariatki (The Madwoman's Dance)" (2:02) rock-infused theatric cabaret music (almost musique concr'te) with interesting call-and-response playfulness between the instrumentalists. Quite creative. (4.625/5)6. "Taniec Czterech (The Four Men's Dance)" (1:37) fun/funny open air, city green music by the local marching band. Nice drumming. (4.375/5)7. "Na Przek'r (Against Everything)" (2:16) opens like some folk rock from one of the Summer of Love's outdoor music festivals--with vocals (DON BREWER-like lead with Gospel church choir backing), like a. moralistic hippy musical. (4.625/5)8. "Nasze Myśli (Thoughts)" (5:10) pensive four chord progression arpeggiated by guitar with organ, drums, and bass backing while lead singer croons like a South American folk singer singing through the city center's public address system (or else LIZARD's Damian Bydliński). The very pleasant and comforting song contains a somewhat-spirited organ solo but is really just more of a nice ballad. Interesting vocal weave at the finish. Reminds me of 1990s QUIDAM. (9/10)9. "Mrowisko (The Hive)" (4:15) unusual opening with drums and organ playing cat-and-mouse-in-the-mirror for the first 35 seconds. Then a pause opens the door for a classical guitar and intermittent bombastic "symphonic" bursts of accompaniment and antiphonal response--something that gets drawn out for a minute, stumbling and fumbling, until finally fully developed at the three-minute mark. From there we get a minute of song with singing. Weird. (So like the 21st Century music of Polish band LIZARD). Yet interesting. And creative. (9/10)10. "Pejzaż Z Pustych Ram (Landscape Of Empty Frames)" (4:31) gentle electric guitar musings accompanied by responsive ghost-vocalese open this before a fully-meted song presents itself at 1:10. Singer Marek Alaszewski sounds like Jacques Brel during the delicate verse, but then things amp up for the chorus, Marek switching voice tones to something more RPI like as choir vocals chase him around like a church choir. Nice bass work from Roman Pawelski as the band and vocalists sustain the chorus intensity from here to the song's end. Very nice: emotional. (9/10)11. "Taniec Głodnego (The Starvelling's Dance)" (2:24) PROCOL HARUM palette and slow militaristic pace as organ swirls, drum and bass keep funereal time, and wooden flute (recorder) presents and carries the lead over the top. The opening motif switches into something more dance-oriented at 1:38 as Roman shifts to a walking bass line. Sounds like a wonderful night for a Moondance (Van Morrison)! Nice! (4.5/5)12. "Epidemia Euforii (Epidemic Euphory)" (3:46) not sure what is meant by this song's title, but the music feels more derivative of a combination of early British Rock and the U.S.'s Beatnik styles. By the time the band really kicks into full gear we're presented something that sounds more like Steve Winwood's first band, The Spencer Davis Group, as well as, at the percussion end, like The Chicago Transit Authority (with, of course, the Damian Bydliński lead vocal voice). (8.875/10)13. "Sen (A Dream)" (1:49) all four members of the rock combo are here represented with Marek dusting off his recorder again to muse over the gentle/calming nature-backed music. (4.375/5)Total time 41:59A very creative band of proficient musicians who create an unusual but very pleasing style of progressive rock: their songs are either isolated vignettes of imagination or conglomerations of such all smashed together. The bottom line is: that it works! I especially like the interesting use of choral backing vocals and full-spectrum and active percussion tracks.A-/4.5 stars; a collection of what feels like experimental and highly-idiosyncratic musical ideas coming from a very creative and skilled quartet of young musicians that results in a minor masterpiece of early progressive rock music. (There is little or no Jazz much less Jazz-Rock Fusion here).

items.body: Review by Thomas1969 — Every time Steven Wilson releases a new album, I think: "Wow, is it that time again?" It also occurs to me that I rarely revisit the albums released after *Hand. Cannot. Erase.* (2015). While every album since then has certainly contained good songs, none have gripped me the way the dark *Grace for Drowning* (2011), *The Raven That Refused to Sing (And Other Stories)* (2013), and the aforementioned album did.What I've missed since then is a certain emotional depth in the music, as well as that "moody" side. Fortunately, we hear that moody side return in the advance track "Requiem for a Village," taken from the album of the same name due out in November. The album cover certainly looks promising. But what about the content?the music itself? "Requiem for a Village" is vintage Wilson: a moody opening, an enigmatic progression, a guitar eruption three-quarters of the way through, busy drumming, and?this is where the real tension lies for me?the quieter passages and mysterious vocals (Wilson is singing more beautifully than ever) at the beginning and end, accompanied by evocative keyboard sounds.Of course, there is a full band behind Steven Wilson?it could easily be called the Steven Wilson Band. Who makes up the band as of 2026? Lead vocals, bass guitar, guitar, Mellotron, keyboards, percussion, piano, oboe, mixing engineer, lyre, producer: Steven WilsonGuitar, backing vocals, synthesizer, Mellotron, co-producer, lyre: Randy McStineDrums: Russell HolzmanSo, it is very much a Steven Wilson affair, but Randy McStine and?most certainly?the new drummer Russell Holzman deserve special mention. They play skillfully?you have to hand it to them?but does it truly *connect*? Does it move me? Richard Barbieri moved me with every keystroke; of that, I remain absolutely certain. I am also left with a nagging feeling?since a new The Pineapple Thief album is coming out next month as well?of whether I am looking forward more to *that* album (featuring Gavin Harrison on drums) or to the new Steven Wilson release. You might say: you still miss Porcupine Tree. That's true. You never really get over that. But what I miss most is the emotional depth found in Porcupine Tree's music. Since *Hand. Cannot. Erase.*, no full Steven Wilson album has truly moved me in the same way. That could change. It might... You probably grasp my point. My ambivalence.A bit of a mixed bag, then, this sprawling track?clocking in at 7 minutes and 56 seconds.

items.body: Review by Finnforest — "After the Darkness, the Light" On their third and final album of the 1970s, Salis flipped the script once again, sounding nothinglike their previous effort five years prior. The Salis brothers were back, but they had a newdrummer and keyboardist in the lineup, and they obviously were hell-bent on forging a new direction.There is no sign of the debut's personality or the acoustic mellow vibe of the second. Here the bandhas shifted to that largely instrumental spacey fusion sound so common in the late '70s. The first reference that jumped into my mind was PFM's "Jet Lag" album, and I wondered if that wasan influence for Salis here, though "Jet Lag" is more adventurous than this. The mix of polishedrhythm section and quirky keyboard parts also reminded me just a bit of some of the instrumentalinterludes on later Cat Stevens albums. Another band this reminds me of is Finch. If you were intothem, you should enjoy these competent but sometimes tedious instrumentals. There are some very coollead guitar passages in several tracks. I suspect the approach is the reason why this album is ratedso much higher than their previous two, but frankly I don't see it. Yes, the longer jams overfloating keyboard atmosphere is going to appeal to progressive rock fans, but I think thecompositions on the first two albums are more interesting to me. Nevertheless, it is withoutquestion another good album by Salis. It all comes down to your tastes, naturally. I find this albumcompetent but pretty forgettable.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — At the time, I thought Strange Little Girls was the last album where Tori Amos pursued a specific stylistic direction; just as she had previously dedicated albums to the sound of the acoustic piano or the clavichord, here she focused on the Wurlitzer (alongside her classic B�sendorfer piano), which gave the record a very special atmosphere. Yet that wasn't the only thing distinguishing the �lbum, which was dedicated to covering songs originally performed by men and giving them a feminine twist. However, rather than focusing on the personas she created for each track, I want to concentrate on the music itself; each version is distinct and received such a unique treatment, akin to applying makeup, that the song was transformed until it became unrecognizable, turning into something entirely new. This reveals the true meaning of reimagining a song."New Age", originally by The Velvet Underground, is transported to another dimension: a cold, futuristic realm, ripped without anesthesia from its quasi-hippie, Buffalo Springfield-esque setting. Tori sings with restraint at first before letting go; her voice sounds perfect alongside the album's other star, guitarist Adrian Belew. While the original held the light of morning, she imbued this version with the shadow of dusk, its diametric opposite.Belew helps make the album more challenging and progressive; his riffs complement the spirit of Tori, which was already unconventional for the time. Then there is "'97 Bonnie & Clyde", originally by rapper Eminem, though it goes without saying that the song is unrecognizable here. It is subtle and modern, yet simultaneously evokes the 1920s, featuring a drum machine that contrasts with the sound of violins and her whispered vocals.The case of "Strange Little Girls" is intriguing; for its creators, The Stranglers, it represented a move toward modernity, embracing new wave after their punk past, while Amos takes it a step further by making it postmodern. The Wurlitzer lends a futuristic air, and her committed, uninhibited vocal performance, bolstered by backing vocals, truly makes the song her own. Matt Chamberlain provides the final touch that perfects the power of this rendition.Depeche Mode's "Enjoy the Silence" is so powerful that one need not dig deep to unlock its full potential. Stripped of all its trappings, just the song itself, a piano, and a few strings, it shone like a mineral catching a ray of sunlight, glowing even from afar.She took 10cc's 1975 track "I'm Not In Love", originally warm and even contradictorily (or paradoxically) romantic, and made it icy, almost Krautrock-esque and mechanical; it features a long introduction where the beautiful original melody is recognizable only in her vocals, yet here it feels more like a threat, even though the original lyrics seemed like a confession born of denial."Rattlesnakes", a song by Lloyd Cole and the Commotions, also retains its original melody, though the tempo has been slowed down; the country, road-trip vibe remains, driven by the sound of the Rhodes piano. However, while the original's string arrangements gave it a friendly, Waterboys-esque feel, this version seems more rooted in the rural landscape of Wim Wenders' "Paris, Texas", which, at the very least, imbues it with genuine emotion."Time", by my dear Tom Waits and taken from the album Rain Dogs, remains completely unchanged; no alteration was needed, as the only shift here lay (significantly) in the vocals. Tom's voice carries powerful tones and deep emotion, tinged with melancholy in this instance, while Tori's version holds its own distinct nuances, rooted in a similarly somber quality but stemming from different sources.Neil Young and his album Harvest need no introduction; they make even those of us who aren't huge fans of country music love it!, And Tori interpreted it as if she were Garbage, with a Portishead-style trip-hop vibe, distorting, transforming, and rocking it out, much like Neil Young had transformed Bob Dylan's "All Along the Watchtower." A double tribute."I Don't Like Mondays", the iconic ballad by The Boomtown Rats (Bob Geldof's band), was a chamber-pop track featuring distinctly New Wave strings, a rich, elaborate sound, and prominent piano work. Tori captured the song's essence while performing solo on the Rhodes; she made it more direct and sincere, less explosive, and instead, something akin to an implosion."Happiness Is A Warm Gun" (originally by The Beatles, of course) features a prominent contribution from Belew, recalling his years alongside Robert Fripp, and evokes the atmosphere of his solo album Exposure, in which the guitar intermingles with audio snippets of George W. Bush; much like Fripp's record, which also incorporated overlaid audio, this concept album cemented modernity as the norm. There is plenty of room for improvisation here, and the creative flight turns progressive once again, with a psychedelic, spacey and cosmic feel.Slayer's "Raining Blood" made people headbang and stomp along to the beat... Tori's version seems to have descended into a netherworld where neither time nor physical matter exists; consequently, it feels and is perceived differently. Her piano is deep and low, it inflicts pain (were we capable of feeling it), and her voice possesses a density equal to that of the guitars in the original. If Slayer's intention was to evoke fear, this version inspires terror.We come to the final track, one by another pianist I greatly admire, Joe Jackson: "Real Men," a classic from his album Night & Day that he always performed live. The original 1982 version already featured a drum machine, keyboards, and an uptempo beat, yet it was imbued with deep emotion through Joe's performance. Consequently, Tori didn't need to alter the song's spirit; aside from performing it as a solo piano piece, an approach she took throughout the album, modifying arrangements only when necessary, she made choices that I feel were spot-on. Just as Joe is a brilliant pianist, so is she; she infused the song with her own piano sensibility, incorporating a few additional classical-style notes. And so, in a manner that feels almost sarcastic given the final track's title and the album's overarching theme, yet while remaining deeply faithful to the defiant spirit of many of the original songs, these twelve covers found a new home.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — The trio format suits the Canterbury scene perfectly. Soft Machine immediately comes to mind, yet a jazz sensibility permeates the French group's sound, whether through the piano or the Hammond organ. As with Soft Machine, vocals are not their strong suit; during the instrumental sections of "Voici la nuit tomb�e," they also lean into a Doors-esque psychedelia.While the classic distorted keyboard sound sets the mood, Yves Hasselmann's vocals occasionally flirt with a classical style reminiscent of Supersister, until the jazz trio element takes over. Atonal passages build great suspense and a French film noir atmosphere, fittingly enough, eventually giving way to further psychedelic sections.However, in other passages, the composition is less daring, settling into a more conventional jazz style akin to that of the previous decade. "Flamenco" follows jazz-style counterpoint, adding Canterbury-esque humor in the vein of Supersister and pushing the sonic boundaries of the trio, with outstanding work from bassist Jacques-Edmond Gour�."Passo" reminded me of Friedrich Gulda's preludes, before shifting into an improvisation more in the style of Keith Jarrett. "Soleil" bears a strong resemblance to Dave Brubeck and "Blue Rondo � la Turk"; the format of short, consecutive tracks suits the trio well following the eighteen-minute suite, as immediacy and speed were Paramount, the idea being that he who strikes first strikes twice, even if they couldn't quite sustain the dramatic tension achieved by their counterparts in Moving Gelatine Plates. The surrealist element was tempered by a classic jazz sensibility that took a bit of the intensity out of the Project, though certainly not its value or quality.

items.body: In September 1827, Hector Berlioz saw the actress Harriet Smithson play Ophelia in a Paris production of Hamlet and fell hopelessly in love. When his letters went unanswered, he turned the obsession into music, completing a symphony in 1830 at the age of twenty-six. It was first performed at the Paris Conservatoire that December, without Smithson in the audience. She heard the revised work two years later, and in 1833 the two were married. The program follows a young artist through five scenes: a reverie, a ball, a day in the country, a march to his own execution and a witches’ sabbath. The last two are opium nightmares, and the woman he loves haunts every scene as a recurring melody, the idée fixe. In the finale her theme returns as a cackling parody on a shrill E-flat clarinet, and bells toll as the Dies irae rises from the depths of the orchestra. Recordings part company on the details: the repeats in the first movement and the march, the optional cornet in the waltz, the bells, and old instruments versus modern. Here are The Classic Review editorial team’s recommendations for the 10 best recordings of Berlioz’s Symphonie fantastique. Royal Concertgebouw Orchestra, Colin Davis Colin Davis gives the listener the whole score: Every repeat is observed, the march’s among them, and the waltz includes the optional cornet part. Davis tightens the drama one movement at a time, and even Berlioz’s oddest sonorities are made to count. The price is a certain restraint. The ball ends in good order rather than a whirl, and the last two movements are held on a tighter leash than the music invites. Complete and played with unbroken concentration, this 1974 recording is the natural place to start. Davis Amazon Presto Apple Boston Symphony Orchestra, Charles Munch Where Davis builds the symphony with steady care, Munch plays it as theater, and this 1962 recording is a touchstone for that raw intensity. The first three movements are ardent, but the real storm is saved for the last two. When it breaks, the march and the witches’ sabbath erupt in a frenzy that still startles, with the whole orchestra driven to the edge. His faster 1954 recording is fiercer still in places, but finer playing and sound tip the balance toward the later version. For Berlioz at his wildest, this is the one to hear. Munch Amazon Presto Apple Orchestre Révolutionnaire et Romantique, John Eliot Gardiner John Eliot Gardiner took his period orchestra into the hall where the symphony was first heard in 1830. He seated the musicians as their counterparts sat in that era, with the violins split left and right, and the 1991 recording still sounds like a discovery. It flows more easily than the period-instrument pioneer before it, and its dynamics stretch from a bare whisper to full force without the inner lines ever blurring. Both repeats are taken, and the optional cornet brightens the waltz. The dry room leaves little halo around the sound, and it is no more thrilling than the great modern-orchestra versions. What it offers instead is the orchestra Berlioz knew, in the very room where his symphony was born. Gardiner Amazon Presto Apple Paris Conservatoire Orchestra, Ataúlfo Argenta Every movement runs faster than usual in Ataúlfo Argenta’s 1957 recording, and the scenes cut past like a film reel run too fast. Argenta skips the first movement’s repeat but takes the march’s, and the playing is not always polished, with some unevenness in the brass. None of that dims the impetuous energy, which carries the whole symphony along like one long, breathless dream. Argenta Amazon Presto Apple French National Radio Orchestra, Thomas Beecham A shadow lengthens through this famous 1959 recording. Beecham takes the story entirely seriously, and his march to the scaffold starts slower than usual, so the threat builds before the procession picks up speed. It is a darker, more measured journey than Argenta’s headlong dash. Beecham leaves out the first-movement repeat, and his mono recording from two years earlier burns hotter. Yet the slow build here pays off in a witches’ sabbath that is truly chilling. Beecham Amazon Presto Apple Orchestre National de France, Leonard Bernstein Every mood swing in the score is played to the full in this 1976 recording. Leonard Bernstein drives the first movement hard, yet he means every one of its quiet, hymn-like closing chords. The waltz has a teasing charm, and the idée fixe drifts through it and is gone. The march to the scaffold is the core of it, a procession that moves the listener to pity. Bernstein’s first New York recording has a sharper edge, and the sound here lacks some depth, but the performance wears its heart openly from first bar to last. Bernstein Amazon Presto Apple Cleveland Orchestra, Pierre Boulez Here the symphony is heard, above all, as a symphony. Pierre Boulez keeps close to the composer’s tempo markings, and the shape of each movement stands out with rare clarity. The Cleveland Orchestra plays superbly, with gorgeous strings and every climax held in firm control, and the disc adds Tristia with the orchestra’s chorus. Compared with Munch, this is a cool performance that keeps its emotional distance from the story. What this 1996 recording offers instead is Berlioz’s design laid out in full view. Boulez Amazon Presto Apple Rotterdam Philharmonic Orchestra, Yannick Nézet-Séguin This 2010 recording turns the drama inward. If Munch’s Berlioz is a fever, Yannick Nézet-Séguin’s is a confession, with the story told from inside the artist’s head as memory and feeling. The country scene is gently drawn, and the distant thunder at its close is kept low. The march stays in proportion, and in the finale the horrors are more dreamed than seen. Anyone after theatrical terror should look elsewhere, but the searching, personal tone is the point, and the disc adds La mort de Cléopâtre, sung by Anna Caterina Antonacci. Nézet-Séguin Amazon Presto Apple Les Siècles, François-Xavier Roth Nearly three decades after John Eliot Gardiner’s period-instrument version, François-Xavier Roth and Les Siècles bring the instruments of Berlioz’s day back to this score, and daylight falls between the lines. Roth went back to the composer’s manuscript before recording, and he lets each episode breathe before the next begins. The country scene is spare and unhurried, its period oboe and cor anglais calling to each other in their own reedy colors. In the witches’ sabbath, the bells come from La Côte-Saint-André, where Berlioz was born. The textures trade weight for light, and the finale closes in with a steady tread rather than an explosion. This 2019 recording is a beautifully observed performance, with every page freshly considered. Roth Amazon Presto Apple San Francisco Symphony, Michael Tilson Thomas From its opening bars, Michael Tilson Thomas’s 1997 recording shows the San Francisco Symphony in dazzling form, its playing at once exact and impassioned. The slow country scene never drags, and the march swings between the hushed and the enormous. For all that power, the last two movements burn less fiercely than the first three. The disc adds two excerpts from Lélio, Berlioz’s sequel to the symphony, and a 2024 remaster brings the recording to Apple Music in Dolby Atmos. items.body: Strikkland are easy to misread if you mistake humour for distance. Henrik Johansson can deliver brutal lyrics while smiling, appear in a red feather boa, play with national flags or deliberately puncture the visual severity traditionally associated with EBM, but none of that suggests embarrassment about the genre. Quite the opposite. The joke works because the attachment underneath it is genuine. They are not standing outside EBM making fun of its conventions; they know those conventions intimately enough to interfere with them. I first saw the Gothenburg duo at E-Only in 2024 and again this year on the much larger Waldbühne at Nocturnal Culture Night. At NCN, something became particularly clear: humour had stopped feeling like something happening around the songs and had become part of Strikkland’s performance language itself. Hard electronic structures, Henrik’s forceful delivery and the physical directness of EBM remained intact, while gestures, costumes and irony continually destabilised the expectation that seriousness must look solemn. Their second album, “Hommage”, makes that tension especially interesting. It openly acknowledges the music that formed Henrik and Henric, while its production deliberately returns to hardware, physical studio equipment and recording practices associated with an earlier era. Yet Strikkland have little interest in turning EBM into heritage preservation. For them, tradition is useful precisely when it can still be disturbed. We spoke about growing into a band after fifty, refusing genre uniforms, why limitation can generate creativity, the ethics of AI, the strange authority of old symbols, and what happens when two people who take EBM very seriously refuse to behave as though seriousness requires a permanent scowl. Strikkland interview Karo: I first saw you at E-Only in 2024 and then again on the much larger Waldbühne at NCN this year. What struck me at NCN was how much more clearly humour had become part of the performance language itself. When did you realise that humour could be structural to Strikkland rather than merely something happening between songs? Henrik: We have always had humour as an important element of what Strikkland is all about. We started the band on impulse and as a fun thing to do. The lyrics are often conjured up at the same time as we are in the studio creating new songs. My texts often tend to drift towards dark stories about space, death, fantasy and the absurd. The humour you get from seeing the band live is something we have developed throughout all the time we have been on stage. We have fun, and that creates what we deliver. Henric: We realised early on that two old geezers would only look ridiculous if we tried to act tougher or darker than we actually are. Besides, there are plenty of bands already biting heads off chickens or dressing up in full combat gear on stage. It has all been done before, and it really didn’t seem like an option for us. Our appearance and the way we behave also evolved from criticism in Sweden after our first live shows in the early days: “Their music is half-decent, but they aren’t a real EBM band because they don’t look or behave like one.” We kind of turned that against the critics, embraced it even more and made it our thing. Karo: At NCN you told me that when you started the band, already approaching your fifties, you briefly considered becoming the “gothiest” band possible before deciding that pretending to be something you were not would be ridiculous. Did starting Strikkland later in life actually give you a kind of freedom younger bands sometimes lack, because you had less need to prove that you belonged? Henrik: Absolutely! Also, later in life you have so many more musical influences to choose from and try to implement into your own songs. Starting a band later in life also means you can afford to have a band and go places to play live without starving and sleeping in the car on the way there. We are doing something today that you thought impossible when you were young. Henric: Being close to 50 when you start a band certainly provides more freedom. Our ambition was never to release records or perform live, but when possibilities opened up, we jumped for it. Speaking for myself, I got a chance to do what I wanted to do in my teens but never got the chance to do. At 50, you aren’t as afraid of criticism or about what others might think as you are at 16 or 17. That helped a lot. Karo: EBM has accumulated a very strict visual and behavioural vocabulary: severity, discipline, confrontation, often a certain cultivated lack of humour. You clearly love the genre, but you also interfere with those conventions constantly. Which parts of EBM do you take completely seriously, and which parts do you think deserve to be laughed at? Henrik: We never laugh at EBM, but we think we can involve irony and humour in the genre and have a laugh at certain aspects of life. Humour and art are always found in the contrasts. I mostly write quite dark lyrics, but we present them with a lot of smiles, humour and dance. Henric: EBM has been a huge part of my life since the 1980s, so it is something I take very seriously. I do laugh at some of the rigidity coming from certain corners of the fanbase, though. Come on, loosen up and dance while you still can. Have fun. At least laugh a little. There are enough bitter middle-aged men in the world, and I don’t want to become one of them. Karo: That is also why “Hommage” interests me. It is explicitly a tribute to the music that formed you, but homage can easily become imitation. How do you honour an artistic language without treating it as something that should remain frozen in the period when you first discovered it? Henrik: The tribute to the EBM bands we grew up with is always there when we make music. In “Hommage”, it is in the basslines, the sounds, the technology and the artwork. I am a curious person, so I constantly look for new music and new bands to listen to. The EBM genre, and Strikkland, keep finding new ways without letting go of the legacy of the bands of the 80s. Henric: Apart from a handful of gems from bands like Kraftwerk, DAF, Nitzer Ebb, Front 242 and a few others which can’t be topped, EBM and electronic music have evolved a lot. In my playlists there are rarely any songs older than two or three years. You can still hear where it is coming from, but it has evolved. If we stick to what we grew up with, there would be stagnation and the genre would surely die out. But thanks to artists like SIIE, Emmon, Plastikstrom and many others, it is still interesting. So I would rather risk going outside the standard formula and at least try to contribute to keeping EBM alive, both musically and visually. Karo: You made “Hommage” deliberately with classic studio equipment, hardware synthesizers and drum machines, and you were very explicit about not using AI. Is that primarily an ethical position, an aesthetic one, or did you simply want the limitations of those tools to become part of the composition? Henric: AI has no place in art. Full stop. For both creative and ethical reasons. When it comes to using hardware versus working “in the box”, it is purely a workflow decision. The tactility of turning knobs and pushing buttons works better for me than using plugins. We are also privileged enough to get to work together with Hans Olsson at Svenska Grammofonstudion in Gothenburg, which is both a studio and a “synthesizer museum”. It would be stupid not to use all of those classic machines if you can. Our first album, “Bodypop”, was mixed there on an SSL 4000E console, so when we got the chance to mix “Hommage” at Hansa in Berlin on their SSL console, of course we took the plunge. And of course we did some additional recordings there as well. I mean, who could resist playing the very same Steinway grand piano that Martin Gore posed in his jocks next to? Karo: There is an interesting contradiction there: Strikkland describe themselves as expanding the borders of EBM, yet “Hommage” deliberately looks backwards in terms of production practice. Can technological limitation actually be more progressive than unlimited technological possibility? Henrik: Well, maybe in a way every EBM band today is expanding the borders of EBM? To stay in the genre, you have to remain within the frame agreed upon, regardless of what technology you use. But it gets more interesting if you drift away towards the border and sometimes cross it, bringing in other influences and expressions. That’s the way music has always evolved. Henric: For me, limitation sparks creativity. There is a certain number of available channels on a physical mixing console. On a computer, you can have hundreds. There are also limitations to hardware synthesizers and effects, and all of this forces me to be creative. As mentioned before, this is a workflow that suits me. With that said, most of our songs start out “in the box” because it is convenient. Karo: Henric writes the music and programming while Henrik handles vocals and lyrics. With such a clear division, where does the personality of a Strikkland song emerge? Does the music arrive with a character already inside it, or can the vocal idea fundamentally alter what Henric thought he had written? Henrik: Often we start with a bassline that Henric has created and then build it together from that point. I get inspiration for the lyrics and write them at the same time as Henric starts to develop the music. When both of us feel ready, we fuse it all together. This is a fast process, so we are very much in line with what kind of music we want to produce. Henric: Let’s put it this way: when Henrik enters the studio, I might have 20 loops that I have worked on for six months, with basslines, drums and maybe a melody ready. If Henrik says, “Great! But can we change this or that?”, that loop goes into the bin. But if he stops, shuts up and starts to write text immediately, I know it is a keeper. Then we combine that idea into a draft by making a rough arrangement, tweaking the text, tweaking the music and finally recording it. When we have enough tracks for an album, we take it to Hans and re-record everything. So, to answer your question, the music inspires the vocals and the vocals give direction to the final piece of music. Neither would be the same without the other. Karo: At NCN, Henrik changed clothes, exaggerated gestures and played with Swedish and German symbols and declarations of friendship. In a genre that has historically borrowed heavily from militarised imagery, does humour give you a way to use those symbols without allowing them to retain all of their old authority? Henrik: When I go to see a band live, I want to be entertained. When I am on stage, I want to entertain and have a good time! To joke around and interact with the audience and get a warm response elates me. I love the contrast of delivering hard-hitting music and brutal lyrics with a smile on my face and prancing around with a red feather boa. So yes, it is absolutely a way to deflate the power of symbols of power. Henric: Personally, I think it is important to reclaim symbols like national flags from fascists and extremists and use them in a positive way. We don’t hide behind humour and irony, but instead use them as tools for communication. Our message is clear. We don’t accept fascists, Nazis or totalitarian regimes, we support Ukraine’s fight for freedom and we advocate free speech. But maybe we have chosen a “lighter approach” to convey this than other bands, mainly because the darker image doesn’t suit us on a personal level. Karo: What I particularly liked was that none of this reduced the concert to parody because the musical foundation remained genuinely hard. Do you consciously protect that balance, making sure the joke never becomes an excuse for musical weakness? Henrik: When we make our music, we never implement humour to start with. Okay, some lyrics are rather absurd and some sound effects we add for fun, but we want our music to be serious and taken seriously. It is mostly when we play live that we joke around. Henric: Some people have clearly written us off as a parody act. No question about that! But either they haven’t seen us perform live or they haven’t understood what we are doing. Irony is a tough nut to crack for some, and others lack humour. One thing is certain, though. We would never release or perform anything that we ourselves thought was weak, and we put a lot of work into our music. Karo: You worked with Hans Olsson at Svenska Grammofonstudion and Hansa Studios on “Hommage”. Did working in spaces carrying so much recording history make you more conscious of tradition, or was the important thing precisely to forget the mythology once you were actually inside the studio? Henric: It took a while for it to sink in once we were at Hansa. We were actually sitting at the same mixing console that was used to make some of the greatest albums of my youth?! Insane! But once that feeling disappeared, it was just another day in the studio and we did our thing together with Hans. Henrik: Hans Olsson suggested mixing the album at Hansa, and I honestly was totally unaware of the history of this studio. Henric was jumping up and down with excitement. We were there for three days and it finally dawned on me how cool it was! There we could use the same machines and instruments that our heroes used. Karo: The larger stage at NCN seemed to suit you surprisingly well. Some electronic acts compensate for space by simply making every gesture bigger; with Strikkland, the additional room seemed to expose more of the interaction between you. Has playing larger stages changed the way you understand what the visual side of the band can do? Henric: We are not that used to playing larger stages. Apart from Subkultfestivalen in Sweden and WGT, most of our shows prior to NCN have been in front of a maximum of 200 to 300 people. I think there is a lot of room for visual improvement when playing the larger stages. We are just two guys and a couple of machines, so in order to put on even better shows we probably need some additional features on stage to make an impact. But we also don’t want to hide behind video walls, smoke and lasers. Guess it’s time to put on our thinking caps and find a Strikkland solution to the problem. But yeah, visuals are important to us, from album covers to how we appear on stage. Henrik: What Henric said. Karo: “Hommage” looked deliberately towards the music that made you. Looking ahead, what would be the opposite gesture? Is there something in the EBM tradition, perhaps even something you personally love, that Strikkland now need to leave behind in order to find out what the band can become next? Henrik: I can’t think of a thing in the EBM tradition that we want to leave behind. When we create new songs, all kinds of new influences colour the final result. Last time we met, the song rotated towards techno music, so who knows? I always get new ideas every time I listen to metal music. There you find my inspiration and trigger to do new stuff for Strikkland. But with that said, there will never be a guitar on stage with us. Body music forever! Henric: I don’t know, to be honest. There are most certainly no holy cows as far as Strikkland is concerned. What we would love to happen is to do even more shows in mainland Europe, and if that means we will have to tweak things one way or another, so be it. If it turns out we have to bite heads off chickens or perform in Pickelhauben in order to get booked, it might be worth a shot! I mean, a lot of people do judge books by the cover, and it would be sad to miss out because of that. We will see what happens and what we come up with. About Strikkland Strikkland are an electronic body music duo from Gothenburg, Sweden, consisting of Henric Ceder, responsible for music and programming, and Henrik Johansson, responsible for vocals and lyrics. Their first documented release, “Predatorial Right”, appeared on 27 March 2020. Their debut full-length album, “Bodypop”, followed on 2 December 2022. The ten-track record was mixed and mastered by Hans Olsson at Svenska Grammofonstudion in Gothenburg, using an analogue SSL 4000E console; Strikkland explicitly connected that production choice to their admiration for classic EBM. Their second full-length, “Hommage”, was released on 28 March 2025. The nine-track album was produced by Hans Olsson, with recording, mixing and mastering work carried out at Svenska Grammofonstudion in Gothenburg and Hansa Studios in Berlin. The band describe the album as a tribute both to the artists who inspired them and to older recording practices. They state that no AI was used in its production, relying instead primarily on classic studio equipment, hardware synthesizers and drum machines.

items.body: ALEO and Menny Flores released “No Voy a Estar” on Mania Records on 18 September 2026. The synth pop single is sung in Spanish over 80s-style synthesizers and a prominent bassline, and marks the pair’s second collaboration on the label after the earlier single “Gracias.” “No Voy a Estar” opens on the line “no voy a estar, no me esperes” (“I won’t be there, don’t wait for me”) turns on the moment late-night calls and unfulfilled promises stop working; rather than dwell on the breakup, the song moves past it. Midway through, the arrangement tightens and Flores’ delivery shifts from melodic verses into a faster, more conversational rhythmic pattern. ALEO produced the track and shares songwriting credit with Menny Flores. About ALEO ALEO is a Grammy-winning producer, songwriter and multi-instrumentalist based in Los Angeles who runs the independent label Mania Records. His production and writing credits include work with Juanes, Young Thug, Swae Lee, Gunna, Lil Baby and A.CHAL, among others. On Mania Records, ALEO has also produced for Parallel 33, including the single “Sowe”, released in June 2026. “No Voy a Estar” is his second single this year alongside Menny Flores, following “Gracias,” and continues a run of ALEO-produced Mania Records releases through the second half of 2026.

items.body: Soft Riot has finished a video for “Ghostwriter,” the closing track on the 2026 album “Crux.” It is the project’s second official video from the record, following “Moving Out Of The Black,” which premiered at the end of April 2026 ahead of the album’s release on 15 May. A premiere date for “Ghostwriter” itself is still being finalised; the video is not yet public. Crux by Soft Riot Jack Duckworth, who records as Soft Riot and is also known as JJD, built the video’s visuals as a graphic, surrealist collage rather than a straight performance piece, with puppet-like character animation reflecting the song’s theme: the sense of ideas for “Crux” materialising, as though something unseen were “ghostwriting” the record. All of the animation was made by hand from physically printed graphics and re-filmed projected textures, a deliberate move away from computer-based tools that Duckworth has linked to feeling increasingly isolated within the digital side of underground music. Duckworth handled all graphics and editing as JJD, with assistance from Leyre Mann Vadillo. “Ghostwriter” closes a nine-track album written and recorded across several sessions between June 2024 and January 2026 at Studio Carillon in Glasgow, with vinyl mixing by Owen Pratt at Flesh And Bone Studios in Tarn, France, and mastering by Josh Stevenson at Otic Mastering. “Crux” is available on streaming platforms, as a download through Bandcamp and Subvert via Possession Records, and on vinyl and digipak CD, including a limited clear vinyl LP on Minimal Kombinat that sold out within a week of pre-orders. A follow-up EP, “Alter,” released in June 2026, carries exclusive, alternate and extended versions of “Crux” material. About Soft Riot Soft Riot is the synth project of Jack Duckworth, a British-Canadian musician based in Glasgow who has released music under the name for around fifteen years, drawing on synth post-punk, darkwave, new wave, Italo and EBM. Duckworth’s roots go back to the mid-1990s art-punk and hardcore scene on the North American west coast, where he played in the first-wave post-punk revival band Radio Berlin (1998-2005) and the industrial synth-punk group A Luna Red (Gold Standard Labs, 1999-2003). As Soft Riot, he has toured Europe repeatedly, sharing stages with acts including Front 242, Absolute Body Control, Parade Ground, She Past Away, Test Department, Selofan, Drab Majesty and Lebanon Hanover, and has played festivals including Ombra Festival in Spain, BIM Fest and Waveteef in Belgium, Kalabalik På Tyrolen in Sweden and Weird Science in Germany. Side-Line has previously covered the Soft Riot albums “You Never Know What Might Come Next” (2016), “The Outsider In The Mirrors” (2018) and “When Push Comes To Shove” (2019), followed by “No.” (2023) and, in 2026, “Crux” and its “Alter” companion EP.

items.body: Twelve years after “Brother,” Morten Harket returns with a new solo album, “Human Grace,” set for release on 27 November 2026 through Warner Music. It is the a-ha singer’s seventh solo album, built from demos and studio recordings made in the years since “Brother,” with some of the material newly arranged and produced for the release. The first single, “Hold Me,” arrives 25 September 2026 and features Harket’s daughter Tomine Harket. A second daughter, Karmen Poppi A. Harket, is featured on the album track “Falling Down.” “Human Grace” runs ten tracks: “Human Grace,” “Hold Me” (feat. Tomine Harket), “Falling Down” (feat. Karmen Poppi A. Harket), “Lord, I Can’t Help You Now,” “Now Your Heart Is Broken,” “Shot of Fear,” “Did I Leave You Behind,” “What Is It You Want With Me,” “The Old Church” and “If I Ever See Your Face Again.” “Did I Leave You Behind” has previously been performed live. Peter Kvint co-produced and co-wrote eight of the ten songs; Ole Sverre Olsen wrote lyrics for six tracks; Jonas Kroon mixed the album, with Erik Ljunggren overseeing post-production, backed by the Stockholm Studio Orchestra and Swedish and Norwegian session musicians. “Human Grace” will be released on black vinyl, beige vinyl, CD and streaming platforms. Morten Harket’s Parkinson’s disease, which he disclosed in June 2025, has affected his ability to control his voice, and much of the album’s vocal work predates the diagnosis, with overdubs added between July 2025 and July 2026. “I have Parkinson’s, and I’ve done the album with its limitations,” Harket stated. He does not expect to tour behind the record, saying of live performances: “That I doubt I can do.” He has described his voice as having partially recovered and said he is “constantly looking for a way back to using my voice for recording.” Harket also left open the possibility of returning to the studio with a-ha. About Morten Harket Morten Harket was born on 14 September 1959 in Kongsberg, Norway. He formed a-ha in Oslo in 1982 with Magne Furuholmen and Pål Waaktaar, and the band’s breakthrough single “Take On Me” reached number one on the US Billboard Hot 100 in October 1985 from the album “Hunting High and Low.” Alongside a-ha, Morten Harket has released six prior solo albums: “Poetenes Evangelium” (1993), “Wild Seed” (1995), “Vogts Villa” (1996), “Letter from Egypt” (2008), “Out of My Hands” (2012) and “Brother” (2014). He has also acted, including the “Kamilla og tyven” films (1988-1989) and “Yohan: The Child Wanderer” (2009), and was made a Knight of the Order of St. Olav in 2012 for his contribution to Norwegian music. Harket disclosed his Parkinson’s diagnosis in June 2025. A-ha’s most recent studio album remains “True North” (2022), with its accompanying documentary. “Human Grace,” out 27 November 2026, is his first solo release since “Brother” and the first new Harket material confirmed since his diagnosis became public.
