items.body:
Fresh off her historic America’s Got Talent win, Nene Royal is heading to Singapore to open for Avenged Sevenfold.

Midas Promotions have announced that the 16-year-old Thai guitarist and singer will join the American heavy metal band for their show on 13 October at the Singapore Indoor Stadium.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Midas Promotions (@midaspromotions)

The announcement comes shortly after Nene, whose real name is Rattikarn Amloy, became the first Thai contestant to win America’s Got Talent. The Phuket native took home the Season 21 title after a run that saw her bring rock and metal to the competition stage with performances of The Cranberries’ 'Zombie', Soundgarden’s 'Black Hole Sun', and The White Stripes’ 'Seven Nation Army'.

Ahead of the final results, Nene also joined Linkin Park for 'The Emptiness Machine', playing guitar and sharing vocal duties with Emily Armstrong. She also jammed with Mexican rock trio The Warning during the finale.

Her Singapore appearance will now put her onstage with another major name in rock. Avenged Sevenfold’s upcoming concert marks the band’s first show in Singapore in over 11 years.

The band — comprising M. Shadows, Synyster Gates, Zacky Vengeance, Johnny Christ, and Brooks Wackerman — will take the Singapore Indoor Stadium stage as part of their 2026 Asia tour.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Midas Promotions (@midaspromotions)

Released on 25 September, Afterglow sees the Singaporean singer-songwriter embracing confidence, ambition, and the importance of putting yourself first. The project pairs sleek pop and R&B sounds with reflections on finding yourself again and knowing when to walk away.

“But it’s also about having fun along the way,” shared Iman. “Dancing around with your girls, celebrating how far you’ve come, and romanticising your own life.”

items.body:
The sweeping soundtrack for The Violinist has arrived.

Released by Milan Records on 25 September, The Violinist (Original Motion Picture Soundtrack) features music by Singaporean composer and Golden Horse winner Ricky Ho and Spanish composer Isabel Latorre. The pair co-wrote the original score for the Annecy-winning animated film, bringing together Eastern and Western musical traditions across 29 tracks.

Featuring intimate violin melodies and sweeping orchestral themes, the score accompanies a story centred on friendship, memory, resilience, and hope. Among its tracks are 'The Pursuit', 'First Duet', 'Sunset Sonata', 'Fall of Singapore', 'A New Sunrise', and 'Strings of a Distant Heart'.

The Violinist spans Singapore and Malaya from the early 20th century through the Japanese Occupation. The film follows two childhood friends brought together by music as war, displacement, and the passage of time reshape their lives.

Produced by Robot Playground Media, The Violinist is an official co-production with Spain's TV ON Producciones and Italy's Altri Occhi, with worldwide sales handled by France tv distribution.

items.body:
Davao-based girl group DAELUX have stepped into the P-pop scene with their pre-debut single, 'Like That'.

Released under Sony Music Entertainment, the upbeat pop track captures the thrill and uncertainty that come with catching feelings for someone — from reading into the smallest signals to wondering whether they feel the same way.

“We were drawn to this theme because the feeling of liking someone and trying to figure out where you stand is something a lot of people can relate to,” shared DAELUX. “There’s excitement, but there’s also that uncertainty when you start overthinking little actions.”

Rather than dwelling on that uncertainty, 'Like That' approaches young love with optimism and candour. Beneath its playful sound is an encouragement to be open about your feelings while remembering your own worth.

Produced by Pao Lofranco and co-written by AndreaH, the track also saw the seven members contributing creative ideas throughout the songwriting process. Its vocal harmonies were developed alongside the group’s vocal coach, Ma’am Shelley, with parts distributed to showcase each member's individual voice.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by DAELUX (@daelux.official)

'Like That' marks DAELUX's first release since partnering with Sony Music Philippines. Comprising Davao natives CK, Alice, Ara, Rhya, Slane, Zyra, and Riri, the group also worked with a Davao-based team on their music and performance video, keeping their emerging P-pop identity rooted in their hometown.

“Being part of Sony Music is a huge opportunity for us,” the group shared. “It gives us the chance to learn, grow, and take our music more seriously as artists.”

items.body:
a1 are celebrating their long-running connection with Filipino fans with a brand-new single.

Released exclusively in the Philippines on 25 September, 'In Love in the Philippines' was written and produced by the British-Norwegian pop group. Inspired by falling in love with both a person and a place, the track serves as the quartet's tribute to a country that has played a special part in their story for more than two decades.

“We’ve shared so many incredible moments with our fans in the Philippines. This song feels like our love letter back to them — and to a country that has given us memories we’ll never forget,” the band shared.

The single arrives ahead of a1 – Love In The Philippines Tour, which will see Paul Marazzi, Christian Ingebrigtsen, Mark Read, and Ben Adams return to the country this October. The group are set to perform in Cebu on 16 October, Quezon City on 17 October, and Santa Rosa, Laguna on 18 October.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by a1 (@a1official)

The upcoming shows follow a1's Valentine's Tour in February, while their previous visits to the Philippines have seen them perform fan favourites including 'Like a Rose', 'Everytime', 'Heaven by Your Side', 'Same Old Brand New You', and 'Caught in the Middle'.

items.body:
The 37th Singapore International Film Festival (SGIFF) has unveiled its latest slate of announcements, with Aamir Khan set to receive the Screen Icon Award and South Korean thriller The Assassin(s) confirmed as this year’s opening film.

Taking place from 21 October to 1 November, the festival will open with The Assassin(s), starring Yoo Hae-jin, Park Hae-il, and Lee Min-ho. Director Hur Jin-ho will attend the Festival Opening alongside supporting cast members Shim Eun-kyung and Park Sung-hoon.

Set against South Korea’s Liberation Day on 15 August 1974, the film follows detective Cheol-gu after a shooting at the National Theater of Korea leads him to question the official account of what happened. Together with a young reporter and newspaper editor, he begins an investigation amid government efforts to suppress dissent.

The film marks Hur Jin-ho’s return to SGIFF following A Normal Family, which previously screened at the festival.

Aamir Khan to receive SGIFF's Screen Icon Award

Aamir Khan will receive this year’s Screen Icon Award, which recognises Asian actors who have made significant creative contributions to cinema.

Khan will also attend a Special Presentation marking the 25th anniversary of Lagaan: Once Upon a Time in India alongside filmmaker Ashutosh Gowariker.

The film follows villagers who form a cricket team in an attempt to avoid paying taxes imposed under British colonial rule. Lagaan: Once Upon a Time in India was nominated for Best International Film at the Academy Awards.

Previous recipients of SGIFF’s Screen Icon Award, formerly known as the Cinema Icon Award, include Michelle Yeoh, Koji Yakusho, Joan Chen, Fan Bingbing, and Youn Yuh-jung.

The announcement follows SGIFF’s earlier reveal that Japanese filmmaker Hirokazu Kore-eda will receive this year’s Cinema Honorary Award. Kore-eda’s latest film, Look Back, will also screen as part of the festival programme.

Anthony Wong, Peter Chan, and more join SGIFF

SGIFF has also announced more filmmakers and actors joining this year’s edition.

Hong Kong actor Anthony Wong will participate in a post-screening dialogue for My Name Ain’t Suzie, his first acting role, while filmmaker Peter Chan and Shim Eun-kyung will take part in SGIFF’s In Conversation With series.

Other guests include filmmakers Koji Fukada and Jacob Cheung, as well as cinematographers Akiko Ashizawa and Tom Harari.

South Korean filmmaker Yim Soon-rye, previously announced as Jury Head for the Asian Feature Film Competition, will also be part of this year’s festival.

More than 25 Singapore productions and co-productions featured

This edition will spotlight more than 25 Singapore productions and co-productions that have received recognition at international film festivals including Cannes, Sundance, Toronto, Venice, Locarno, and Melbourne.

Among them are Ang Geck Geck’s Ah Girl, Nelson Yeo’s The House on the Moon, Koji Fukada’s Nagi Notes, Edwin’s Sleep No More, Phuttiphong Aroonpheng’s The Burning Giants, Kamila Andini’s Four Seasons in Java, and 9 Temples to Heaven.

Ah Girl, 9 Temples to Heaven, The Burning Giants, and Four Seasons in Java will also compete in the Asian Feature Film Competition.

Local animation will feature across the festival’s short film programmes too, including EXYL’s Singapore God, Calleen Koh’s RIP ME, LOL, Mark Wee’s A Tree, Nah Yee Chern’s Everything’s Peachy, and Shara Tay’s Kiss Me Climax.

SGIFF introduces Junior Explorers and live performances

The festival is also expanding the ways audiences can experience its programme.

For the first time, Junior Explorers will offer relaxed, sensory-friendly screenings for younger audiences, opening with stop-motion animation Brave Cat.

Meanwhile, SGIFF’s Undercurrent section will open with three live performances combining moving images with other disciplines. Corporeal Forms: Four Stories incorporates Taiwanese puppetry, The Compression Zone features live video gaming, while Imagination + The Rest Is My Ghost brings together analog film techniques and music performance.

SGIFF Pro will also return in an expanded format with the previously announced Parallax, Off Campus, and Pitching Forum programmes.

The SGIFF Film Fund is also returning after a short hiatus. Applications for its SEA-SHORTS and SEA-DOC grants will run from 5 November to 5 December.

A post shared by Singapore Int'l Film Festival (@sgiffest)

items.body: Text by Hideo Kanno 神野秀雄 『小曽根真 クリスマス・ジャズナイト2026』 “For Someone” TRiNFiNiTY featuring アナ・マリア・ヨペック 2026年12月19日(土) 19:00 2026年12月20日(日) 15:00 Bunkamuraオーチャードホール (東京都渋谷区) 小曽根真(p)、アナ・マリア・ヨペック(vo) 小川晋平(b) きたいくにと(ds) S席9,500円 A席8,500円（全席指定・税込・未就学児入場不可） 【チケット発売】 ●MY Bunkamura先行発売＜先着＞ 2026年9月24日(木)10:00～9月26日(土)23:59 オンラインチケットMY Bunkamura https://mybun.jp/ozone-xmas2026 （座席選択可能） ※9月27日10:00より同URLで一般発売開始 ●一般発売 2026年9月27日(日) 10:00～ Bunkamura、チケットぴあ、イープラス、ローソンチケット オーチャードホール公演とその発売の詳細は、 Bunkamura公式ウェブサイト 『小曽根真 クリスマス・ジャズナイト』は、渋谷Bunkamuraオーチャードホールを会場に、ピアニスト小曽根真がパートナーで俳優の神野三鈴とともにプロデュースし、毎年ジャンルを超えてさまざまなミュージシャンとのコラボレーションで感動のステージを創り続けてきた年末恒例のイベントだ。2006年のパキート・デリヴェラ(cl, as)をゲストに迎えたモーツァルト・プログラムを第1回に2026年で19回目を迎える。 今年は、“For Someone” TRiNFiNiTY featuring アナ・マリア・ヨペック。小曽根の重要な音楽活動のコアとなっている気鋭の若手を擁したピアノトリオTRiNFiNiTYに、ポーランドで絶大な人気を誇るヴォーカリスト、アナ・マリア・ヨペックを迎えたステージとなる。TRiNFiNiTYは、小曽根が信頼する小川晋平(b)、きたいくにと(ds)と結成したピアノトリオで、ファーストアルバム『TRiNFiNiTY』を2024年にNYで録音。何度かヨーロッパツアーを成功させてきたが、今年11月のヨーロッパツアーを経てのクリスマス・ジャズナイトとなるので、ヨーロッパの空気の中で熟成し研ぎ澄まされたステージを楽しめそうだ。 アナ・マリア・ヨペックは、パット・メセニーとの共演盤『Upojenie』(2002年)やブランフォード・マルサリスとの共演でも注目されたが、小曽根との共演は2009年録音の『Road to Chopin』に始まり、小曽根はアナ・マリア・ヨペックの『Haiku』に参加している。日本とヨーロッパで共演を重ねてきて、最近では、TRiNFiNiTYヨーロッパツアーの一部を共にして、初期ECMの重要な拠点であり、小曽根が参加したECM盤『Gary Burton / Real Life Hits』、『gary Burton / Whiz Kids』も録音されたドイツ・ルードヴィヒスブルクBauer Studiosでセカンドアルバム『For Someone』の録音にも参加した。 Bunkamuraは2027年1月4日より大規模改修工事のため全館休館となるので、オーチャードホール休館前最後の『小曽根真 クリスマス・ジャズナイト』となる。 【東京以外の公演】 12月13日(日) 15:00 福岡 NCBホール (※小曽根真＆アナ・マリア・ヨペック デュオ) 12月15日(火) 18:45 浜松 アクトシティ浜松 中ホール 12月16日(水) 19:00 兵庫県立芸術文化センター KOBELCO 大ホール 12月18日(金) 19:00 埼玉 フカガワみらいホール (川口総合文化センターリリア)

items.excerpt: Arshan Najafi‘s Zenosyne takes its title from John Koenig’s neologism describing the unsettling sensation that time seems to accelerate as we grow older. items.body: Arshan Najafi‘s Zenosyne takes its title from John Koenig’s neologism describing the unsettling sensation that time seems to accelerate as we grow older. The album focuses on the paradox behind that sensation. As Najafi explains in the accompanying interview, the music emerged from a period in which he felt psychologically frozen while time rushed relentlessly onwards. This tension between stillness and acceleration defines the album’s two long-form electroacoustic compositions. Built from live improvisations using a piezo microphone attached to an external hard drive alongside the sonification of raw digital data, Zenosyne makes surprisingly little ceremony of its unusual sound sources. The hard drive becomes another resonant object, its vibrations feeding a semi-generative system that Najafi actively steers. Algorithmic processes introduce an element of instability, but his intervention remains central to the shape of the music. The opening “Binary Bloom” begins with almost imperceptible movement. Sustained electronic tones slowly develop interference patterns and harmonic beating, gathering momentum from within. Energy and apparent speed continue to increase without reaching a conventional climax, and the accumulated tension eventually dissipates. “Static Rotation” expands this language through a more active dialogue between pure tone and electronic noise. Its materials circulate around an unstable centre, creating perpetual motion with little sense of arrival. Najafi places considerable trust in microscopic change. Much of the musical activity remains concentrated in the lower and middle registers. Rhythm and dramatic contrast play relatively small roles, while subtle redistributions of spectral energy, minute shifts in timbre and constantly evolving resonances determine the form. Musical time is stretched sufficiently for these small changes to acquire unusual weight, sharpening our awareness of its passing. To get an idea of Arshan Najafi’s live process, here is a recording of one of his no-input mixer and computer sets, followed by an interview about the making of Zenosyne. Zenosyne takes its title from John Koenig’s neologism and yet the album doesn’t seem to represent memory nostalgically. Instead, both “Binary Bloom” and “Static Rotation” seem to suspend chronological time altogether, creating spaces in which microscopic changes become more significant than linear progression. How did the idea of Zenosyne shape your compositional thinking? Were you interested in evoking the psychological sensation of accelerated time, or in constructing an alternative temporal experience in which conventional notions of duration begin to dissolve? I chose the title Zenosyne because it perfectly captured my state of mind during the composition process and still does. I was experiencing this overwhelming feeling of staying completely still – almost a sense of uselessness or incapability – while watching every day pass by in a flash of light. The music reflects that paradox. The suspension of linear time you noticed in these pieces wasn’t necessarily a conceptual design to challenge musical duration, but rather a direct mirror of that personal, psychological standstill. It is the feeling of being frozen in place while time accelerates around you. Your previous releases, from Imaginary Crisis to Live at Daa Theater House, have consistently explored live electronics, improvisation and the instability of sound in performance. Zenosyne continues that trajectory, drawing on live recordings made with a piezo microphone placed on an external hard drive alongside the sonification of raw digital data. What attracted you to treating a storage device not simply as a technological object but as a resonant instrument? Did working with the physical vibrations of digital memory alter the way you think about the relationship between information, sound and materiality? I have to admit, the reason is a bit less poetic than treating the drive as a metaphor for digital memory! I have a habit of attaching piezo mics to anything that I basically can. Frankly, I don’t see much point in recording traditional acoustic instruments anymore. That’s one of the main points of electronic music for me: it obliterates the need for conventional instruments. It gives us the freedom to choose the most mundane surface or object as a sound source and manipulate it into an entirely new form. The hard drive was just a fascinating object to harvest raw frequencies from, which the computer then allows me to further process. Both pieces were improvised live in Max/MSP before being shaped during the mixing process in Ableton Live. Listening to the album, there is a constant negotiation between systems that appear algorithmic and gestures that feel spontaneous or instinctive. How do you understand improvisation when working with generative processes? Do you see yourself directing the system, collaborating with it, or responding to behaviours that emerge unexpectedly during performance? I definitely see myself as the director of the system. I design a semi-generative algorithmic environment that responds to incoming signals based on parameters I’ve dictated beforehand. I call it “semi-generative” because I intentionally build it to a point where it still requires my interaction to continue its work; it cannot sustain itself without being steered and not sound boring to me. I view live improvisation fundamentally as a technique of composing on the fly. Because there are physical, unpredictable elements – like the random fluctuations of the hard disk spinning in “Static Rotation” – I have to remain hyper-aware and react to sudden gestures, not to mention I often cause those sudden gestures myself because I feel it’s needed at that particular moment. It’s a constant dialogue between the rules I set and the behavior the system throws back at me. Your work moves fluidly between sound, image and text—you are not only a composer but also the author of Twenty Wrong Turns. Across these different media there seems to be a recurring interest in fragmentation, ambiguity and the ways meaning emerges from incomplete information. Does Zenosyne belong to that same broader artistic inquiry? More generally, how do writing and sound composition inform one another in your practice, and are there ideas that can only be explored through one medium rather than the other? To be completely honest, I haven’t consciously intertwined my music and my writing so far. I tend to treat them as separate practices that serve different purposes. However, the connection that I do see between these mediums is the word “composition” itself, as I fundamentally treat them the same way. That’s the whole point for me. While they usually exist on their own, I might occasionally bring them together – it really just depends on how I feel about a certain project. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items.body: To complement her interview in The Wire 512, Slovenian improvising pianist and bandleader Kaja Draksler creates an exclusive Wire mix Kaja Draksler studied jazz at a music-oriented high school in Ljubljana, later enrolling at the Conservatory of Amsterdam. There, her instructor, the British composer Richard Ayres, asked her the simple question,“What do you want to do?”, which set her on a path that would chafe against the jazz orthodoxy. In August Punkt.Vrt. Plastik, her long-running trio with Swedish bassist Petter Eldh and German drummer Christian Lillinger, released their fourth album, Kompress, while another of her groups, matter 100, releases its debut True Or False this October. This exclusive mix, she explains, is “more of a collage, where I mostly take excerpts from different pieces, placing them one after the other, and, at times, one of top of the other. The track selection is a mix of my own music and music I love, with a bit of a focus on piano and voices.” Tracklist Kaja Draksler “Prst, roka, laket” (excerpt) Vaqif Mustafazadə “Bizim Bakı Gecələri” (excerpt) Luciano Berio “A La Femminisca” Christian Lillinger “Poliform” (excerpt) Punkt.Vrt.Plastik “EKV” Vince Staples “Get Paid” New London Chamber Choir & James Wood “Serment” (excerpt) Georges Aperghis “Recitation 10_ left part, 1st version” Nina Simone “Who Am I” Irena Z Tomažin “Rain” (excerpt) Pauline Oliveros “Horse Sings From A Cloud” (excerpt) J Gallus “Mirabile Misterium: De Nativitate Circumcisione Et Epiphania Domini Huelgas Ensemble” matter 100 “Rushing Through The Night” (excerpt) Czajka & Puchacz “Wacky Compass” (excerpt(s)) MIA “Sunshowers” (excerpt) Cecil Taylor “Pt 4 Glossalalia” (excerpt) Craig Taborn “Glossolalia” Kaja Draksler Octet “Come See” (excerpt) Andrew Parrot “De Torrente” Judith Berkson “Castle” Ellen Arkbro “For Organ And Brass” (excerpt) matter 100 “Alternating Current” Read Peter Margasak’s full interview with Kaja Draksler in The Wire 512. items.body: The Bug’s Ladybug 2 pairs his heavy, hypnotic bass pressure with Friday Night Plans’ hushed vocals, turning six versions of “Miss U” into a dark, immersive journey where dub, shoegaze, and electronic melancholy slowly dissolve into one hypnotic flow. Bass pressure meets quiet melancholy Ladybug 2 by The Bug / Friday Night Plans   The second chapter in the Ladybug series arrives just over a month after The Bug’s encounter with Dis Fig. The premise remains intact: Kevin Richard Martin entrusts his universe of bass pressure and deceleration to a different female voice, allowing each contact to alter its direction. This time the chosen presence is Friday Night Plans, the project led by Japanese vocalist Masumi. In 2023, Martin named Visitors his album of the year; three years later, that act of listening becomes a collaboration, taking shape in the six variations of Miss U released by Pressure. The artwork anticipates the character of the record. Masumi’s face, hidden behind dark glasses, emerges from a field of weathered white, almost erased by a layer of photographic dust. The music also withholds any sharp definition. Her voice feels close and already remote, the rhythm distorts the perception of time, while the bass presses forward relentlessly and casts a dim light around itself. This is sound that narcotizes, shifts the center of listening and carries the listener elsewhere through a calm troubled by unease. Miss U is approached six times, through reductions and deformations that alter the weight of its individual elements. Martin works with recurrence, with the memory of what has just been heard, with the expectation of an impact that may arrive late or dissolve entirely. The Broken versions sharpen this logic: the song loses its outline and enters a haze where dub meets the languor of shoegaze and certain strains of electronic mel​ancholy from the nineties. Keyboards float, the central matter grows rough, the foundation preserves an enormous power. Everything moves slowly and with absolute discipline, even when it seems close to collapse. Masumi avoids any display of force. Her singing is hushed, melancholy, almost oblique; it brings a controlled fragility into a sound system capable of swallowing her whole. That disparity feeds the attraction of Ladybug 2. Her voice skims the surfaces, disappears for long stretches, then returns like a thought that sleep had only hidden. Martin gives her a simple and memorable melodic line, surrounding it with echoes and deep expanses of absence. The result retains a secret pop element, perceptible even in its most disintegrated forms. “Masumi allows herself to be absorbed, becoming color and breath, encouraging an unbroken hypnotic continuity. The first volume moved through successive intensifications; this one favours dissolution.” ~Mirco Salvadori The comparison with Ladybug 1 is unavoidable and clarifies the distinct character of these two episodes. With Dis Fig, the voice seemed to act from inside the music, pushing each version towards a further degree of emotional exposure. Vanishing carried the weight of a wound spoken aloud; its subsequent mutations extended the narrative and allowed new tensions to emerge. Friday Night Plans adopts a more elusive presence. Masumi allows herself to be absorbed, becoming color and breath, encouraging an unbroken hypnotic continuity. The first volume moved through successive intensifications; this one favors dissolution. From that choice arise both the record’s particular allure and its mildest limitation. Ladybug 2 possesses an extraordinary sensory pull, wrapping itself around the body and suspending thought; across the sequence, its emotional transformations feel less profound than those heard in the previous chapter. Some versions extend a state that has already been achieved, refining the same vertigo and adjusting its density. The experience continues to seduce as the journey assumes a more circular form. There is less risk, less drama, and a reduced ability to change meaning with each passage. It would be unfair to read this restraint as fatigue. Martin is defining a series built upon the responses of different voices to his musical grammar, and Ladybug 2 demonstrates how readily that language can welcome distant sensibilities. The production has an almost tactile precision. The bass takes on physical dimensions, pauses open sudden drops, vocal fragments cross the mass with exhausted grace. Even the most rarefied moments maintain their pressure. The music seduces through a stubborn slowness and transforms repetition into an act of conscious surrender. “Its six forms construct a single dark, sensual and estranging flow, from which the listener emerges with the sense of having lost contact with the outside world for a while” ~Mirco Salvadori Ladybug 1 therefore retains a slight advantage. It possessed a clearer emotional center and a dialogue between voice and sound capable of producing new consequences. Ladybug 2 chooses a more uniform beauty, less lacerating and entrusted to immersion. Its six forms construct a single dark, sensual and estranging flow, from which the listener emerges with the sense of having lost contact with the outside world for a while. It is an intensely realized work, meticulous throughout, endowed with a force that grows with the volume and with the willingness to surrender to its pace. The highest point in the series still belongs to the first encounter. This second episode broadens the design and changes the path taken by the voice. The Bug and Friday Night Plans deliver a record capable of numbing and transporting, less devastating than its predecessor and equally serious in the pursuit of its own spell. Ladybug 2 prolongs the moment following the impact, when the senses slow down and reality loses its clarity. It finds its truth there, within a submerged melancholy that keeps pulsing in silence. Ladybug 2 is available on Pressure. [Bandcamp] Ladybug 2 by The Bug / Friday Night PlansThe post The Bug / Friday Night Plans :: Ladybug 2 (Pressure) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items.body: When the final sound fades, the small white emblem at the bottom of the cover comes to mind. A wave reduced to calligraphy, discreet while the blue occupies everything. Wind Paths works in much the same way: it passes through the listener, leaves behind a faint vibration and entrusts the air with carrying it away. A form capable of appearing and dissolving within a few minutes Wind Paths by Philippe Deschamps   The cover already offers a statement of intent. A shifting blue, crossed by pale brushstrokes, occupies the entire field, leaving a small white mark near the lower edge. It could be water observed at close range, air made visible, a photograph taken in motion during a crossing. The image refuses to settle. Wind Paths follows the same impulse, entrusting its identity to whatever passes, bends and changes density. Philippe Deschamps gathers wind, waves and rain into music that is brief and lucid, animated by a calm that retains its sense of movement. Four pieces and just over ten minutes form a single current. The compact running time keeps every element clear of decorative contemplation. The chords move slowly, changing color by small degrees; the guitar disperses its outlines; the synthesizers hold open an even light, gently varied from within. The field recordings enter the wider fabric discreetly. Sea and rain shed their role as illustrative background and become pressure, an irregular pulse, a measure beyond human intention. The record listens to the landscape as it transforms it. The new gesture lies in the voice. Deschamps trained as a Baroque countertenor and draws on that experience here, freeing it from text. The vocal tones stretch, overlap and take on the quality of warm currents. No phrase reaches for​ meaning. The body emerges through breath, then merges with guitar and recorded air. This fusion forms the emotional centre of the EP. It offers a fragile presence. The listener recognises a human figure and immediately watches it dissolve into the broader movement. It is a simple decision on paper, decisive in its effect. Deschamps’ path has been leading towards this synthesis for some time. Introduced to the piano as a child, later a singer, bassist and guitarist in rock and post rock groups, then trained in film sound at La Fémis, the French composer has developed an ambient body of work since 2022, nourished by natural phenomena and mental images. “Blue Baths,” “Forest of my Nights,” “The Silence of Pallas,” “Remember the Clouds,” “Endless Vanishing Lines,” and “Entering the Ocean” mark the stages of a coherent inquiry. Ocean, sky, darkness and distance provide a different organizing principle each time. Wind Paths distils that inquiry even further. The voice enters the frame and alters the relationship between landscape and memory. Intensity develops through accumulation and minute alteration :: His experience in cinema emerges through the precision of each entrance and fade. Deschamps understands the weight of a sound placed an instant earlier or later, and knows how to let a detail acquire prominence without demanding it. Here, that sensitivity produces a fluid montage. Forms follow one another through affinity, carried by a slow pulse that resembles breathing and, at times, the movement of the tide. There are no spectacular peaks, refrains or turns designed to reclaim the listener’s attention. Intensity develops through accumulation and minute alteration. At certain points, a low line supports the entire field; elsewhere, the texture grows lighter and the voice seems to arrive from an immeasurable distance. Few materials, carefully chosen. The record’s ambient purity grows from this economy. Its sound world possesses body and depth, and maintains an almost tactile transparency. Silence appears within the gaps and along the fading edges of notes. Even the fuller passages leave an open area where the wind around the listener, distant traffic or movement elsewhere in the house can still be heard. The music welcomes such intrusions. Its open character encourages a porous relationship with the present. Wind Paths can drift at low volume and preserve its identity; under closer listening, it reveals subtle changes, harmonies slipping sideways and voices layered with restraint. Such control brings its own risk. At times, the music’s gentleness brushes against a beauty held too safely, polished until friction and surprise have almost disappeared. Its brevity sharpens the issue: certain openings withdraw just as they acquire an unexpected inflection. The ending arrives early and leaves a desire for one further stretch, perhaps a little less serene. This limitation also clarifies the nature of the project. Wind Paths chooses a form capable of appearing and dissolving within a few minutes. It asks for attention without insisting upon it. The title speaks of invisible paths, and the music realizes that idea with remarkable coherence. Each element follows its own direction, guided by shared currents. The voice rises, the guitar fades, the harmonies change their angle. Deschamps has created one of his most lucid works, bringing together his vocal training, cinematic sensibility and ambient practice within a form that feels accessible, intimate and precise. When the final sound fades, the small white emblem at the bottom of the cover comes to mind. A wave reduced to calligraphy, discreet while the blue occupies everything. Wind Paths works in much the same way: it passes through the listener, leaves behind a faint vibration and entrusts the air with carrying it away. Wind Paths is available on Silent Sonic. items.body: Hawgood has tied Folk Reels to the idea of a mobile archive, a repository for scattered works, old tapes and encounters. Live At Still Point 2026 introduces a welcome fissure into that archive. To preserve also means admitting loss and giving it an audible measure. A work that fully embraces the loss it suffered and transforms it into living matter Live at Still Point 2026 by Ian Hawgood   A live album promises to bear witness, a weighty claim, perhaps too weighty. It evokes the idea of an event fixed once and for all, destined to return unchanged with every listen. Live At Still Point 2026 favors a memory with sections erased, passages heard only by those present at Brimscombe Mill that afternoon. The recording preserves the core of Ian Hawgood’s performance, while the contributions of two laptops used for processing were never captured in the file. A tangible absence, then, which has become the defining character of the work itself. The released sound recognizes its own limits and reveals them with rare candor. For Hawgood, the concert marked his return to performing before an audience after seven years. That fact carries more weight than a line in a press release, since his artistic journey has always sought a human dimension in the act of listening. A British sound engineer, founder of Home Normal and custodian of Folk Reels, he has built an extensive catalog around care, collaboration, tape and field recordings. At Still Point, that principle reconnects with the risk of the moment and a freedom still capable of play. Twenty five minutes, a single movement. At first come rustling sounds, calls whose source is difficult to place, brief electrical flashes. They​ resemble tentative contacts taking the measure of the air. Then a deep mass expands, gathering everything happening around it. Figures from We Are But Dream are bent and pushed towards a different sense of duration. Hawgood uses SYNTRX, Buchla sequences, sounds gathered outdoors and computers running AudioMulch, instruments from different eras surrendering their names to a single current. The music grows unhurriedly and gathers body through accumulation. A melody seems about to declare itself, then immediately chooses a less determinate form. This hesitation gives the work its intensity. No backdrop inviting distraction, no contemplative postcard. Hawgood’s ambient music asks for attention in a low voice and makes perceptible the time sound requires to change its nature. From time to time, an impulse punctures the continuity, an oblique jolt roughens the balance. It happens, that is all. The performance retains a vulnerable quality, even a slight awkwardness, precious in an age obsessed with polish. Depth becomes almost physical :: In the central stretch, depth becomes almost physical. The volume rises, the fabric thickens, while the pressure avoids all monumental emphasis. Hawgood proceeds through successive degrees of proximity: one colour enters another, the drone slowly alters its light, the breathing becomes irregular. It takes time to realize that the initial landscape is already elsewhere. At the point of greatest rarefaction, the current loses substance and seems about to fade out. The music accepts this descent. From there emerge more clearly defined figures, a gentle pulse, circling scales that bring energy without breaking the spell. The ending gathers motion and a strange, purposeful serenity, as though the sound had found a way to continue after almost dispersing. Tim Diagram’s photograph translates this condition well. Trees seen from below, pale clouds, a second pattern of foliage superimposed upon the sky. The image holds two temporalities and allows them to interfere. The album likewise contains what happens and the imprint of what escapes. The material lost from the two computers compels a reconsideration of what a document can mean. The audience heard a broader version, traversed by elements that are now irretrievable; the album offers an autonomous trajectory, barer and perhaps more exposed. Fidelity lies in the gesture, its openness to chance and the human scale of what has been preserved. Hawgood has tied Folk Reels to the idea of a mobile archive, a repository for scattered works, old tapes and encounters. Live At Still Point 2026 introduces a welcome fissure into that archive. To preserve also means admitting loss and giving it an audible measure. The still point evoked by the title becomes a magnetic centre around which everything changes: intensity, distance, density, memory. This is where the album’s achievement lies. Its beauty arises from a restrained decision: to release what survived without consoling reconstruction and to entrust absence with an active role. At the end, an unusual feeling lingers. Has one listened to a concert, or to the memory that a concert produced inside a machine? The question matters more than any answer. Hawgood offers twenty five minutes freed from the pose of the celebratory live album and the smoothness of the ambient product. The sound breathes, falters, gathers strength and recedes. In that movement it carries with it the Still Point community, the apprehension of returning, the pleasure of experimentation and the part that no medium will ever be able to hold. A work that fully embraces the loss it suffered and transforms it into living matter. Live at Still Point 2026 is available on folk reels. items.body: Giulio Aldinucci has made an album that seems acquainted with the unnamed part of human nature, the part that surfaces in sleep or in the few seconds before news capable of changing the course of a day. Rhythm is felt through changes in pressure Materia by GIULIO ALDINUCCI   At first there is weight. A quiet, almost geological pressure that arrives before recognition, touching the body before it reaches the mind. Materia begins in that dark place. Sound has volume, temperature, even something resembling a will of its own. It advances slowly and alters the scale of things, like a sudden bank of fog moving in. Sight loses its authority and the ear becomes a larger organ. Giulio Aldinucci has made an album that seems acquainted with the unnamed part of human nature, the part that surfaces in sleep or in the few seconds before news capable of changing the course of a day. The composer, born in Siena, Tuscany, reaches this point after years devoted to landscape, memory and the voice stripped of semantic meaning. The experience developed under the name Obsil and the chapter that began with Tarsia have shaped a coherent body of work, nourished by field recordings, choral presences and electronic transformations. Borders And Ruins examined the nature of territory; Disappearing In A Mirror and Shards Of Distant Times shifted the tension towards identity and memory; Real sought a personal reality within the excess of digital mediation. Materia, Aldinucci’s fifth album for Karlrecords, condenses that history into an essential gesture: taking a tightly packed mass of sound, carving into it, paring it back and searching for what is already alive​ inside. The album was released on September 18, 2026. Here accumulation and subtraction become emotional acts. Aldinucci gathers frequencies as scattered memories might be gathered after years apart, then removes the excess and listens into the space left behind by what has disappeared. Time, too, acquires substance. It is broken into minute units and reassembled according to an order that escapes the familiar pulse. Rhythm is felt through changes in pressure, through inner tides, through the way a distant voice rises from the haze and immediately loses its face. These are slow movements filled with secret life. Their apparent stillness is alive with motion. The six pieces form a single body lasting just under 43 minutes. Density remains the active principle, capable of changing state while retaining its gravity. The depths below sustain the journey with a telluric continuity. Above them appear distorted choirs, echoes, drifting particles and sounds that preserve a human trace after language and origin have fallen away. The titles sketch a constellation of absence: “Not Here,” the shadow cast by noise, ash and distant waves, the absolute finality of “Never,” evening, then light caught in a dream. The music receives these images and preserves their indeterminacy. Each one works within the act of listening, removed from plot and close to the freedom of involuntary association. “Materia finds its human center here. The album’s grandeur springs from this dizzying proportion: an immense sound holds a tiny gesture, perhaps a mouth drawing breath, perhaps a syllable worn away by time.” ~Mirco Salvadori The voice is central. It rises like a collective memory without face or biography, suspended between comfort and alarm. At times it resembles someone calling across an immense distance; elsewhere it takes on the substance of a thought formed in the body before words. Aldinucci understands the power of vocal fragments and frees them from any narrative duty. What remains is breath, impulse, a tremor that reminds the listener of human fragility. Materia finds its human center here. The album’s grandeur springs from this dizzying proportion: an immense sound holds a tiny gesture, perhaps a mouth drawing breath, perhaps a syllable worn away by time. “Come Luce, In Sogno,” chosen as the advance single, offers a discreet way into the album. The light invoked by its title contains dust and density. It filters through opaque layers and produces figures already moving towards dissolution. Dreaming becomes a mode of knowledge. A detail can expand until it fills the entire field of perception, while an enormous event contracts into a brief vibration. This instability runs through the whole work. Time seems to lengthen; then an almost imperceptible shift alters the landscape. Sound retains warmth and a question that has yet to find words. The cover helps reveal the character of the work. A white façade multiplies concave modules, dark openings and curves that look identical only at a glance. The eye finds order, then differences, shadows, stains and minor signs of wear. It is a serial form made vulnerable by time and by the material from which it is built. Aldinucci’s music behaves in much the same way. It turns repetition into change, raises immense structures and allows irregularity to bring them alive. Each surface hints at another depth. No answer comes. The desire to look again grows stronger. The concentration of the sound demands complete attention. A moment’s distraction can break the spell, and some passages deliberately court saturation. This is an exacting choice. Materia requires time, an appropriate volume and a measure of solitude. In return it offers a rare experience, moving listening beyond taste and into consciousness. Its forms entrust their appeal to a slower force, like the memory of a place never visited. There is familiarity and a faint fear. The unknown takes on an intimate temperature. “Sound appears as something that precedes its maker and continues beyond its listener, bound to the same matter as bodies, air and thought.” ~Mirco Salvadori Throughout Aldinucci’s career, recording the world has carried the value of a living archive. A landscape could hold a story; a procession could deliver into the present voices already receding into the distance; an ordinary noise could open a passage through perception. Materia brings this practice close to an elemental dimension. Here substance comes before place and contact before narrative. Sound appears as something that precedes its maker and continues beyond its listener, bound to the same matter as bodies, air and thought. This is where its power lies. The album speaks of the human condition through feeling. The need to give chaos a shape meets the fascination of whatever resists a final form. Every cut removes part of the original mass; subtraction reveals an unforeseen outline. The music breathes between these impulses, tightens, withdraws and fills out again. At times it seems about to disclose something. Then that something changes substance and becomes pure listening. Materia is expansive, gathered into a fierce intensity and charged with physical mystery. Giulio Aldinucci reaches one of the most mature expressions of his artistic language and gives contemporary ambient music an album with moral as well as sonic weight. When the final vibration ends, silence feels altered, thicker, almost conscious. Within that silence passes an intuition that cannot quite be held: perhaps the human spirit is precisely this restless substance, seeking form while knowing that every form is temporary. For just under 43 minutes, Materia gives it a body and lets it sing. Materia is available on Karlrecords. items.body: Kim Cascone’s book Post-Digital Music gives sound artists the conceptual thought tools that help open up connective valves between the unconscious and conscious minds, stimulating the growth of imagination. This collection of essays is also essential reading for the continued critical discourse around issues of electronic music production and reception. Beyond knobs, plugins, and technique Some books about music making take a very materialist approach. They look at sound as a purely physical phenomenon. They look at art making as just a matter of sliding the right dials and turning the right knobs (and they love to turn knobs). They ignore the subtle side of being a musician, the synchronistic clues that align to tell an artist they are on the right path of creation, the inner knowing of when to start on a certain project, when to halt on another one, and when it might be good to revive a work left behind. There are enough books that focus on the hardware and software of music making, even as they ignore the realware of imagination. Without imagination such tools mean little or nothing. Kim Cascone’s book Post-Digital Music gives sound artists the conceptual thought tools that help open up connective valves between the unconscious and conscious minds, stimulating the growth of imagination. This collection of essays is also essential reading for the continued critical discourse around issues of electronic music production and reception. Electronic music isn’t about having a stylish se​t of tools, a modular set up that looks good on social media, or a digital studio with all the latest plugins. The tools won’t accomplish much without a musician who has grown what Goethe called “new organs of perception.” This is a phrase Cascone uses throughout his writing as a way to convey the necessity of training intuitive skills, skills at noticing the subtle, skills that can help an individual create pieces resonate with the interior life of their prospective audience, rather than just regurgitate shiny audio baubles whose sounds never reach beneath the surface.None of this is to discount the training and skill set needed to develop as a musician, songwriter or composer on the material level, but it has been shown again and again that people without the traditional pedigree of talent and virtuosity can make compelling music, while the works of virtuoso’s can be lifeless and boring. Technical chops are only half the battle. If it was all about technique, Hollywood movies would be a lot better than they are and so-called B-Films from the past would suck, but I’ve found the opposite to be true. A mind and spirit keyed in to the imaginative side of the world allows an artist in any medium to tune their own subtle senses to act as antennae for incoming seeds and ideas. Once transmuted those seeds can then be recast into the field of cultural life. The eighteen essays collected in Post-Digital Music act as a corrective to the material focus prevalent in so much of electronic music discourse over the past several decades.   The essays themselves span the years 1999 to 2026 and show the evolution of Cascone’s mature thought. Many of these pieces have been around in various publications and posted online, and I had read a good chunk of them over the years before this slim volume arrived. It’s nice to have them collected all in one place, and the book can easily be tucked into a laptop bag or backpack to peruse between setting up for different gigs, recording sessions or any other time when an injection of deep thought or intellectual stimulation is required. Issues that Cascone brings up in the first short essay, “Residualism,” crop up throughout the work and are looked at from different angles all the way to the last essay “0’00” and Vertical Time.” And while they are organized sequentially in the order they were written, I have found that there are about three main topics, along with various interrelated subfields, that the essays flock and organize themselves around. The first of these topics, and a major overarching theme of his work in general is one many people are afraid to look at: failure. Cascone looks at “The Aesthetics of Failure,” ruminates on “Modulating the Boundaries of Failure” and pokes around into the possibility of failure as a window from which the future leaks out in “Errormancy: Glitch as Divination.” After a few decades of thinking about failure, and working with it in artistic computer music, he still hadn’t extracted or unpacked all that could be gleaned from its study. He included an interview titled “The Failure of Failure,” which goes beyond the notion of working with software at the edges of their prescribed ability, and takes a critical look at the failure of experimental music and art to glitch out the larger system of society. Perhaps the failure of these genres and subgenres within electronic music to change things in larger society also relates to the continued problems around performing electronic music. His essay “Laptop Music” traces the issues around live electronic music performance, specifically with computers, and it remains just as pertinent as it was when it was written in 2004. He quickly delineates the history of different kinds of music performance in the west, showing how the placing of electronic musicians on stages, and the audience in seats, as in your typical theater situation, upsets our notions of what a music performance is and should be. By way of example, I had the opportunity to see William Basinski earlier this year, and he played in a theater. He was on the stage with a tape loop, a laptop and a mixing board. I was very happy to hear this music done live, and I sat with my eyes closed for most of the show as the sounds washed over me at volumes levels I would never breach at home. When I didn’t have my eyes closed, I mostly paid attention to his video projections. His adjustments of the mixing board, computer, and loop were all very understated, and the video was in many respects its own kind of visual drone. Yet even as a fan of him, and even as someone who has played electronic music live myself with laptops and other knobby gear, the expectation around of musical performance as a kind of visual spectacle of virtuosity remain in place. As Cascone put it, “The laptop musician is conceived as a medium conducting a séance, whose tricks of table knocks, wall rapping and spectral voices broadcast from nowhere are orchestrated to feign the effect of authenticity where none really exists. Thus the cultural artifact produced by the laptop musician is deemed a counterfeit, leaving the audience unable to determine a use-value.” There still has not been much a “recuperation of codes that move away from the use of spectacle, that establish aura, and show the audience how to differentiate ‘representation by the machine’ from ‘repetition of the machine.’” Many in the audience relied on the aura of expectation created by Basinski’s albums in the live setting, or on his comedic pre and post show banter as a way to come away from the evening feeling satisfied. “The laptop musician is conceived as a medium conducting a séance, whose tricks of table knocks, wall rapping and spectral voices broadcast from nowhere are orchestrated to feign the effect of authenticity where none really exists. Thus the cultural artifact produced by the laptop musician is deemed a counterfeit, leaving the audience unable to determine a use-value.” ~Kim Cascone The other early essays remain just as relevant. The issues Cascone raised, now decades ago, are still with us. Sometimes there has been a bit of mutation along the fringes of the field, but where things have remained static, the major points are still at play. It must be remembered that electronic music is still very young as an art. The post-digital is even younger with its general focus on computer music. Perhaps a definition of just what Cascone means by Post-Digital is in order. In “Residualism” he talks about how Post-Digital music making is about the “deconstruction of audio by manipulating the prima materia itself” and how this has led to the recognition of the aesthetic value of sonic artifacts that were previously considered to be in the background. The art becomes a matter of subtracting information until only residues are left behind. While this simplifies the theoretical basis Cascone lays out, this approach and its aesthetic ramifications can be considered another core theme of the book. Because those artifacts had often been generated by pushing technology and software to the breaking point, is one of the reasons behind his intense focus failure, and how it can be a gateway into new forms of aesthetics. Another theme that emerges is a trinity around music, metaphysics and imagination. There is spiritual substance in the book, and in the works created by artists who are tuned in to the subtle fields. Essays in this grouping of include “Subtle Listening,” a text based on the workshops Cascone used to give. (These differ in form and substance from Pauline Oliveros’ work with Deep Listening, though I see the two as complimentary.) He also explores the metaphysical side in pieces such as “The Avantgarde as Aeromancy” and “The Transcenditial Imagination.” Other pieces such as “Organs of Subtle Perception” and “Imagination, Idea, Will, Manifestation” get to some of the core precepts around his percepts. His essay on aeromancy written in 2013 reflects on the artists relationship to time. Over on the blog at the Silent Records Bandcamp page, Cascone continues to write about time, about the hyper-present and how the effects of the simulacra and our immersion in online worlds pushes us into a vertical experience of time. He distinguishes this sense of verticality, of being removed from the clock-a-day world of linear horizontal time, from the kind of natural verticality we experience in moments of creative flow and time spent outside in nature.For the artist working on the horizons, at the boundaries, these distinctions are important for the work of tuning into the subtle senses and fishing for big ideas. In the essay he writes, “The past has become embedded in the future, reducing what we experience as ‘the present’ or ‘now’ -as simulacra, a plastic bauble bouncing upon the infinitesimal fulcrum where two streams intersect. One beckons from the past, the other seduces from the future. The plastic bauble of ‘now’ is all that exists today. All of time is trapped inside of it, containing a chimeric environment constructed from a trick of light, a sleight of hand, a conflation of nostalgic past with a tantalizing future.” And he continues with this salient advice: “For a real avant-garde to exist -again- we need to reestablish a ‘long-view’ perspective, recover from our collective amnesia, and locate ourselves in the larger historical landscape. By moving outside the manufactured environment and allowing the stream of time full passage through our psyches, we can return to an intuitive process of artistic divination.” “Like the artist, the audience also needs to be able to open the valve to the unconscious. Digital media in its current incarnation works as a firehose blasting the senses. Overstimulation is part of the issue. To tune in, sometimes the first step isn’t turning on, but turning off.” ~Justin Patrick Moore Now we are even more in the blurspace of the simulacra than we were in 2013. For those of us who wish to see such a return of the avant-garde as Cascone does we need to take regular time for reflection. If one of the tasks of the artist is to give reflection back, gestation periods are necessary, as is frequent time spent outside the outer focused hyper-present world, and inside the inner focused world of imagination. What bubbles inside the cauldron of a new avant-garde may take time to brew. In the world of outer of immediate action where each new piece and release vies for attention with the rest, the long term view tends to get shunted off and replaced by short term commodification, i.e. the market forces that cultivate the hyper-present simulacra for their own harvest. The larger gains that come from time spent swimming in the reflecting pool of imagination are not as apparent, not as immediate, but the long term effects could be much larger than those produced by the shiny baubles of momentary attention. For every force there is a field, and for the final grouping of general ideas I see in this book is the cluster around these words: aura, grain, and field. Field recordings have been at the heart of many approaches to electronic music for quite some time starting with the academic part of the tradition. Following the explosion of electronica, ambient, and then the plethora of interconnected subgenres, many electronicists began employing field recordings as a way to lend their pieces an organic integrity they sometimes lacked when based purely on digital sources. Ideas around the use of field recordings, and what a field actually is, all get explored at a deep theoretical level that is often missing elsewhere in the discourse.   Along the way we get to learn about Cybernetics and Systems Theory (always fun and always essential) as well as flocks and the swarming behavior of genres, and how they form. All of these subjects tend to get woven into each other, one area emphasized here, another there. Reading them together, it is hard not to feel the desire to get creative. The intellectual stimulation gives me the desire to put more critical imagination into the work of making electronic music and the conversations around the field. Perhaps the greatest advice to the aspiring artist included in the book is to “lessen ones dependence on digital tools” and his admonition, via Werner Herzog, to “Read, read, read…” he suggests that composers be “voracious readers and keep a physical notebook of ideas and projects. By relying less on digital tools you will gain a valuable context for your work.” That in itself is very much another kind of Post-Digital framework. As the book began with focusing perceptions on the boundaries and edges in “Residualism,, so it ends with a piece focusing on one of the great Zen koans John Cage left behind in the form of a musical composition. It is a seldom talked about piece of music that he wrote, 0”00”. It is a work that has no duration, and in many ways, it only exists in the mind. By going back to this ground zero, we are left in a kind of recursive mobius strip, zeroing back in on zero itself. Cascone again cautions against getting too caught up in the speed race of digital acceleration. He also reminds us that the collective suite of digital tools that now exist to make things by command, i.e., AI, while in some ways resembling the chance operations and recombinatorial procedures of the earlier avant-garde expemplified by John Cage, do not in fact resemble the actual facts of his work. Cage did his chance operations in a slowed down way. His use of the I Ching was part of a contemplative artistic process, not just punching in commands at a whim. As such, until we can regain our composure and pull ourselves away from the immersive grip of the hyperattentive state induced by the constant influx of media and data made possible by what Cascone has often called McGovCorp, it will remain difficult for sophisticated artworks in any medium to find a receptive audience. Like the artist, the audience also needs to be able to open the valve to the unconscious. Digital media in its current incarnation works as a firehose blasting the senses. Overstimulation is part of the issue. To tune in, sometimes the first step isn’t turning on, but turning off. Post-Digital Music (Essays) is available on Silent Records. [Bandcamp]The post Kim Cascone :: Post-Digital Music: Essays (1999–2026) (Silent) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items.body: Columbus’s Pinta, Niña and Santa María sail through “Delfín del Mundo” alongside pineapples, cockerels, chocolate, tobacco and caipirinhas, a roll call of conquest and tropical produce chanted over a psychedelic cumbia. “Delfín del Mundo” is the third and final single from Desertropical, the new EP from Dr. Rayo, due in October on Costa Rican label Lácteo Cósmico. The project belongs to Red Jesus, a Chilean-Mexican percussionist and producer who spent 2014 to 2020 on Mexico’s independent circuit. Now based in Madrid, he launched the project with a sold-out night at Moby Dick. Red Jesus made the track with Barzo, the San José-born DJ and producer who runs Lácteo Cósmico and has remixed Janelle Monáe and Erykah Badu. He came to Madrid for a short visit, and the pair recorded most of the instruments live at Dr. Rayo’s base. Barzo then built the electronic production on top of those takes. The earlier singles “Mexicali Tropical” and “Owl on Cocaine” opened big and dramatic, while “Delfín del Mundo” settles into a mid-tempo sway built on a slow-burning bassline, live percussion and a vocal delivered close to a chant. The vocal carries a message of pride in Latin American roots, and the cacao, tobacco and pineapples in the lyric were growing in the Americas long before Columbus’s ships arrived. Desertropical gets a launch party at Madrid’s Siroco at the end of September, with Spanish dates to follow in Seville, Oviedo, Gijón, Logroño and Santander. Stream “Delfín del Mundo” HERE The post Daily Discovery: Dr. Rayo x Barzo – Delfín del Mundo appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: Review by kenethlevine — The odd title for this difficult third album is somewhat reflected in the content, which, while still emphasizing skilled acoustic interplay, has seen its Celtic edge gone dull, and with it most of the earlier spark. The band seems to be channeling a theatrical FAIRPORT or MELLOW CANDLE, though a less committed ISB, SIROGYRA or JAN DUKES DE GRAY might be more a propos, or even a disoriented Lindisfarne as seen on a few contemporaneous albums, but without that group's prior success as a triggering event. It's like a live performance of new material in which jamming and vocalise fill in overly busy and inauthentically complex arrangements. One of the big misses is the inclusion of the unsubtle "Don't Forget the Animal" phrasing on 3 tracks, a theme handled better, though well short of masterfully, on a full length bonus track available with the group's debut. Still, "Is it Me" carries on the understated folk of its predecessors while POLLY BOLTON's best vocal contribution to date is in the ballad "I Heard Somewhere", combining with Martin Jenkins on-point violin. Overall though, this is a dispirited effort that fits the band about as well as the wrong pantaloons.

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — What starts out sounding like a Funk-Jazz outing of the highest quality seems to turn taward the R&B, Disco, Black Dance, and even Adult Contemporary/Smooth Jazz charts. But then we are only getting started: soon we find ourselves treated to one absolutely amazing journey through Power Fusion of the highest caliber. 1. "Master Funk" (3:42) Al is playin' it all on this (not really, but a lot of the tracks!) There is a Brothers Johnson-meets-Billy Preston-and-The Hues Corporation feel to this one. Whereas the song feels a bit like a one-trick pony novelty song, there are definitely some praise-worthy elements to the music: these funk masters are definitely talented! (8.875/10)2. "Baker's Daughter" (5:34) the quartet takes a long route to introducing the full structure of this one, using wah-wah-ed "underwater" funk bass, ample cymbals and drums, broad keyboard swaths, and treated soprano saxophone to introduce the sound palette over an extraordinary two minutes time before Al power drums his way into establishing the pace and power of the Smooth Power Fusion. Stu and Welton kind of hold space trying to keep up with Al's frenetic pace while Gary seems to take great satisfaction on delivering his Jerome Richardson-like melodic soprano sax solo over the top. Stu gets some solo time in the fourth minute for his piano, Chick Corea-style, as Al's drumming keeps pushing, pushing, and pushing. Great performances from Al, Gary, and Stu; I just wish Welton had a little more room and confidence to spread his wings a little. (9/10)3. "Come into My Life" (5:10) a sensual, ARP Odyssey strings-rich opening that is marred a bit by and "out-of-place" chunky & forward bass. Stu is playing some nice grand piano as Al handles drums lite and the Odyssey and Gary belts it out like a castrati with his soprano sax. Nice and relaxing, even appropriate for those late night date-ending "drinks" that couples resort to in order to warm-up and commit to sexual interplay. (8.875/10)4. "Nyctophobia" (7:00) finally we get some Stanley-Clarke/Jaco Pastorius-level bass play from Welton Gite! They're off to the races for this one with Gary Bartz plying his skills with ease on his soprano sax. As much as I usually dislike this particular instrument, I have to admit that Gary makes it sound like a walk in the park (and I know it's not!) If I had to walk through scary dangerous street-alleys in the dark of the late night, the intrepid spirit that Gary displays with his soprano sax is the kind of fearless courage I would want at my side (or coursing through my veins). Stu's MiniMoog solo in the sixth and seventh minutes takes that instrument to extremes that no one, not even Jan Hammer or Chick Corea, ever took it! Everybody's performance on this piece is jaw-dropping--and they keep it going for all of its seven minutes. (14.75/15)5. "Virtue" (8:23) a drumming clinic in which Al seems to be playing a medium-paced straight-time rhythm track but his tom-tom and cymbals cry out for forgiveness as they are so mercilessly (though almost lackidaisically) abused! Though Fender Rhodes is the first instrument to join (and try to match Alphonse's energy), it's Stu's grand piano and Gary's alto sax that the listener soon finds each screaming out "hard bop" Jazz. Meanwhile, Welton's bass is being beaten silly like it's on a DOUG ROUCH or PERCY JONES outing. In the fourth minute Stu's electric piano begins flying all over--through a complete review of the Herbie-Chick lexicon. And then there's the MiniMoog-dominated sixth minute: exhibiting yet another "outside the box" display of synth creativity. This is Power Fusion at its absolute best, folks! (19/20)6. "Poobli" (5:30) Smooth Jazz with a funk-cool vibe reminiscent of some of Earth, Wind & Fire's most groovin' dance tunes--all thanks to Welton and Al's cool, ultra-laid back rhythm track and Stu's dreamy Fender Rhodes play in the middle. Gary's plays some mean and unusual tenor sax lines to toy with the main melody lines, later retweeted by Al's ARP Odyssey strings and Stu's MiniMoog--which Gary must see as a challenge to his manhood as he takes off into new and extraordinary heights. Why this guy isn't a household name when it comes to discussing saxophone players I do not know! He may be the one that makes me finally appreciate, even like, the saxophone! (9.333/10)"The Mouzon Drum Suite" (8:31) : (18.21/20) = 9.10 - 7. a) "Jazz-Rock-Improvisation" (2:23) solo drumming . . . with effects. (4.425/5) - 8. b) "Out of the Desert" (1:45) steady simple, metronomic drumming with lots of percussion instruments played and over the top--especially the ones that bend and twist pitch. (4.333/5) - 9. c) "Colors of Africa" (2:39) gong opening followed by kalimba, marimba, twizzles, shakers, cymbals, and hand drums of all shapes, sizes, and elements (clay, wood, metal)--plus kit drums and true African chant vocals! Awesome! (5/5) - 10. d) "Total Swing" (1:44) virtuosic display at the traps. Sped up at the end. (4.45/5)Total Time: 43:50Al is a drummer who at first did not impress me as much as the other "greats" but, over time I've come to experience and appreciate both his skills and his creative talent as well as his commendable abilities beyond the drum kit and percussion trunk. He has, here, created a truly marvelous masterpiece of fully-developed and fleshed-out Jazz-Rock Fusion.A/five stars; a veritable masterpiece of eclectic Jazz-Rock Fusion--one that centers fully in the domain of the Power Fusionists. HIGHLY recommended.

items.body: Review by Sean Trane — Out of Central/East Serbia's most ancient city Nis, comes this fusion quartet that is lead bypianist Ilijic, a competent rhythm section and an electric guitarist that is looking to run awaywith the spotlight. They can make you think of a GoGo Penguin trio with an added electric guitarist,and the least we can say is that they hold this flattering comparison quite well.A live album, encompassing most of Eyot's studio discography, as the recordings rank from '15 to '23 and tracks played from their hometown Nis all the way to Munich and even New York and O-Yokohama.Some Balkan gigs and Western Europe gigs are also present in this selection. As you've guessed,we're dealing more with some kind of "best of" live, rather than a whole concert set list. Over thetwo disc (just under one hour each), you'll be bombarded with some brilliant instrumental interplay,though there is a sense of repetition over the full listen, but one track features a two-horn, whichis a welcome sonic change, if only temporary. IMHO, listen to only one disc at a time, because anoverdose is around the bend.

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — A longtime Jazz veteran of Brasil's music scene catches the "fusion" bug, travels to the USA to collaborate with some of New York City's finest studio musicians. The album was recorded in 1970 at A&R Studios in New York City and then released by Cobblestone Records sometime later in the year.1. "Coalhada (Yogurt)" (3:00) big band jazz that happens to use electric piano. This sounds like Doc Severinson's late night band with Johnny Carson. The song's end is a fadeout during some very animated and dynamic full-band interplay. Nice full-band cohesion. (8.875/10)2. "Hermeto" (4:22) sounds like a Eumir Deodato and Burt Bacharach team rendering of "You Are the Sunshine of My Life." Hermeto's electric piano play fits so nicely over the Smooth Jazz orchestral arrangement. Nice lead flute solo from (probably) Hermeto himself. (9.125/10)3. "Guizos (Bells)" featuring Googie Coppola (6:20) gentle, atmospheric jazz stripped down to Ron Carter, Hermeto's sensual electric piano, Airto's cymbal and brush play, with Flora Purim's wordless vocalese floating within and above it--and, later, a breathy flute. The orchestra makes its presence known in bigger and bigger ways toward the end of the fourth minute, swelling just before Hermeto's sexy little keyboard dance duet with Ron. Flora and low brass return around the five minute mark, prompting the horn-led orchestra to swell again. Beautiful music (that reminds me very much of the intro "Storm at Sunup" section of Gino and Joe Vannelli's opener to their great 1974 album of the same name)! (9.12510)4. "Flor Do Amor (The Love Flower)" (5:51) opening with a beautiful small chamber arrangement of wind instruments that turns to strings for support and takeover around the 20-second mark before melding together to support a lovely lower register flute lead. The harmonic orchestral support is wonderful! Brass take over in the lead position of the "dance," giving Hermeto time to get situated at his electric piano for a turn. Then it's back to flute for the end of the fourth minute, back to keys for the fifth, dueling/dueting with flute (there are so many accomplished flute players credited in the line-up chart that it's hard for me to believe that Hermeto doesn't use one or more of them to play off of: Hubert Laws! Joe Farrell! Jerome Richardson!) (9/10)5. "Alicate (Pliers)" featuring Flora Purim (4:00) this one sounds very much like a Burt Bacharach song with the orchestra providing most of the melody leads for the first 1:45. Then an odd almost "bass" or bamboo flute enters, playing really low, really breathily. This must be Hermeto due to the Amazonian flavor/flare being presented here. Return to orchestral dominance for the rest of the third and fourth minutes (with lots of wonky, animal-sounding brass), and then fade out. (8.875/10)6. "Vel�rio (Mourning)" featuring Flora Purim (8:38) organ, bass, and low-end flute(s) and female vocalese open this one while a taped recording of tribal conversation plays beneath. The whole vibe here is one of the Amazon jungle. Even the violins that enter in the middle of the second minute and the other orchestral instruments seem to be trying to capture or emulate jungle noises. Then in the second half of the third minute Airto's lone violin-like berimbau goes completely solo, sounding like the fast-rushing of an on-coming railroad train. The fifth minute sees a return of the wooden flute (heavily reverbed), which plays solo for a complete minute before petering out and being supplanted by a faded-in piano--who continues the on-rushing train theme--until the end of the sixth minute when the orchestra's trumpet section announces itself sharply, being joined by other brass, winds, strings, and percussion instruments in a very theatric motif that begins to "fall apart" like a drunken debauch at the end of the eighth minute. The chaos is then displaced by piano, bowed bass, and tambourine playing an "old-fashioned" barroom jazz bit to the song's end. Interesting! Not my favorite but I appreciate the creativity behind the song. (17.5/20)7. "As Marianas (The Marianas)" (4:34) full orchestra playing music that sounds like the warm up music to a grand ball or art museum exhibit. This may be jazz (of the Nelson Riddle-Glen Miller kind) but it's nowhere near anything I'd apply the Jazz-Rock Fusion term to. It's also kind of lame, like a sleepy, sloppy version of "Born Free." (8.375/10)8. "Fabiula" (3:51) more "old" strings-dominated cinematic music that may be big band created (I hear the individual instruments like flutes, horns, and Spanish guitar) but it, again, fails to even come close to the musics I would term "J-R F" (or any other kind of fusion). Maybe "orchestral-bossa nova lite" would best describe this soporific fare. At least this one is far more sophisticated and melodic than the previous disaster. (8.875/10)Total time: 40:46B/four stars; Oh! how one really poor song can drag an entire album down from near-masterpiece status to good/worth your attention. Side One is definitely deserving of all your Jazz-Rock Fusion enthusiasm whereas Side Two may bore you to tears--especially if you have an aversion to languorous strings-dominated orchestral jazz and attempts to replicate the sounds of the jungle using musical instruments.

items.body: Review by WizardGirl420 — I write this review in 2026 of an album I listened to extensively when it was released in 2008. Iremember listening to it nonstop for days on end. for years I couldn't listen to THE BEDLAM INGOLIATH without feeling transported in time to 2008-09. So I put it away, so I could live in thepresent.Recently I decided to pick up this album again. It still feels vital. so full of energy. At thisstage in their career the Mars Volta were firebrands of creative energy, one of the leading lightsof the 00s prog rock revival. Their well-earned Grammy win for WAX SIMULACRA, a lead single fromBedlam, was the crown to commemorate this creative peak, before they eventually declined and splitinto assorted side projects. (the followup, OCTAHEDRON, is a significant drop in quality in myopinion, which I don't think they ever got much better from. But I digress.)The album opens with a slam with "Aberinkula". The Mars Volta's trademark complex, salsa-influenceddrum patterns and highly effected guitar is a relentless blast of rocking. I love Rodriguez-Lopez'sguitar style, there's the noisiness from his experience in hardcore punk, but he's obviously verywell-versed in jazz and latin styles with a healthy dose of psychedelia. The heaviness barely letsup as the album smoothly flows into "Metatron". Everything flows together smoothly, actually; thedynamic and mood shifts between the songs feel so natural."Ilyena" is my personal favorite. Extremely catchy, and the electronic noise gives you a nice breakfrom the punk-influenced intensity that defines the album. The rest of the album follows a similarstyle of punk heaviness, electronic distortion, prog rock composition and latin rhythms. Veryunique, very catchy, very loud and very gripping.FRANCES THE MUTE and DE-LOUSED IN THE COMATORIUM might be overall better, and have probably beenmore influential on subsequent prog-minded artists. But THE BEDLAM IN GOLIATH remains a personalfavorite of mine and I think is a great piece of 2000s heavy.
