items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — An unusual yet fully-progressive undertaking of setting literary stories to music using jazz-fusion artists.1. "The Sinking Spell" (4:40) Robert Wyatt's distinctive voice enters with some effect applied while the four musicians, Steve Swallow, Jack DeJohnette, Carla Bley, and Terje Rypdal apply their talents to constructing a loose and reactive soundtrack to Robert's rendering of this Edward Gorey story. Terje is particularly flamboyant (almost in a Steve Hackett way!) while Carla, Steve, and Jack are pretty dynamic in their own right. Perhaps Robert's best, most unique performance on the album and maybe the best collective Jazz-Rock Fusionary exposition as well. (9.125/10) 2. "The Object Lesson" (5:00) piano, bass and swelling cymbal crashes back Robert's rather flat/monotone delivery of this story. Eventually the musicians fall into a kind of groove with Jack DeJohnette's rock drumming and Terje Rypdal and Carla Bley's Canterbury organ saw-like expressions. The music is not great, not fully-formed or composed for much other than dramatic support, but it works (it's better than the story being told). (8.75/10)3 "The Insect God" (5:00) some truly top-notch Jazz-Rock Fusion is used to present another sobering and not-for-children's-ears story. The music quartet of Bley, Rypdal, Swallow, and drummer Jack DeJohnette are all on the same page of aggressive and insistent delivery while Robert and spoken-word "backing vocalists" render their fast-talking approach to dramatic story-telling. (8.75/10)4 "The Doubful Guest" (4:45) finally! some thoroughly-composed music! It's a challenging weave of off-timed hi-speed drum and keyboard music in which Steve and Terje contribute long-held, pensive notes on their respective instruments. All the while Robert delivers a near-spoken word story with a little more flair and enthusiasm than the past two. The overall weave really works--has no glaring flaws or inconsistencies. I like the way the musical performances ramp up toward the end: especially Terje's guitar shredding and Carla's breadth of synth strings chords. (9.125/10)5 "The Remembered Visit" (6:25) voice with syncopated bass and synth-strings pulses, adding piano and Mellotron "ooo"s and "aaah"s, then treated electric guitar notes and some background drumming. In the third minute the drums and bass play get more animated--still orchestral and reactive, though, more than "song" oriented. Where Robert's delivery starts out dramatic and engaged, it begins to sound a bit like rote reading in places. But then things slow down for the background vocal-supported passage in the fifth minute--which has the effect of seeming to bring Robert back into the spirit of the story. From there out he feels fully-present in his story-telling. Effective. (8.875/10)6 "The Hapless Child" (7:00) Robert Wyatt's distinctive voice and vocal/story-telling stylings are here backed by music that feels more like theater music: it's incidental and yet has a personality all its own--as if taking on the characteristics of Robert's story's characters. Nothing is flowing or timed, almost all of it feels impressionistic and reactive more than composed and prescribed. There is one theme that feels prepared: the whole-band motif that starts at 2:58 when Robert starts singing about the start of Charlotte Sophia's boarding school experience, but at 4:20 everything devolves to simple piano--just before launching into a more dynamic and drum-and-guitar-driven theme. What a horrifying Dickensian tale! Carla Bley's odd chord choices hold the whole thing down but it's Steve Swallow's obtuse bass notes and Terje Rypdal's sharp, stinging guitar notes that bring forth and amplify the Poe-like atmosphere of the story. Wow! What an experience! Definitely not your typical bed-time story! Even children's theatre would be scarred and marred for decades if they brought children in to hear this one! Still, it is a rather powerful and effective delivery mechanism. (13.25/15)Total Time:I have to admit that I was not prepared for either the album's total dedication to story telling nor it's dark and rather dismal, even desolate, Dickensian/Brothers Grimm/Edgar Allen Poe story lines. While I love the literate nature of the stories, I'm a bit disturbed by their unsettling subject matters. At the same time, I appreciate these adventurous musicians for their commitment to the expansion of that which music and Jazz-Rock Fusion can do. B/four stars; though admirable to take on such an odd and ambitious undertaking, I feel that the stories and music do not always match as well as the artists/producers may have wanted. Nor are the instrumental performances and song/soundtrack compositions as polished and coordinated as well as one might expect or desire from this stellar line-up.

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — A surprisingly-sophisticated and highly-entertaining album from a group of University of Illinois college students! Released on Brunswick Records in July of 1972.1. "The Monster Bride" (10:36) a very proggy, early King Crimson and Yes-like opening of bass, organ, clarinet, and delicate cymbal play turns in the second minute toward proggy brass rock--more like ELP meets BS&T. In the third minute the motif starts to smooth out before suddenly switching direction toward more light and playful circus music and then, in the fourth minute there is an equally sudden directional change toward more avant/eclectic Jazz-Rock Fusion before going Crimson and Zappa in the fifth. This is all quite tightly-performed and very sophisticated and unpredictable! It must have been something to compose and then pull off as a band in 1970s studio conditions. By the time we get to the end of the sixth minute everything slows down to a cymbal-supported droning organ for a Peter Hammill-like male vocal to enter and sing. Very Crimsonian! Flute and piano pick up from here with a very pretty, almost CHICAGO-like melody presentation and passage which builds and builds, horns entering and gathering forces over bass, guitar, and drum's rhythm track. At 5:22 everything stops for some percussion-backed dramatic very theatric narration of a sexually-piqued scene of the monster's reaction and response to the birth of his bride and child--which then leads to a finishing burst of CHICAGO-like brass rock. Very interesting! The sophistication of the compositions (and ability to pull it off in the studio) is the most impressive part. (18.375/20) 2. "Spiders (In Neals Basement)" (5:57) an accented male voice singing a sly lyric of film noir's detective-type music, like musical themes for scenes in a New Orleans juke joint or Chicago flop house. The music, performances both instrumentally and vocally are so colorful and spry. Great brassy theater music and great entertainment! Amazing that these were just a bunch of college kids! (9.333/10)3. "Witches Theme And Dance" (9:47) a brass rock song that opens like a LIGHTHOUSE song with great pace and energy before dropping down into a slow, plodding motif over which the gang issue some great four-part vocal harmony vocals. These guys must've done music theater or high school theater music. Bassist Neal Rosner is quite impressive (and, thankfully, placed forward in the mix), sounding a lot like Goblin or PFM's bassists. More stunning theatric stop-and-start composition performed with ease and professional precision over/within which electric guitar, voices, slide flute, and other mildly scary Hallowe'en noises contribute their solos and incidentals. Nice trilly flute solo in the final third--augmented by awesome "distant" flugelhorn. The finish is just perfect for the "lesson" of the witchy allegory. Another gem of a song; these guys are so creative and so talented! (18.875/20)4. "A Brief Message From Your Local Media" (9:59) here the band conjures up a four-part suite. It opens sounding like something from Aaron Copeland before organ, bass, hi-hat & bass drum lay down a soft carpet for a lone vocalist to begin his GREG LAKE-like "In the Court of the Crimson King" imitation. Obligatory flute joins in as "Greg" reaches his third verse--arpeggiated guitar chords and increasingly MICHAEL GILES-like drumming, as well. Around 4:30 there is a break in which narrator delivers a brief spoken-word summation of the contributions of Henry Ford to the workings of modern society, which is then followed by the development of a new motif of rather up-tempo organ- and flute-driven Jazz-Rock--which gains Latin elements in the eighth minute to give it a LEONARD BERNSTEIN West Side Story feel but then about a minute later the music moves more toward a pop/theatric-Brass Rock form similar to the snarky Hair, Godspel, and Pippen phenomenons. The music ends with a fading out calliope and military drums sound. Interesting. Though still delightfully creative and astonishingly sophisticated, the cohesiveness of this one is questionable (but, then, so is the flow of the typical radio or television programming!). (18.125/20) - a) "The Garden"- b) "The Assembly Line"- c) "Electric Man"- d) "Question"Total time 36:19Jazzy, brassy Crimsonian prog rock that sounds quite mature for a bunch of Illini students--and it's so entertaining, even addictive! Incredible for a debut album.A/five stars; a surprisingly-sophisticated and well-polished display of delightfully-entertaining compositions and performances. Who knew?! And, Whatever happened to?

items.body: Review by alainPP — Green Carnation presents the third album in the "A Dark Poem" trilogy, nodding to the likes of Anathema and Katatonia. It delivers an oppressive, heavy, and meditative sound with dark progressive roots."Unconditional Artificial Chemistry" opens with a spacey feel, suddenly cut through by an exuberant, thick, heavy guitar; the monolithic vocals help transport the listener to another planet. The track narrates the dangers of AI, unfolding seamlessly while building an all-encompassing, progressive intensity. It shifts to include a crystalline piano in the distance, with musical grandeur that straddles the line between doom and Opeth-esque gothic metal, creating an oppressive atmosphere. There is a spellbinding melancholy'a blend of Anathema, Mogwai, Katatonia, and early King Crimson. "The Messiah Complex" features a melting guitar arpeggio, with vocals that abruptly break the ethereal, charming, and hypnotic mood. Melancholic, mysterious keyboards add a layer of solemnity that oozes progressive structure, while the dominant vocals allow the mantra-like atmosphere to spill over. The decrescendo finale is simple and effective'steady and unstoppable'serving as a musical paradigm."Broken Souls, Common Enemies" features a prominent New Wave-style synth driving the rhythm. The riff, the languid vocals, and the guitar's plaintive melody evoke emotion, discovery, and complexity in a track that is heavy without flaunting it. A shift to screamed vocals over a machine-gun riff'reminiscent of The Gathering in their early days'reasserts the track's intensity and complexity, bolstered by Wright-esque keyboards. A break featuring an ethereal flute and a melting, Western-style acoustic solo follows. Vocoded vocals amplify the majestic atmosphere, launching a stratospheric guitar solo worthy of the genre's titans'a truly stunning moment. Finally, "A Dark Poem - Orchestral Suite" begins with otherworldly vocals introducing wind instruments'including Ingrid's flute'as the orchestral arrangement takes center stage. An orchestral suite worthy of *Fantasia*'a classic pastoral anthem recounting Rimbaud's "Ophelia," performed by the Kristiansand Symphony Orchestra and its opera choir. Then comes the break: a return to archaic vocals, a primal sound reaching its zenith'is this the birth of prog? A dark, unsettling, yet colorful and pastoral atmosphere, pierced by illuminating trumpets; it is a masterpiece right up to the final note, with a soaring violin flourish creating a moment that transcends time.Green Carnation takes its final bow with this triptych finale'punchier, spellbinding, and invigorating. It is a crowning achievement, blending dystopian lyrics about our society with majestic, solemn melodies. Classy, ​​dreamlike, and immense progressive post-metal'featuring a sound that left an indelible mark on me from their very beginnings, delivering a powerful impact this September.

items.body: Review by brainsuccasurgery — Despite having been around for some thirty years (their first album, released in 1993, was produced by Eroc, former drummer of Grobschnitt), very little has been written about this German band in the progressive music press, with the exception of a few wonderfully insightful reviews published in 2001 to mark the release of their masterpiece, *Fantasma*. In those insightful lines, everything was said?from the impeccable vocals of Oliver Philipps?the heart and soul of the band?which stir us with emotion in airy, nostalgic atmospheres, to Everon's distinctive taste for Rush at its most melodic. Incidentally, the influence of the fathers of Canadian hard-prog on a band from our good old continent is rare enough to warrant special mention. For good measure, among the similarities or influences more or less acknowledged by Everon, we should also mention the prog metal of Vanden Plas, the even more symphonic style of Sylvan, or the more neo-prog sound of Pallas. And despite my fear of intriguing or horrifying some readers, I'll also take the liberty of pointing out Oliver Philipps's avowed fondness (see his website) for Nik Kershaw.But it's through a subtle affinity for Rush that *North* really bursts onto the scene, with a mind-blowing and compact "Hands ", driven by an unstoppable melody yet free of any lulls or orchestral flourishes (here, a few keyboards with a discreet but essential presence)?exactly as Oliver Philipps intended, having momentarily had his fill of his own sumptuous arrangements.A track remarkable for its ability to encapsulate the very best of its creator's aspirations, "Hands" reassures us of Everon's intentions: to succeed in creating something that is both simple and grandiose. This is something the band's two previous albums, *Flesh* and *Bridge*?which were not substantial enough despite the extravagant 14-minute title track "Flesh"?partially failed to achieve; curiously, both were released in the same year (2002). The next track, "A Brief Encounter", is the biggest surprise on the new album: constructed like a sort of "Turn of the Century" in tune with our times (read: with a testosterone boost), complete with acoustic guitar and piano parts, it unabashedly reveals the depth of Philips' love for the universal sound of Yes. The greatest (and consistent) melodic shortcoming?at least on the early albums?has, over time, become a strength. Straight to the point: emotion. UnforgettableOliver is a tremendous singer who has never stopped improving since a debut album that was nearly disastrous in that regard (a young Greg Lake's voice, uncertain and poorly anchored to confusing melodies) to reach a level that only the very best have attained. On that note, on *North*, be sure to listen to "Test of Time", opulent prog metal with a brief cello intro. Or the tormented "North" ("I remember I wrote 'North' on an unbelievably stormy day" (O. Philipps), with its false string section richer than a cathedral door.Olivier Philipps is also an excellent musician (guitars, keyboards) who puts his performance at the service of the richness of the melody?and not the other way around. He's fairly sparing with solos but increasingly generous with pure emotion, as on "Wasn't It Good" (6:33), the most poignant track on *North*, my favorite track, and probably also Oliver Philipps's favorite on this album: "Actually, in my humble personal opinion, this kind of song is the essence of what Everon is all about" (O. Philipps). At the beginning, with a touch of nostalgia, a piano begins to float heavily through the ether, the melody detached from its harmonic body, a sphere of thought undulating at the end of a long string. And when the guitar solo comes in?which seems as simple as pie, so much so that even my thick, clumsy little fingers think they can play it?you find yourself hoping never to hear another lukewarm review of Everon.The edgy "Woodworks", a highly successful instrumental, as if to retrospectively disprove the famous review mentioned above, which noted that instrumentals had never been Everon's strong suit (a claim already contradicted at the time by the intro to "Venus" in 1997, as beautiful as anything by Dave Bainbridge), helps lighten the emotional load somewhat after bringing us to our knees. And Judith St�ber's enchanting voice on the ballad "Islanders" gently lifts us back up. And we stand tall as we listen to the glorious and energizing "Running", convinced that *North* is a truly ambitious album, a classic?and not just another heavy prog record?a formidable magnetic force that, while not reaching the absolute pinnacle of modern progressive rock, succeeds where so many others have failed, starting with Everon himself up to this point: to bring together in a single artistic work 10 crisp, simple, and clear melodies, set in 10 rings of precious metal, resting on 10 harmonic velvet cases. With the uncertain style of their early days having given way to a confident musical personality, Everon's music?that of their new album in particular?can fulfill the deepest progressive aspirations hidden within us. There's no doubt that *North* could give Everon the place it deserves: on the podium. At last!

items.body: Eight tracks, two of them longer than eight minutes and one past eleven: Fields of the Nephilim built their third album around length. Beggars Banquet released “Elizium” on 24 September 1990, two years after “The Nephilim” had taken the gothic rock band from Stevenage to number 12 in the UK. The new album peaked at number 22. It turns 36 this year, and it remains the last studio record by the line-up of Carl McCoy, Tony Pettitt, Peter Yates, Paul Wright and Alexander “Nod” Wright. The band recorded “Elizium” in 1990 at Park Gate Studios in Battle, East Sussex, with additional recording and mixing at Astoria in Hampton Court. Andy Jackson, the engineer on Pink Floyd‘s late-1980s records, produced the album with the band and engineered the sessions; Jon Carin added keyboards. McCoy wrote the lyrics and the five members share the music credits. The title respells Elysium, the afterlife of Greek religion, and “At the Gates of Silent Memory” opens with the voice of Aleister Crowley reading from his poem “At Sea” in a 1920 recording. Beverley Carruthers shot the front sleeve, and Sheer Faith and Chris Bigg designed the packaging. ‘Elizium’ tracklist, singles and reissues The album runs 48 minutes and 3 seconds: “(Dead But Dreaming)”, “For Her Light”, “At the Gates of Silent Memory”, “(Paradise Regained)”, “Submission”, “Sumerland (What Dreams May Come)”, “Wail of Sumer” and “And There Will Your Heart Be Also”. Beggars Banquet issued it in the UK on LP, CD and cassette, with Rebel Rec. and SPV handling the German-speaking countries. “For Her Light” came out as the lead single in July 1990 and reached number 54 in the UK; “Sumerland (Dreamed Version)” followed in November 1990 and peaked at number 37. Music On Vinyl repressed the album on LP in 2011. Beggars Arkive marked the 30th anniversary on 11 December 2020 with a 180-gram dark green vinyl edition, and on 5 April 2024 released an expanded double LP on brick red vinyl. That edition spreads the album over three sides and adds four tracks on the fourth: “Sumerland (Single Version)”, “For Her Light (Two)”, “Submission Two (The Dub Posture)” and “Sumerland (Dreamed Version)”. John Dent handled the analogue transfer and Sean Magee cut the vinyl master. About Fields of the Nephilim Fields of the Nephilim formed in Stevenage, Hertfordshire, in 1984 around vocalist Carl McCoy, bassist Tony Pettitt, guitarist Paul Wright, drummer Alexander “Nod” Wright and saxophonist Gary Wisker. Peter Yates joined on guitar in 1985, the year the band released the “Burning the Fields” EP on its own Tower Release label. Jungle Records reissued it and financed the “Returning to Gehenna” EP in 1986. Situation Two, the Beggars Banquet imprint, signed the band in 1986 and released the singles “Power” and “Preacher Man” ahead of the debut album “Dawnrazor” in May 1987. The second album, “The Nephilim”, followed on 5 September 1988 and entered the UK chart at number 12, with “Moonchild” reaching number 28 as a single. The stand-alone single “Psychonaut” peaked at number 35 in May 1989, and the band moved up to the parent Beggars Banquet label for “Elizium” in September 1990. The two-night Festival of Fire at London’s Town & Country Club in 1991 produced the live album “Earth Inferno”, released on 25 March 1991, and the concert video “Visionary Heads”. McCoy left later that year. Pettitt, Yates and the Wright brothers continued as Rubicon with singer Andy Delaney, releasing “What Starts, Ends” in 1992 and “Room 101” in 1995, while McCoy formed Nefilim, whose only album “Zoon” appeared in 1996. McCoy and Pettitt announced a reunion at the Zillo Festival in Germany on 15 August 1998. Jungle Records issued the single “One More Nightmare (Trees Come Down)” in May 2000 and, in October 2002, the album “Fallen”, compiled from 1997 to 2001 recordings and disowned by the band as unauthorised. “Mourning Sun”, the first new Fields of the Nephilim studio album since “Elizium”, came out on 28 November 2005. A new line-up returned to the stage at the London Astoria in May 2007 and headlined M’era Luna in 2008. The double live album “Ceromonies (Ad Mortem Ad Vitam)”, recorded at Shepherd’s Bush Empire, appeared on McCoy’s Sacred Symphony label in April 2012, and the single “Prophecy” followed on 17 March 2016. Guitarist Tom Edwards, a member from 2008 to 2016, died in January 2017, as Side-Line reported in Fields of the Nephilim / Adam Ant guitarist Tom Edwards dies aged 41. Beggars Arkive has since reissued the Situation Two and Beggars Banquet catalogue: the 30th anniversary “Elizium” in December 2020, an expanded “The Nephilim” in October 2023, the four-track expanded “Elizium” in April 2024 and a remastered “Dawnrazor” in December 2025. McCoy and Pettitt lead the current line-up with guitarists Gavin King and Adam Leach. Thirty-six years after its release, “Elizium” closes the first chapter of that catalogue, the final album of the original five-piece before “Earth Inferno” documented its last shows.

items.body: Tanner McGraw sings and John Beckmann stays off the microphone on “Nothing Is Missing”, the third single from Utopia PKWY, out on 25 September 2026 with a video. Utopia PKWY is the new project of Beckmann, the New York songwriter and producer behind The Mortal Prophets, and the single precedes the project’s first album, “Debut”, due on 6 November 2026. Beckmann wrote and produced the track alone; McGraw takes the lead vocal and Lawson Mars adds backing vocals. Utopia PKWY mix post-pop hooks with synth-wave-tinged psychedelia, and bring keyboards, theremins and sitars into the arrangements. The single follows “I Knew You Would Be Trouble”, released on 3 July 2026, and “Sleep In Moving Colors”, released on 14 August 2026, both with official videos on the project’s YouTube channel. The “Nothing Is Missing” video was not yet public at the time of writing, so the player below carries the second single, whose video upload is titled “I Sleep In Moving Colors”. Beckmann described the new song as “Less a song than a philosophical hallucination, more like a midnight transmission from the far side of grief – where loss doesn’t disappear, it simply changes frequency and keeps humming beneath the skin.” The project takes its name from Utopia Parkway in Queens, the street where the Surrealist artist Joseph Cornell lived and worked. Beckmann calls McGraw and Mars, his two younger collaborators, the “kids in the neighborhood”. Both singers already appeared on the two most recent psychedelic dream-pop albums by The Mortal Prophets, and Utopia PKWY moves that line-up into brighter, more melodic songs. ‘Debut’ tracklist and release dates “Debut” runs to ten tracks: “I Knew You Were Trouble”, “Sleep In Moving Colors”, “Nothing Is Missing”, “If I Could Steal One More Kiss”, “You Talk Like Every Feeling”, “What Disappears”, “Come In Waves”, “Glitter And Doom”, “Fall Into You” and “Dreaming I’m A Rock Star”. The tracklist spells the opener “I Knew You Were Trouble”, while the single and its video carry the title “I Knew You Would Be Trouble”. The closing title also appears on The Mortal Prophets’ July 2026 album “Ain’t No Fool”. The earlier Utopia PKWY singles are on Spotify and Apple Music; the album page on the official site lists the release dates for all three singles and the album. About Utopia PKWY Utopia PKWY is the 2026 side project of John Beckmann, a New York singer, songwriter, producer and visual artist who has recorded as The Mortal Prophets since 2022. That project opened with the EP “Stomp The Devil” on 8 July 2022 and the album “Me And The Devil” on 9 December 2022, both built on reworked blues standards. “Dealey Plaza Blues” followed on 28 July 2023, the ambient guitar album “Guitarworks” on 22 December 2023, the EP “Sleeping In My Bed” on 15 March 2024, the opera “Hanussen: The Enigmatic Clairvoyant” on 15 April 2024, the EP “ICNCLST/” on 20 August 2024 and “Laurel Canyon – Lost Sessions (1966-69)” on 29 November 2024. In 2025 came “Ghost Land” (17 January), “French Summer” (16 May), “Guitarworks II” (28 July) and the covers EP “Under The Influence” (5 December). The move toward dream-pop and psychedelia began with “Hide Inside The Moon”, released on 2 January 2026, the first Mortal Prophets record with Tanner McGraw on lead vocals. “Not Here, Not There” followed on 3 April 2026 with McGraw and Lawson Mars sharing the vocals over synth-wave keyboards, theremins and sitars, and “Ain’t No Fool”, with Jake Burden on vocals, arrived on 3 July 2026. On the same day Beckmann launched Utopia PKWY with “I Knew You Would Be Trouble”, again with McGraw and Mars singing, and released “Sleep In Moving Colors” on 14 August 2026. “Nothing Is Missing” on 25 September 2026 is the last single before “Debut” on 6 November 2026.

Uboa’s ‘Meltdown’ performance from Roadburn 2024 Roadburn commissioned Uboa to write two original works for its 2024 fes
items.body: Uboa releases the live album “Every Reactor Four a Friend (Live at Roadburn 2024)” through The Flenser on 22 September 2026, with a vinyl edition to follow as part of the label’s Membership Series 8 Exclusive. The three-track release is a recording of “Meltdown,” a piece Roadburn commissioned Uboa to compose for its 2024 edition. Uboa’s ‘Meltdown’ performance from Roadburn 2024 Roadburn commissioned Uboa to write two original works for its 2024 festival: “Calm Down,” a quieter piece, and its counterpart “Meltdown,” performed alongside TOomD’s “Shut Down.” “Every Reactor Four a Friend” is the live recording of “Meltdown,” captured from the mixing desk at Roadburn and later remixed and reworked, since some onboard vocal effects and microphones were missing from the available stems. The title refers to Reactor Four at Chernobyl, the reactor that melted down in the 1986 disaster. Musically, the release leans on power electronics and cut-up harsh noise, closer to the extremity of Uboa’s 2018 album “The Sky May Be” than the more intricate construction of her recent records. Uboa described the themes behind the performance directly: “It’s about embracing the overwhelm rather than shaming oneself for it. All the shame, anger and overwhelm was put in this short performance.” She added: “Sometimes it’s fine to just crash the fuck out. Sometimes it is necessary.” The album runs three tracks: “Dys,” “Do Not Comply In Advance” and “Ascension Threshold.” Every Reactor Four a Friend (Live at Roadburn 2024) by Uboa The Flenser also published a full-album stream of the performance: All Bandcamp proceeds from “Every Reactor Four a Friend” go toward covering Xandra’s gender-affirming surgery costs through 21 October 2026. About Uboa Uboa is a solo power electronics and noise project active since 2010, based in Melbourne, Australia. Early releases “Sometimes Light” (2010) and “Jouissance” (2013) were self-released before the 2018 album “The Sky May Be” arrived on the Australian label Art As Catharsis. “The Origin of My Depression” followed in 2019, initially self-released before The Flenser reissued it on vinyl after Uboa signed to the San Francisco label in February 2023. The Flenser then released the 2024 studio album “The Great Impossible Light,” featuring contributions from Blood of a Pomegranate, Otay:Onii, Charlie Looker and Haela Hunt-Hendrix of Liturgy. Uboa performed three sets at Roadburn Festival in Tilburg, Netherlands, in April 2024, including the live debut of “The Origin of My Depression” performed in full alongside the commissioned pieces “Calm Down” and “Meltdown.” “Every Reactor Four a Friend (Live at Roadburn 2024)” is the recording of that “Meltdown” performance, released through The Flenser two years on.

Peaceful In Daylight Spelling Misery Unsafe State Merchants Of The Wave The record pairs electronic textures with serrated guitar work, running through recurring images of water, predatory animals and religious dread across its ten songs. CD and LP copies can be ordered directly through Bat-Cave Productions, with a download code included. About Gossip Collar Gossip Collar formed in Boston in the dark basement scene at the tail end of the pandemic, bringing together members previously involved with The Showcase Showdown, Spitzz and Secret Hearts. The band’s lineup is Victoria on vocals and guitar, Tom on guitar, Mark on bass and Megan on drums. Gossip Collar released a self-titled debut album on April 7, 2023, followed by spinning silk for parasites on October 31, 2024. Eaten of Worms, out September 4, 2026 via Bat-Cave Productions, is the band’s third album. items.body: Berlin-based darkwave act Night Nail has released “Vile Train”, a gothic rock single that previews the band’s fourth studio album, Infinite Fountain, due November 6, 2026 through Icy Cold Records. The song arrives with an official video directed and edited by Jean De Oliviera. ‘Vile Train’ single details “Vile Train” was mixed and post-produced by William Faith at 13 Studio in Chicago, with co-production by Night Nail in Berlin and additional vocals and guitar from VV & the Void. Frontman Brandon Robert said the track drew its initial inspiration from a visit to Pompeii, where a fresco depicting an angel and a demon in an embrace suggested “dark and brutal truths about love sung in a twisted but beautiful way.” The video reunites the band with director Jean De Oliviera, whose previous work with Night Nail includes “Hollow Day,” “Little Armenia” and “Narcoleptic Dream Catcher.” Shot in black and white, it cuts between Robert and bassist Ilija Gavrilenko performing among amplifiers and outdoor scenes set among stone arches and fountain basins. A full tracklist for Infinite Fountain has not been announced. The album also includes mixing and post-production work by Sven Wolff of Patenbrigade: Wolff. Night Nail plans to support the release with shows across the US, UK and Europe during 2026 and 2027. About Night Nail Night Nail formed in Los Angeles in 2013 and relocated to Berlin in 2018, the same year the band’s debut album, LA Demons, appeared on Cleopatra Records. March To Autumn followed in 2020 through Cold Transmission, and Fates Explained arrived on Metropolis Records in 2023, mixed and mastered by Pete Burns of Kill Shelter; Side-Line covered the single “Fates Explained” at the time. The band followed with the archival release Early Demons and Demos and the remix album Fates Remade in 2024, after earlier singles including “Narcoleptic Dream Catcher” and “Cracks In My Heart”, the latter featuring Luna De La Torre on vocals. Night Nail’s catalogue connects darkwave electronics with gothic rock’s appetite for emotional extremes, a combination built up over four albums and multiple labels since the band’s Los Angeles beginnings. “Vile Train” and the forthcoming Infinite Fountain, out on Icy Cold Records, mark the band’s next chapter and its first full-length since 2023’s Fates Explained. Follow Night Nail: – Bandcamp – Spotify – Website

items.body: IAMX, the solo project of Chris Corner, is running a silent auction of two stage-used items from the 2026 “Recollections” tour: a bass guitar played on stage by touring bassist Gözde Düzer and a rhinestone-covered mask worn by Corner during live shows. Both auctions close on 27 September 2026 at midnight CEST, while the tour is mid-way through a run of Scandinavian dates. The bass guitar was played on stage by Gözde Düzer, who tours as IAMX’s bassist and also records as Aux Animaux. It is signed by both Düzer and Corner and comes in a hand-stencilled hard case made for the tour. The second item is a handmade mask Corner wore onstage throughout the “Recollections” shows, covered in rhinestones with black fur ears and gold detailing. Both listings are running through the band’s official shop and close at midnight CEST on 27 September 2026. IAMX tour dates for 2026 and 2027 23 September 2026 – Oslo, Norway – John Dee 24 September 2026 – Malmö, Sweden – Plan B 25 September 2026 – Helsinki, Finland – On The Rocks, with Aux Animaux 13 November 2026 – Santiago, Chile – Santiago Gothic Treffen 14 November 2026 – São Paulo, Brazil – Madame Club 24-25 July 2027 – Cologne, Germany – Amphi Festival 31 July – 1 August 2027 – Thale, Germany – Unter dem Himmel About IAMX IAMX is the solo project of British musician Chris Corner, who co-founded the trip-hop group Sneaker Pimps in Hartlepool in 1994. After a fourth Sneaker Pimps album went unreleased, Corner kept the songs, moved to London and released them as the debut album “Kiss + Swallow” in 2004. Later albums include “The Alternative” (2006), “Kingdom of Welcome Addiction” (2009), “Volatile Times” (2011), “The Unified Field” (2013), “Metanoia” (2015), “Unfall” (2017), “Alive In New Light” (2018), the acoustic rework album “Echo Echo” (2020) and “Machinate” (2021), followed by “Fault Lines¹” (2023) and “Fault Lines²” (2024). IAMX opened 2026 with the single “Artificial Innocence” ahead of a European tour, and Corner discussed his songwriting approach in a Side-Line interview in May. Gözde Düzer, who tours with the band on bass and theremin and records on her own as Aux Animaux from Stockholm, spoke to Side-Line in March about joining the IAMX live band and touring with Chris Corner. The “Recollections” tour has since carried the band through Scandinavia this week, with dates in Chile and Brazil to follow in November and festival shows at Amphi Festival and Unter dem Himmel booked for the summer of 2027. This week’s silent auction of stage props from the tour runs alongside that live schedule.

items.body: Depeche Mode, the English electronic band from Basildon, Essex, released “Some Great Reward” on 24 September 1984 through Mute Records. The album turns 42 this year. It was the band’s fourth studio album, and it reached number 5 on the UK Albums Chart and number 3 in West Germany. Most of the record was made in West Berlin. Sessions began at London’s Music Works studio and moved to Hansa Mischraum, where the band also mixed the album. Daniel Miller produced it with Depeche Mode and Gareth Jones, who had engineered the previous record and was promoted to co-producer here. The band carried over the sampling approach it had started on Depeche Mode’s ‘Construction Time Again’, building rhythms from struck metal and concrete rather than drum machines alone. Martin Gore wrote eight of the nine songs; Alan Wilder contributed “If You Want”, the last song he wrote for a Depeche Mode album. Dave Gahan sang lead throughout, with Gore taking the vocal on “Somebody”, recorded live with Wilder on piano. The nine-track album runs “Something to Do”, “Lie to Me”, “People Are People”, “It Doesn’t Matter”, “Stories of Old”, “Somebody”, “Master and Servant”, “If You Want” and “Blasphemous Rumours”. Mute had issued “People Are People” as the lead single on 12 March 1984, six months ahead of the album, followed by “Master and Servant” on 20 August 1984 and the “Blasphemous Rumours” / “Somebody” double A-side on 29 October 1984. Both later singles drew objections over their sexual and religious subject matter, and some radio stations declined to play “Master and Servant”. Brian Griffin photographed the sleeve at Round Oak Steelworks near Stourbridge, continuing the industrial imagery he and designer Martin Atkyns had used on the previous cover. The album title is a line from “Lie to Me”. The Some Great Reward Tour opened three days after release and ran to the end of July 1985, taking the band through the UK, Europe, North America and two shows behind the Iron Curtain, in Budapest on 23 July and Warsaw on 30 July 1985. The 14 December 1984 concert in Hamburg was filmed and issued as the band’s first live video, “The World We Live In and Live in Hamburg”. About Depeche Mode Vince Clarke, Martin Gore, Dave Gahan and Andy Fletcher formed Depeche Mode in Basildon, Essex, in 1980, taking their name from a French fashion magazine. The band signed to Daniel Miller’s independent label Mute Records and released the synth-pop debut “Speak & Spell” in 1981. Clarke left after that album to form Yazoo with Alison Moyet, and Gore became the band’s main songwriter. Depeche Mode continued as a trio for “A Broken Frame” (1982), then expanded to a four-piece when Alan Wilder joined for “Construction Time Again” (1983), the album that brought sampled industrial sounds and Gareth Jones into the band’s productions. “Some Great Reward” extended that partnership and gave the band its first US chart single, “People Are People”, which reached number 13 on the Billboard Hot 100 in 1985 after a delayed run there. Mute followed the album with the compilation “The Singles 81>85” in October 1985, then “Black Celebration” (1986), “Music for the Masses” (1987) and “Violator” (1990), which produced “Personal Jesus” and “Enjoy the Silence”. Wilder left in 1995 after “Songs of Faith and Devotion” (1993), and the remaining trio released “Ultra” (1997), “Exciter” (2001), “Playing the Angel” (2005), “Sounds of the Universe” (2009), “Delta Machine” (2013) and “Spirit” (2017). Fletcher died in May 2022. Gahan and Gore released “Memento Mori” as a duo in 2023 and toured behind it, documenting the Mexico City dates in the concert film “M”. Forty-two years on, “Some Great Reward” remains the point at which the Berlin sessions, the sampling and the leather-and-steel visual language settled into the form the band carried through the rest of the decade.

items.body: With Hor-Cheret, we welcome a new project presented as a collaboration between members of Vortex, Nam-Khar, and Delta Komplex, complemented by a few more artists. The project’s name alludes to Horus, the child of Isis and Osiris in Egyptian mythology. With an album title referring to an ancient nomadic law of hospitality, Hor-Cheret offers an intriguing metaphor and, in my view, a critical perspective on today’s world. It certainly offers food for thought, but above all, this is music to be discovered. From the very first notes, a distinct Ritual influence emerges through the percussion and the use of traditional acoustic instruments. While the percussion reinforces the album’s ritualistic character, the listener gradually discovers a dark atmosphere shaped by deep sound waves. Elements of Dark-Ambient and Industrial music are clearly present. An Ethereal female voice occasionally takes on a narrative role while simultaneously enhancing the sense of mysticism. The male voice also serves a narrative function, while some of the lyrics possess a distinctly poetic quality. This is a superbly crafted album in a genre that suffers from a lack of quality projects and inconsistent production standards. Hor-Cheret’s debut is a release to be savored and cherished. (Rating:8½). Listen to “In The Shadow Ov Power”: In The Shadow Ov Power by HOR-CHERET About Hor-Cheret Hor-Cheret is a new collaborative project pairing members of Vortex, Nam-Khar and Delta Komplex with additional contributors, presented on Dunkelheit Produktionen. Its name references Horus, the child of Isis and Osiris in Egyptian mythology. Nam-Khar is the ritual ambient project of Romanian musician Konchog Gyaltsen, active since 2009, previously paired with Vortex on “Nag-Hammadi” in 2022 and “The Sarajevo Spiral” in 2024. Delta Komplex is a German electronic band founded in 2019 around Minu-Schirin Samimi and Tufana, known for the 2022 album “Veils”. “Nanawatai”, Hor-Cheret’s debut album, was released on 7 November 2025 in a limited handnumbered digipak edition.

items.body: Two pizzas, a boombox, and a demo CD-R were enough to keep Michael Mayer and Wolfgang Voigt out all night. In Mayer’s recollection, their first encounter with the music of young Regensburg producer Markus Guentner began in a Cologne park. The listening session continued as they wandered through the city, playing the same three tracks over and over. Something in those recordings had altered the evening sufficiently that neither man wanted to switch them off. “We knew that we had found something outrageously beautiful and we wanted the whole world to listen,” Mayer recalls. A quarter-century later, that encounter offers a useful way into In Moll. Music associated with introspection and solitude first won over two of its most consequential listeners in the open air, among streets and other people. It could change the character of a place, and the quality of the time spent there. As the album’s 25th anniversary is celebrated this September, those possibilities remain central to its appeal. Its return through Rafael Anton Irisarri’s Black Knoll Editions on November 6, 2026 also brings a substantial restoration: the complete album will finally be available on vinyl, including the previously omitted “In Moll 4.” The photographs from around the album’s creation bring its history back to an everyday scale. There are headphones around Guentner’s neck, rows of mixer controls, a Technics T-shirt, and him as a young man sitting on a sofa with his arms folded. They place a face and familiar surroundings beside music often discussed in terms of vastness. Guentner was about twenty when In Moll appeared. Its compositional assurance can make that easy to forget. Markus Guentner around the time of In Moll’s original release. His Regensburg EP had appeared on Kompakt in 2000. “Regensburg 1” and “Pilot” followed on the inaugural Pop Ambient 2001 compilation, alongside music by Dettinger, Ulf Lohmann, Joachim Spieth, and others. The series gave a name and a shared home to an area of experimentation within the label’s wider electronic community. Melody could remain immediate even as the familiar structures of a song dissolved; repetition could carry an emotional charge without being organized around a dancefloor payoff. Kompakt’s account of Pop Ambient emphasizes pop as an attitude, connected to subculture and Pop Art. That distinction helps recover the uncertainty and excitement of the early records. Producers were investigating what happened when the machinery of club music was allowed to move at another pace. A phrase might expand until its texture became as absorbing as its tune. Bass could give weight to an otherwise suspended passage. The space surrounding a sound became part of the composition. In Moll belongs to the cultural interval those experiments opened up. In the chillout and comedown era, electronic music had acquired a life in the hours surrounding the club: the quiet room, the trip home, the morning when exhilaration gave way to more complicated feelings. Dub minimalism’s treatment of bass and empty space met a distinctly post-industrial sadness. Guentner gave that meeting an unusually intimate form, allowing warmth and unease to occupy the same stretch of music. Wolfgang Voigt’s GAS was an obvious contemporary reference point, with its dense textures and softened rhythmic presence. Guentner developed a more private expression within related territory. In his April 2002 review for Pitchfork, Mark Richardson recognized the connection while drawing attention to the album’s industrial unease and enclosed spaces. That early response is useful now: the music’s beauty has always accommodated discomfort. Its emotional proximity to post-punk is easy to understand. Solitude, urban stillness, and longing held under restraint have sustained entire bodies of work in that tradition. In Moll, whose title translates as “in minor,” gives those feelings an electronic form. The low frequencies suggest weight and distance; small melodic details offer something close enough to hold. Melancholy becomes a relationship between the individual and the space around them. You can imagine the deserted street as readily as the room overlooking it. That relationship gives the ten-minute “In Moll 3” particular significance. The album’s most popular track, selected as the anniversary edition’s second single, is an especially apt introduction to its darker emotional register. Its heavy synthesizer layers and deep echo give it a substantial, almost architectural presence. Within that scale, the melodic pull remains personal. The tension between those qualities helps explain how a piece of such duration can become the record listeners return to most readily. Ten minutes also allows a different kind of encounter with a piece of music. A feeling can occupy the foreground, recede, and become apparent again as attention shifts. For listeners drawn to coldwave’s inward concentration or dream pop’s prolonged emotional suspension, “In Moll 3” offers a natural point of entry. Its place at the centre of this anniversary campaign makes sense: it gives newcomers enough time to discover the album’s proportions, and returning listeners a reason to settle into them again. Watch the visualizer for “In Moll 3,” with music and video by Markus Guentner, below: Born in Regensburg, Germany, in 1981, Markus Guentner discovered electronic music at thirteen and secured his first weekly DJ residency while still a teenager. His listening extended across shoegaze, dream pop, indie rock, pop, ambient, and techno, giving him an appreciation for both the directness of a melody and the expressive possibilities of texture. Those interests informed a musical life rooted in his hometown, where he later co-founded the SUBLIME collective in 2006. The connection to the broader post-punk family also has a concrete history. In 2005, Guentner worked with 4AD founder Ivo Watts-Russell on The Hope Blister’s Underarms and Sideways, supplying the reworkings that formed its second disc. His version of Talk Talk’s “Such a Shame,” featuring Dana Grey, had meanwhile carried his affection for pop into a club setting through Ware Records. These projects reflect a musician whose interests could move naturally between a song’s emotional clarity and the possibilities of abstraction. Across releases for Kompakt, Ware, Warner, Sending Orbs, and Affin, Guentner has continued to move between minimal techno, beatless composition, and extended drone. Collaborations with Rafael Anton Irisarri, Julia Kent, Brock Van Wey (bvdub), Joachim Spieth, and zakè have brought other approaches into contact with his own, sustaining an exchange between musicians whose work shares an interest in depth and duration. His association with A Strangely Isolated Place began in 2012 with Talking Clouds, released through the label’s Places Series. Theia followed in 2015, beginning the loosely connected trio of albums completed by Empire and Extropy. These records gave his bass drones and slow melodic developments a larger, cosmic setting. In 2024, Kontrapunkt brought eight collaborations together, with contributors including Arovane, Abul Mogard, Benoît Pioulard, Karen Vogt, and Hollie Kenniff. Guentner’s work also extends into graphic design and cinema. His longstanding partnership with Joachim Spieth includes shaping Affin’s visual identity, while his music has featured in Drake Doremus’ Equals. That attention to the relationship between sound and image continues in the new visual presentation he has designed for In Moll. For Irisarri, the influence of In Moll reaches directly into his own beginnings. He first heard the album shortly after its 2001 release, while still discovering what he wanted to express through electronic music. “Markus showed me entirely new possibilities for what electronic music could communicate,” he recalls. His assessment of its importance to his project The Sight Below is unequivocal: “The Sight Below would not have existed without IN MOLL paving the way.” Brock Van Wey, better known as bvdub, remembers a similarly personal recognition. In his anniversary recollection, he describes hearing an unfamiliar producer articulate feelings he was struggling with far away: “it was as if that album was made to comfort me.” Their eventual friendship brought the additional pleasure of finding kindness in a musician he had admired for years. Such accounts give the word “influence” some substance. A record helped someone feel understood; that listener went on to make music of his own. Irisarri’s stewardship of the anniversary edition gives that history a particularly satisfying continuation. An artist whose possibilities were expanded by In Moll has now undertaken its new analogue remaster. The restoration of “In Moll 4” corrects a long-standing difference between the original formats: the piece was included on CD, while the vinyl edition left it out. Its first appearance on vinyl restores the seven-part sequence to the format, preserving the full span of the work. For an album so dependent on the relationship between duration, density, and release, completeness has an artistic value as well as an archival one. Guentner has also designed a new visual presentation for the edition, extending his involvement beyond the recordings themselves. The album returns with the care of its maker and of a musician it helped inspire. Richardson, looking back in the accompanying press materials, calls it “one of the finest ambient releases of the 00’s.” The strongest argument for that assessment lies in how readily the record can still enter the present. Heard in 2026, its patient pacing and emotional economy feel entirely current. Contemporary interest in slow music and environmental listening gives fresh context to choices Guentner was making twenty-five years ago. He understood how a recording could become part of a room while retaining its own complicated emotional life. In that sense, the world has gradually caught up with In Moll: more listeners have found reasons to seek the concentration and depth it has offered all along. That brings us back to Mayer and Voigt carrying a young producer’s music through Cologne. The circumstances belong to another time; the discovery remains available. Put on In Moll, give it an hour, and notice what happens to the room. In Moll (25th Anniversary Edition) is due November 6, 2026, through Black Knoll Editions (BKE025), with digital and black or white double-vinyl editions available to pre-order. Bandcamp currently lists December shipping estimates for the vinyl. “In Moll 4,” the first single, is available now. Listen below and pre-order the anniversary edition here. items.body: Infrarosso Se mi guardi, cambio forma Come fuoco nell’oscurità Infrarosso Barcelona-based duo VILLANELLE have figured out something plenty of club records forget while staring lovingly at their own machinery: rhythm gets interesting when there is a body inside it. Infrarosso, the debut single from Jessica Bellomo and Carmilla Sioux, runs on that friction. Synthesizers press forward with clean, metallic authority, the bassline prowls beneath them, and the beat keeps tightening the room until Bellomo’s voice becomes another pressure point in the arrangement. Their shared connection to rock and darker electronic music comes through two distinct histories. Bellomo is an Italo-Argentine interdisciplinary artist whose production, DJ sets, and live work span dark disco, electro, breakbeats, EBM, techno, and trance. Sioux began as a bassist in the post-punk scene before moving into electronic music as a DJ and producer, founding From Hell To Disco in 2024. VILLANELLE gives those experiences a shared form, bringing their understanding of club music into close contact with songwriting, visual presentation, and the possibilities of performing together. The writing of Infrarosso began with the instruments. Sioux developed the foundations of the bassline, and Bellomo built layers of synthesizers around it. The music took shape before the words, giving the duo a structure against which to test melodies, vocal rhythms, and different languages. That sequence helps explain the close relationship between the arrangement and the singing: the voice developed through a conversation with sounds already in motion. Traces of Pet Shop Boys appear in the chilly economy, Ladytron in the clipped sensuality, and Boy Harsher in how desire folds into sensual repetition. VILLANELLE draws from their influences without turning the song into a résumé. The bassline has enough shape to carry the track by itself, but the synth layers keep introducing new angles, giving the arrangement a strange sense of forward motion even when repetition becomes the hook. Analog warmth and digital precision meet in a track that keeps its emotional temperature unsettled. Italian gradually became the natural language for the song. Friends independently imagined the instrumental with Italian vocals, reinforcing a direction the duo were already discovering through experimentation. Its musicality, warmth, and sensual undertone suited the track’s character. As Bellomo worked through melodies, spoken-word phrases, rhythm, and rhyme, the provisional title Infrared became Infrarosso. The choice took shape in the act of singing, with the sound of the words helping determine what the song would become. Infrared suggests a presence beyond ordinary sight, something registered through heat when appearances offer little guidance. The opening line, “Se mi guardi, cambio forma”—“If you look at me, I change shape”—adds another complication: being seen can change us. Read as a statement about intimacy, it suggests the strange adjustments people make under another person’s attention, when attraction and exposure become difficult to separate. The title offers a way to sense what remains beneath those changing surfaces. The phrase Sotto la pelle, “under the skin,” became central to the duo’s conception of the track. Bellomo circles a few elemental ideas—heat, skin, darkness, disappearance—and treats language as percussion, stretching words across the beat until meaning and sensation start leaning into each other. The lyrics ask what survives between two people when the world loses light and only sensation remains. There is romance in that image, though VILLANELLE leaves enough tension in the track to imbue that romance with a bit of salt rather than sugar-sweetness. This approach also reflects the poetic dimension behind the project’s name. For Bellomo and Sioux, words participate in the rhythm and atmosphere of a composition, with repetition giving a phrase room to change emphasis. On Infrarosso, the voice works almost as another instrument, adding movement while preserving space for an emotional response. The lyric’s economy allows small shifts in delivery to carry considerable weight; the same words can feel inviting or uncertain depending on how they sit against the beat. Nicole Krämer’s video extends the same fascination with body and machine through darkness, movement, and controlled physicality. It belongs to the broader visual language VILLANELLE are developing around the music, where nocturnal elegance and bodily presence reinforce the tension within the songs. The imagery suits a track built around pressure and restraint, where sensuality comes from withholding as much as release. Read alongside the opening lyric, the camera introduces a further layer to that exchange. A song about changing under another person’s gaze becomes a performance offered to the viewer’s attention. Movement gives the rhythm a visible form, while the words continue to point toward something that cannot be understood through appearance alone. The relationship between music and image grows from that shared concern with what a body reveals and what it keeps private. Watch the official video for Infrarosso below: Live performance has helped the duo understand how these ideas reach an audience. They describe their debut at Stella Nomine as an early lesson in how strongly people could connect with the material while hearing the songs for the first time. Repetition offered listeners a point of entry, while the duo’s physical stage presence and visual interaction added another means of communication. In their account, the response in the room helped clarify what VILLANELLE could become. That experience makes the stage an essential part of the project’s development. A repeated phrase can establish familiarity within an unfamiliar song; a gesture or an exchange between performers can give its tension a visible expression. For music so concerned with perception and proximity, a live setting brings those ideas into a shared space. The audience encounters the people responsible for the sounds, and the performers discover how those sounds affect others. Released September 10, 2026, Infrarosso introduces a duo already thinking beyond one song. An album is planned for spring 2027, with further exploration of the relationship between voice, instruments, electronic production, and the body. Their debut establishes the terms with considerable assurance: post-punk’s rawness, Italo’s melodic appeal, and electronic music’s physical force all have a place in the conversation. The duo describes the intention behind Infrarosso as “music intended to be felt — somewhere beneath the skin.” Across the recording, the video, and their account of performing live, that idea takes a concrete form. A bassline becomes a framework for synthesizers; a voice finds its language inside their patterns; movement carries the song into view. By the time an audience answers, the private sensation has become something people can share. Listen to Infrarosso below and order the single, out now via From Hell To Disco, here. items.body: You said we’d never change You said we’d never fall I held on to every word I believed it all Forever is an ambitious promise to make on behalf of two people who are still changing. Romance encourages this sort of confidence, giving even the most cautious among us the vocabulary of someone who has personally inspected the future. When the relationship ends, those assurances acquire a different meaning, and the person who believed them has to wonder how much of the deception they helped along. Leipzig’s Kalte Steine turns that uncomfortable recognition into the cool, deceptively buoyant synthpop of “Love Is A Lie.” Following the social suffocation explored in “Drowning,” the single brings the question of dishonesty into a more intimate setting, where two people discover that sincerity offers little protection against making promises they cannot keep. A breathy exclamation hangs in reverb as the title refrain begins, with cool synthesizer tones underneath. Bubbly figures and bell-like notes soon brighten the arrangement, joined by a danceable drum-machine beat whose straightforward momentum gives the song its immediate pop appeal. There is an easy catchiness to these parts, each phrase leaving enough room for the next to register. The declaration that love is a lie becomes remarkably easy to sing along with. Buzzing synths and guitar tones gather beneath the first verse, while a brief metallic ripple of programmed percussion adds a small disturbance to the steady beat. The vocal sits high in the register, smooth and quietly sorrowful, carrying disappointment through its tone as much as its words. Deep bass strumming adds weight below, grounding the brighter electronics in the song’s private reckoning. The arrangement keeps moving even as the singer returns to assurances that have become difficult to hear. Initially, the lyrics give that disappointment a familiar address: “You said we’d never change / You said we’d never fall.” Every promise belongs to someone else, and the singer occupies the apparently straightforward position of having trusted the wrong person. The repeated title sounds conclusive enough to close the case. Yet the second verse quietly changes the pronouns: “I said we’d never change / I said we’d never fall.” The same words now come from the person who has been condemning them, making the earlier accusation considerably harder to sustain. “I promised you forever / Like it could be true / Oh I believed it too” supplies the song’s most revealing admission. Both people have mistaken the intensity of a feeling for evidence that it will last. Desire makes the promise persuasive to the person speaking as well as the person listening, complicating the chorus’s sweeping verdict. Through the repeated “Promises,” the post-chorus keeps returning to that shared vocabulary, setting “Words of love / Hearts on fire” beside “A web of lies / Built on desire.” What once sounded reassuring has become a reminder of how willingly both participated. When the chorus returns, melodic guitar figures add detail without crowding the hook, their economical phrasing intricate enough to reward attention and direct enough to stick. A laser-like synth accent introduces a little electronic whimsy, suggesting the beginnings of acceptance within the song’s disappointment. That small, almost playful touch suits a lyric that has gradually surrendered its claim to innocence. By the end, “Love Is A Lie” sounds like something the singer is still trying to believe, perhaps because admitting that the love was real and the promises failed is harder. Listen to Love Is A Lie on Spotify below: Love Is A Lie continues the English-language direction heard on “Crying Out” and “Drowning,” extending a catalogue that also includes “Shattered,” “Dysthymia,” “Wüste aus Beton,” and “Kinder der Nacht.” As explored in our earlier feature on Kalte Steine, the project has moved between personal fracture, urban alienation, and nocturnal escape. Here, its attention settles on the distance between what lovers mean and what they can reasonably promise. items.body: I’ll always wait for you The promise that someone will wait forever has enjoyed an excellent reputation in love songs, considering how uncomfortable it can become outside them. Patience can deepen into devotion, but it can also give obsession an alibi, allowing someone to call an inability to let go proof of a superior kind of love. London trio Black Doldrums explore that uneasy territory on Waiting, a song whose tenderness comes with the unnerving suggestion that nobody has agreed on when the waiting should come to an end. The third single from Repetition Compulsion, due November 13th, 2026, via Fuzz Club, carries a particular connection to the band’s previous album. Written around the same time as In Limerence, it extends that record’s preoccupation with longing and romantic fixation into a love song that sounds both consoling and quietly bereft. Its accompanying video takes those feelings out into the city, where a solitary attachment becomes an increasingly threatening pursuit. A deep, humming bass and the heavy thud of drums establish the song’s measured pace, while a cool, jangling guitar melody moves between high, glassy notes and lower, mournful phrases. There is something of The Chameleons in the guitar’s arcing melodies, and of The Cure in the funereal weight beneath it. Sheets of icy synthesizer widen the space around the instruments, giving the opening a peculiar calm: everything sounds composed, even as the melody suggests that something has gone terribly wrong. When Kevin Gibbard begins singing, the synthesizers settle into warmer mid-range tones, bringing a little bodily comfort to that cold room. His voice carries some of Andrew Eldritch’s solemn authority in a slightly higher register, with an exposed ache that also recalls Ian Curtis. Beneath him, the guitar takes on an increasingly Cure-like character, its clear notes ringing against the low end. Then the chorus rises into “I’ll always wait for you,” stretching the promise into a lament. The guitar’s answering jangle supplies the small, involuntary chill, the sort that travels up an arm before the mind has decided whether the feeling is pleasure or dread. For all that unease, the song began in an ordinary moment of affection. Gibbard wrote the lyrics early one morning while waiting for Sophie Landers to wake up, with the themes of their second album still close at hand. “When we were going through the finished mixes of the second album, Sophie noticed this recurring theme of limerence, which pushed ‘Waiting’ further in that direction. I liked the idea of writing about waiting for someone you love, that if you love someone enough, you’ll wait forever. I wrote all the lyrics in one go, early one morning, while I was literally waiting for Sophie to wake up. I just started jotting it down.” Landers also supplied the idea behind one of the recording’s stranger details, asking for a sound that would suggest a spirit departing its body. Gibbard found his approximation through a Mellotron, voice synthesizers, and pitch bend: “Sophie wanted something that sounded like a soul leaving someone’s body. So I played around with a Mellotron and voice synths with pitch bend to create something similar. It seemed to fit nicely because it has this really haunting sound.” That imagined departure hangs over a song devoted to staying. The warmer synthesizers offer closeness, while the guitars and spectral vocal textures suggest distance, absence, and the possibility that a promise might outlast the person it was made to. There is considerable romance in Waiting, though very little reassurance that romance will make anyone happy. The video’s darker premise took shape during a recent viewing of Taxi Driver. Landers recognized connections between the film and the band’s interest in limerence, particularly its treatment of loneliness, idealization, mental distress, and destructive fixation. Black Doldrums developed those observations into a story about an isolated, obsessive man following a woman through the city, with his sense of control destined for a nasty correction. Gibbard and Landers occupy a nocturnal world of café booths, shuttered shopfronts, graffiti-covered brickwork, and stretches of nearly empty pavement. He sits alone with a cup, writes on a loose sheet of paper, and eats in a café; she walks through the streets in a black leather jacket, occasionally looking back. The editing brings their separate movements into an uncomfortable relationship, while red-lit close-ups of her eyes interrupt the greenish darkness outside. The ordinary business of getting through a night begins to feel charged with the possibility of being watched. As the distance between them closes, the action moves into a narrow pedestrian underpass, its fluorescent lights leaving little room for either figure to disappear. Landers walks ahead while Gibbard follows, until a look back changes the balance between pursuer and pursued. The closing image gives heartbreak an abruptly physical form, making the familiar business of giving someone your heart seem like an offer best considered carefully. Watch the video for Waiting below: Gibbard and Landers formed Black Doldrums in London, initially working as a duo built around guitar, drums, and vocals before expanding into a trio. Their 2022 debut Dead Awake and 2024 follow-up In Limerence, both released through Fuzz Club, brought their early interests in psychedelia, drone, and reverb into a more concentrated gothic post-punk form. Extensive UK and European touring followed, including arena dates supporting Archive and their own headline shows. Repetition Compulsion completes the band’s interconnected “State of Mind Trilogy,” exploring the emotional patterns people carry into relationships, memory, and self-understanding. Across eleven songs, the record expands those concerns into inherited behaviour, politics, and mental wellbeing. Waiting provides a particularly intimate connection between the trilogy’s final two chapters, holding affection and fixation close enough for their resemblance to become unsettling. The album arrives November 13th, 2026, on 180-gram neon-yellow vinyl limited to 350 hand-numbered copies, 180-gram ultra-clear vinyl, and CD. Pre-order the album here. Listen below and order via Bandcamp. items.album: Boston’s GOSSIP COLLAR Explore Faith, Fear, and the Frailty of Flesh on Gothic Post-Punk LP “Eaten of Worms”
items.excerpt: His curved neck bent right back to see the swan Dreading the four steps up and over to where we ran I reached the viewing point and I sit here watching and waiting But then sometimes life’s unkind Boston’s GOSSIP COLLAR makes post-punk as though somebody locked Ladytron in an abandoned theater with a deathrock band, a stack of Killing Joke records, several reels of damaged fairy-tale film, and instructions that nobody gets out until dawn.
