items.body: His curved neck bent right back to see the swan Dreading the four steps up and over to where we ran I reached the viewing point and I sit here watching and waiting But then sometimes life’s unkind Boston’s GOSSIP COLLAR makes post-punk as though somebody locked Ladytron in an abandoned theater with a deathrock band, a stack of Killing Joke records, several reels of damaged fairy-tale film, and instructions that nobody gets out until dawn. Somewhere behind the electronic throb and serrated guitar on their latest offering, the EATEN OF WORMS LP, there is also the emotional breadth of the Chameleons, a little Breeders crookedness, and that marvelous early-goth conviction on bass guitar. The band began with best friends playing and dancing in a dark Boston basement at the tail end of the pandemic, drawing together members of The Showcase Showdown, Spitzz, and Secret Hearts. They describe this incarnation as their “dark punk chapter,” which sounds about right, though “chapter” seems almost too civilized for music filled with drowning sailors, torn bodies, predatory birds, collapsing circuses, religious dread, and people standing beside freezing seas wondering precisely when existence developed such a personal vendetta. There are obvious ancestral spirits here: Xmal Deutschland, Parálisis Permanente, early Siouxsie and the Banshees, the strange congregation that gathered around the London Batcave when punk discovered it could wear theatrical makeup without surrendering its teeth. They sound less interested in reconstructing 1982 than in asking what happens when those old poisons get poured into present-day arteries. Their live pedigree adds another clue. GOSSIP COLLAR have shared stages with The March Violets, Pink Turns Blue, Rendez-Vous, Haunt Me, House of Harm, Fotocrime, and Sympathy Flowers, placing them comfortably among bands for whom darkness still needs rhythm, muscle, and enough propulsion to keep bodies moving even while the songs are busy describing spiritual ruin. Throughout the songs on EATEN OF WORMS, nature rarely provides comfort. Seas threaten to swallow people, birds wait for flesh, wolves pursue deer, plants cut skin, rain destroys, and the night contains forces that clearly have not received the memo about personal boundaries. GOSSIP COLLAR’s apocalyptic fairy tale grows out of this collision between childhood imagery and adult terror, where forests, animals, oceans, and old religious symbols have all turned slightly hostile. Edgar Froese once said, “There is no death, there is just a change of our cosmic address.” GOSSIP COLLAR sound perfectly capable of furnishing the house he moved into. Disguise My Heart opens with a saxophone-like drone, its low complaint quickly overtaken by a deep, quick-moving bassline and drums that strike with the urgent physical force of Joy Division’s Love Will Tear Us Apart. The guitars pick out a cold, melodic figure before heavier layers gather around it, giving the song a density that makes the vocal seem to travel from somewhere beyond the instruments. Witchy and windblown, the voice calls through the mix with a banshee’s sense of occasion, stretching the distance between the rhythm section’s forward charge and the solitary figure waiting beside the Northern Sea. Freezing water, aching eyes, and blood threatening to turn cold give emotional injury a bodily presence; the guitars seem to press against the skin as insistently as the memories. Even as the drums push onward, the song remains fixed on that desolate stretch of coastline. Heartbreak becomes architectural here: eventually you stop carrying it around and simply move into it. Scavengers follows with a sheet of cold guitar and an insistent bass throb, burying an unusually inviting melody several layers into the disturbance. When the arrangement briefly catches its breath, the bass leads the voice into view, exposing the sharp, declamatory cadence beneath its witchy inflections. There is an anarcho-punk edge to the delivery, a sense that these words are being hurled across a room even as the guitars make that room feel enormous. That force suits a song whose speaker lies broken, bleeding, and apparently available to whatever happens to be circling overhead. The hook keeps drawing the ear back through the commotion while memories collect like personal debris beside the body. Death may happen quickly, destruction takes its time, and the promise of resurrection supplies a final complication. Apparently even carrion birds are going to have to wait their turn. A brief arc of distortion introduces Big Top Comes Crashing Down, followed by a jagged guitar figure that rings with the blunt insistence of a tolling bell. Once the drums and bass hit, the riff acquires a crooked melodic momentum, turning its initial severity into something almost indecently catchy. Above it, the vocal echoes with a thunderous breadth, making the performance feel much larger than the cramped emotional circumstances it describes. White greasepaint goes on, the smile gets rehearsed again, and another day disappears beneath the effort of remaining presentable. That circling guitar figure becomes an apt accompaniment to the work of doing it all again tomorrow. The image of someone maintaining the same expression for ten years on Exmouth Street carries the ugly comedy of a photograph that has outlived everybody’s patience. Keep smiling hard enough and sooner or later your face becomes part of the prison. Haerisis gives the bass room to announce itself, opening with a thick, deliberate strut locked to the drumbeat. Sustained guitar tones spread above that steady march, and the clearer placement of the vocal lets its chanting insistence register more directly. The arrangement has a substantial physical weight, with dense guitar chords and more melodic lines carrying on around a groove that remains easy to follow through all the theological panic. Blood, broken bones, forbidden chalices, frozen streams, wolves, and deer crowd the lyrics, turning belief into a landscape where almost everything can injure you. The sustained tones lend those images a sense of scale, while the rhythm section keeps their violence close enough to feel. There is something particularly effective about the orderly tread beneath all this religious dread: the song advances with the certainty of a procession whose destination nobody has thought to question. On Dead Thing, a heavy wash of guitar gives way to the splash and momentum of the drums, with the opening density settling into a firm support for the melody. Another weighty riff sweeps through the arrangement, while a persistent guitar drone keeps pressure on the spaces between its movements. The vocal sounds cavernous, its thunderous resonance making each phrase seem to return from the far end of a large, inhospitable room. Those overlapping guitar textures give the song’s fascination with self-destruction considerable force. Lions are led by their manes, weapons are made, and human ingenuity eventually discovers the convenience of turning its own inventions inward. Scars become evidence and shame becomes inheritance, yet the drums maintain enough movement to make the plea for dancing feel entirely plausible. Tenderness enters through the side door wearing funeral clothes, and the rhythm section has already made room for it. Why Me? begins with eerie chimes and a low drone, suggesting an old piano being played somewhere beyond the inhabited rooms of a house. A thick bass figure gradually establishes the song’s tension, recalling the stalking movement of the Cure’s A Forest with considerably more weight behind each step. The vocal holds its heat close, sounding troubled and intimate against the spacious opening. Around the halfway point, heavier guitars enter and the arrangement settles into a cold gothic-rock groove, increasing the pressure while keeping its movements controlled. That restraint gives the lyrics’ grotesque physical imagery additional bite. Red lips, internal screaming, and organs hanging from trees turn desire into a form of captivity, while the bass continues its patient inspection. The fascination directed toward the speaker feels increasingly forensic, as though somebody has been pinned beneath a collector’s glass and asked to appreciate the compliment. The uneasy string-like tones and warbles that open Peaceful in Daylight make its title seem optimistic well before the kick drum lands. Arcs of cold guitar stretch across the entrance, then the full beat pushes the song into motion, carrying heavy riffs and a vocal whose witchy bite grows sharper against the instrumental weight. Seaweed, dense smoke, cutting thorns, broken walls, injured skin, and abandoned nests accumulate in the lyrics, filling the song with evidence that something has gone badly wrong. The arrangement gives that damaged environment a restless physical life; every forward push seems to uncover another unpleasant detail. An old-school rock guitar solo adds a flash of theatrical excess, briefly letting the instrument take over the voice’s fevered work. Daylight may make this place easier to inspect, but there is very little in the music to suggest that inspection will bring reassurance. Spelling Misery initially gives its guitar melody a clear view of the room. The figure rises and falls over a solid rhythm section, its easy memorability providing a point of reference before heavier guitars and dark vocals crowd into the arrangement. Further melodic details appear as the song progresses, with a recurring gothic-rock guitar phrase adding small complications to the surrounding force. Those returns keep the ear attached to the song even as its family portrait becomes increasingly difficult to look at. Anger lives in the blood, a father kills the fatted calf in nervous rage, and memory falters under the effort of naming what has happened. Biblical promises of shelter follow: arrows will fail, feathers will cover the vulnerable body, and fear might be held outside for another night. The returning guitar figure offers a little steadiness amid those appeals, though the heavier passages make the promised protection feel precarious. Unsafe State opens with a buzzing synthesizer pulse and cold electronic tones, briefly suggesting a turn toward synthwave before the melodic resonance of the post-punk guitars establishes its place on the record. The vocal sits more clearly in the mix, and its somber delivery makes the song’s vulnerability unusually exposed. Where other tracks enlarge their distress through dense guitars and cavernous echoes, this one allows the words to feel nearer, with the electronic repetition giving them an uneasy regularity. Eyes lose their rhythm, time becomes a dark tunnel, and the speaker digs until their nails hurt while dead souls call from somewhere nearby. The guitar melody carries that distress with a fragile clarity, giving the song an emotional directness that makes its domestic setting especially troubling. Home is supposed to provide some distance from danger; here, danger has apparently obtained a key. The closing Merchants of the Wave begins with a bassline that shifts up and down, setting a rolling motion beneath a classic post-punk guitar figure. Broader gothic-rock arcs develop around that melody, while the ghostly vocal seems suspended above the rhythm section’s steady movement. The arrangement gives the record’s returning ocean imagery a physical shape: friends venture onto dangerous seas, boats pitch, beds shake with frantic dreams, and tears become indistinguishable from salt water. The bass keeps the song moving beneath those anxious visions, its rises and falls suggesting the uncertain footing of people trying to remain upright. Prayer repeats because repetition may be the only available defense against forces too large to negotiate with. The sea that opened the album as a place of private emotional exposure becomes a shared source of fear here, carrying the possibility that somebody loved might disappear beyond reach. GOSSIP COLLAR keeps returning to bodies under pressure: freezing, bleeding, scratched, exposed, dissected, exhausted, threatened with consumption or drowning. Yet these bodies persist. They dance. They pray. They disguise themselves. They paint their faces. They get abandoned to scavengers and announce plans to rise anyway. Musically, that stubbornness comes through in the combination of deathrock abrasion and electronic precision. Imagine Ladytron discovering a box of Killing Joke singles beneath the floorboards, then recruiting the Chameleons to widen the horizon while somebody from the Breeders quietly rearranges the furniture. Beneath all the gothic architecture runs punk’s ancient belief that anxiety becomes considerably more useful once somebody gives it a bassline. That may be why GOSSIP COLLAR’s particular apocalypse remains so inviting. Civilization has collapsed, the circus tent is falling, the sea wants your body, God may or may not be answering correspondence, and several animals appear to have questionable intentions. Fine. There is still a song playing downstairs. Might as well dance before the scavengers get here. Listen to EATEN OF WORMS below and order the album, out now via Bat-Cave Productions, here. items.album: Album Premiere: A celebration of brotherly LØVEGOD
items.excerpt: It’s said that the best friends make you a better version of yourself: they challenge you, encourage you, and help your better qualities shine. items.body: It’s said that the best friends make you a better version of yourself: they challenge you, encourage you, and help your better qualities shine. If that concept is prompting some personal reflection…well, I’ll leave that to you. But the idea also, arguably, applies to music. The best splits and collabs celebrate the best traits of all bands involved.LØVEGOD, the new split from German heavyweights Love•Love•Love and Ølgod, proves the better-together principle. The former’s rollicking post-hardcore/noise rock collides with the caustic doom/sludge of the latter for a celebration of all things reverb and abrasion. Love•Love•Love opens the album with muscular, in-your-face rippers engineered to start mosh pits. Walking a narrow tightrope between energizing groove and cutting harshness, it’s hard to sit still while listening to their bruising bops. In contrast to their friendly-sounding name, Love•Love•Love feels like they’re trying to start a fight…and having the time of their lives doing so. Ølgod picks up the caustic challenge laid down by Love•Love•Love and respond with devastatingly heavy grooves. The fighting intensity established in the first half of LØVEGOD is channeled into slow-burning anthems of despair, stretched and blown out into wallowing pits of misery. The core sound of the album doesn’t falter, but the delivery fundamentally alters the mood. Fans of noisy, scalding grooves will find themselves delighting in the contrasting points-of-view unveiled by both Love•Love•Love and Ølgod.Interestingly, both bands make good use of clean(ish) vocals that cut through rough-and-tumble riffs with mesmerizing clarity, adding a haunting layer to bludgeoning, crushing tracks. The emotion conveyed, however, shifts between the two sides: Love•Love•Love delivers a fervent, almost manic high while Ølgod reaches a plaintive, searing low. Strikingly similar methods with startlingly different results. Friends that make each other better by turning up the intensity of their best traits. LØVEGOD will be released tomorrow via Electric Valley Records. Pre-order here and prepare yourself for grrrrroooooves. Listen to the full album below. Follow Love•Love•Love and Ølgod on Bandcamp.

items.body: I recently wrote about an innovation currently taking place in noise rock, where noise rock bands that have embraced everything from more elaborate and thoughtful songwriting to unsettling electronic experimentation on their 2026 releases. Some that I didn’t mention have taken on a spacious, extended approach to the genre while others have embraced a dense, radical brevity. Bands across the genre have been stretching and morphing the style into previously unknown forms over the last few years, but it feels like this year has been especially fruitful in this regard. Tankerlow’s sophomore effort Slagroom can safely be added to the growing list of innovative noise rock that has been released this year, and it stands among the best.On Slagroom, Tankerlow employs a variety of sonic and dynamic approaches. Several tracks slowly unfold with a drone-like quality. There is an openness to those tracks that allows them to breathe and bloom on their own without being forced into a preconceived form by the composers. This natural pacing gives the impression that the members of Tankerlow exhibited considerable restraint, especially within a genre known for its compositional density. This restraint is most prominent toward the end of “Ergo/Ogre” when the song gets so quiet that the listener can hear the buzz of the amp underneath vocalist Guy Azulay’s unsettling, quiet moans. Yet, within that restraint is an impressive, free-wheeling aptitude for experimentation. That experimentation is prominent throughout the album, and not just with the more expansive tracks. Hammered dulcimers, pitched-down looped vocals that sound like a horn, and feedback accidentally created in the studio are all features on the groove-oriented “Formula Baby.” This combination of various compositional approaches and experimentation give each track their own character, a trait that is sadly hard to find in noise rock.What is at least partially responsible for that experimentation is the fact that the band spent over “two consistent and meticulous years in the studio,” which also explains the high quality of Slagroom’s production. Slagroom is, simply put, the best-sounding noise rock I’ve heard all year. Aspects of the album’s mix and sonic qualities oscillate between warmth and intimacy and coldness and harshness. Many of the album's sounds have an industrial quality, but they all come through the mix with analog-like warmth and clarity. Primary vocalist Azulay’s spoken-word vocals on tracks like “DIN” sound as if he is an unwell man standing right next to you on the subway, calmly detailing his mental deterioration in broken sentences. At other times, Azulay’s vocals explode into ranting and raving fury, such as during the tortured refrain in the middle and end of “Plasticine.” The opening guitars on “Ergo/Ogre” are subdued jabs, cutting into the mix like a cold butter knife. But that guitar contrasts wildly with the clanky, claustrophobic walls of chaotic distortion that envelop the listener in the song’s more climactic moments. Other aspects of the production are more subtle, such as the kick drum in “Glory Hole” that suddenly has more gain added to it during the song’s climax. According to the band, Slagroom explores “the concept of duality and the conflicts that arise from the battle of opposites,” and that notion is represented in nearly every aspect of the album. Slagroom is a rewarding but unsettling listening experience in part because the result of so many of those “battles of the opposite” is purgatory — a sense of being perpetually stuck in the gray, struggling to answer questions on identity, capitalism, and fame. But this, along with the experimentation and assiduous attention to detail, is what makes Slagroom such an intriguing listen and one of the most engaging noise rock releases this year. Of all the innovative releases put out under the noise rock banner this year, Slagroom is easily one of the best. SLAGROOM by tankerlow

items.body: 「この規模において、想像力は装飾ではない。インフラである」。スペキュラティヴアーキテクトのリアム・ヤング（1979-）が、ロンドンにあるバービカン・センターの個展「In Other Worlds」で掲げた言葉だ。ギャラリーの問いに留まってきたスペキュラティヴデザインを、産業と資本の現場へ接続するその賭けを、自らもアルゴリズミックデザインを事業として営む佐野虎太郎氏が、当事者の視点から読み解く。（artscape編集部） 立体駐車場に吊るされた、最後の人工物 展覧会の終わり、観客はバービカン・センターの立体駐車場「Car Park 5」へと誘われる。コンクリートの柱に黄色で「5」と記された、まぎれもなく現役の駐車場である。その薄暗い空間に、ワイヤーで1枚のパネルが吊るされている。そこに書かれていたのは《Emissary》──人類の文明が沈黙した後も航行し続けるよう設計された、「最後の人工物」としての宇宙船。NASAジェット推進研究所のエンジニアとの協働で構想されたこの架空の探査機は、征服のためではなく記録のための船であり、「傷ついた惑星から逃げるためのロケットではなく、それと向き合うための船」であると語られる★1。 「In Other Worlds」は、オーストラリア出身の映像作家でありスペキュラティヴアーキテクトという肩書きをもつリアム・ヤングの、英国初の大規模個展である。SCI-Arc（南カリフォルニア建築大学）で修士プログラム「Fiction and Entertainment」を率いるヤングは、映画産業におけるワールドビルディング（架空の世界を、地理・技術・統治・儀礼まで含む一貫した設定として構築する手法）を建築・都市の思索に持ち込んできた人物だ。本展は《World Machine》（2026、新作）、《After the End》（2024）、《Planet City》（2021）、《The Great Endeavour》（2023）、《Future Present》、《Emissary》（2024）の6つの「世界」で構成される。映像、都市模型、アン・クラブトリーによる衣装、グラフィックノベル、フォレスト・ソーズやスペース・アフリカらによるサウンドスケープが、ギャラリー「The Curve」から駐車場までを貫く1本の動線に配置されている。SF作家のキム・スタンリー・ロビンソン、AI研究者のケイト・クロフォード、ジオエンジニアリング研究者のホリー・ジーン・バックといった書き手が各「世界」のナラティブに参加していることも記しておこう。 展覧会の掉尾に置かれたステートメントに、このような一節がある。「この規模において、想像力は装飾ではない。インフラである」★2。本稿はこの一文を軸に本展を読解する。ヤングはスペキュラティヴデザインを、ギャラリーで問いを発する営みから、社会が未来を建設するための基盤へと運び出そうとしている。ただし運び出された先で、想像力は産業と資本の語り口にも組み込まれていく。筆者はアルゴリズミックデザインをファッションの領域で実践し、それを事業として経営する立場にある。スペキュラティヴデザインの語彙で教育を受け、その批評性を「実装」と「市場」のなかで運用せざるを得ない当事者として、本展のこの両義性を読んでみたい。 「In Other Worlds」より。Car Park 5に設置された幅16メートルのLEDスクリーンに映し出される《Emissary》（2024、約11分）［筆者撮影］   スペキュラティヴデザインの二つの系譜 「スペキュラティヴデザイン」（思索的デザイン）という言葉の来歴を、ここで簡単に振り返っておこう。通説的な系譜はロイヤル・カレッジ・オブ・アート（RCA）のアンソニー・ダンとフィオナ・レイビーに始まる。ダンは『Hertzian Tales』（1999）でデザインを問題解決の道具ではなく問題提起の媒体として再定義し、二人が率いたRCAのデザイン・インタラクションズ学科（2005年開設）がこれを教育として体系化した。「こうなるだろう未来」ではなく「ありうべき未来」を扱うデザインとして、スペキュラティヴ／クリティカルデザイン（以下、SCD）はダン＆レイビーの共著『Speculative Everything』（2013）を頂点に2010年代前半に制度化され、日本でも輸入学問的に受容された。しかしその形式──ギャラリーの白壁に置かれた思索的プロトタイプ──が誰に向けて何を変えるために問いを発しているのかについて、スペキュラティヴデザインはなお余地を残していた。ダン＆レイビー自身も2015年にRCAを離れて以降、プロダクトの形を借りた問題提起から、社会的想像力そのものの設計へと軸足を移していく。SCDの最初の波は、批評のための批評という袋小路と、美術館制度への快適な収容という二つの限界を抱えたまま一段落した。 ヤングの実践はこの系譜と重なりつつも、もうひとつ別の系譜も引いている。建築的ワールドビルディングの系譜だ。その先駆者であるアーキグラム（1960年代英国の前衛建築集団）の《ウォーキング・シティ》（1964）やスーパースタジオの《連続的モニュメント》（1969）が試みたのは、単体のプロダクトに問いを込めることではなく、都市と惑星のスケールで「別の世界の全体像」を描くことだった。同様にヤングもまた、2008年にロンドンで共同設立したシンクタンク「Tomorrow’s Thoughts Today」でも、ケイト・デイヴィスと共同で率いるリサーチスタジオ「Unknown Fields」でも、ヤングが一貫して扱ってきたのは「世界」の単位である。Unknown Fieldsはリチウム鉱山やコバルト採掘地など、私たちのテクノロジーを支える「見えない風景」への遠征そのものを方法とし、地球そのものをフィールドとしてきた。SCDの思索的プロトタイプとは、扱う対象のスケールも方法も異なる。モスクワのストレルカ・インスティテュートで哲学者ベンジャミン・ブラットンが率いた教育・研究機関「The New Normal」（2017–2019）に中核教員として参加し、都市を計算の「スタック」（層状に積み重なった惑星規模の計算基盤を指すブラットンの用語）として捉える語彙を得たことで、この系譜は本展の《World Machine》に流れ込む。 「In Other Worlds」より。4番目の世界《The Great Endeavour》の導入パネル。「大気を修復するには、空そのもののスケールで建設しなければならない」［筆者撮影］   見えないほど「大きな」技術への畏怖 ただし、SCDが生まれた2010年代初頭と現在とでは、思索の前提条件が根本的に異なっている。本展は、この変化に自覚的であるように見える。 第一に、生成AIの登場である。もっともらしい未来のイメージは無限にたやすく生成され、スペキュラティヴなイメージの希少価値は暴落した。実際、《After the End》のヴィジュアルにも初期生成AIを思わせる質感が横溢しており、ヤングもそれを隠そうとはしない。それでもなおワールドビルディングに固有の価値があるとすれば、それはイメージの表面ではなく、世界設定──エネルギー収支、物質循環、統治形態、儀礼──の一貫性と厚みにこそ見出される。6つの世界が複数のメディアで同一の世界設定を多角的に「実装」していたのは、その価値の所在への応答だと読める。 第二に、巨大インフラ企業の台頭である。2010年代のSCDが問うたのは「目に見えないまま個人の生に浸透していく技術」への恐怖、いわば製品スケールの未来だった。しかし現在、未来を最も大規模に建設しているのはハイパースケーラー★3であり、恐怖の対象は「見えないほど大きな技術」へと移った。データセンターの電力需要は原子炉の再稼働を促し、AI企業の設備投資は国家予算に匹敵する。新作《World Machine》が描くのは、この現実の延長にある世界だ。渓谷が回路になり、塩湖がプロセッサになり、サーバーは岩盤に沈む。先住民（ファースト・ネーションズ）のコミュニティが、化石時代の金属を溶かして大地に還す「更新の儀式」を執り行なっている。「惑星規模のAIを夢見ることは、地球そのものが機械になることを再想像することだ」（《World Machine》会場パネルより）★4。重要なのは、これがAIインフラを告発する作品ではないことだ。すでに建設されつつある「機械惑星」を、別の所有、別の儀礼、別の物質循環のもとで建設し直せないかという思考実験である。SCDが「問いを投げかけて立ち止まる」場所で、ヤングは「どう建て直すか」まで踏み込む。 本展の入口に掲げられた「未来は水のように私たちに押し寄せてくるものではない。それは創造の行為であり、私たちが一瞬一瞬、共につくるものだ」★5という言葉は、一見するとダン＆レイビーの「望ましい未来」と地続きに見える。だがここで実践されているのは、問いを発するデザインではなく、世界を建設するデザインだ。「想像力はインフラである」とは、デザインの思索が美術館制度から出て、政策、資本、技術開発の現場と直接に接続されるべきだという宣言にほかならない。 人間のいない風景──『Machine Landscapes』からの連続性 この「建て直す」という態度がどこから来たかは、ヤングが編者を務めた建築誌『Architectural Design』の特集号『Machine Landscapes: Architectures of the Post-Anthropocene』（2019）と並べると見えてくる。同号は、人間のためにつくられていない建築──データセンター、全自動港湾、物流倉庫──を「ポスト人新世の建築」として概念化し、人間中心設計の終焉を悲嘆ではなく観察として引き受けた。本展でも人間はほとんど映らず、映るとしてもインフラの巨大さを測るスケール・フィギュアとしてである。ドローンショットの幾何学的な人工景観が喚起する「テクノロジカル・サブライム（技術的崇高）」の美学は一貫している。 ただし、決定的な転調がある。『Machine Landscapes』の機械景観が「すでにそうなってしまった世界」の診断だったのに対し、本展の機械景観は「そうなるべき世界」の処方として提示される。診断の道具だった人間不在の風景が、修復の風景として反転されている。《Planet City》が最も明快だ。100億人が単一の超高密度都市に集住し、残る1億4200万平方キロメートルを野生に返す。「この世界で私たちの最大の建設は、建てないことを選んだ土地である」（ヤング、本展より）★6。人間の退場が、疎外ではなく贈与として語り直される。診断から処方へのこの転調こそ、想像力を「インフラ」と呼ぶことの実質である。 Climeworksとフィクションの往復 その宣言が最も鮮烈に、そして最も危うく表われていたのが、駐車場のセクション《Future Present》である。7面のLEDスクリーンには、実在する再生可能エネルギーと農業テクノロジーのサイトを取材したドキュメンタリー映像が流れる。そのなかに、直接空気回収技術（DAC。大気中のCO2を化学的に直接捕集する技術）を開発するスイス企業Climeworksへのインタビューが含まれていた。 印象的だったのは、インタビューの内容ではなく、その配置である。Climeworksのエンジニアが自社のCO2捕集モジュールを語る映像は、展覧会の構成上、直前のセクションで観たばかりの《The Great Endeavour》──大気を石に還す惑星規模の炭素除去インフラを、「私たちの世代の月面着陸」としてのジオエンジニアリングとして描いたフィクション映像──と地続きに接続されるよう置かれていた。観客は、洋上にそびえ立つ架空の巨大炭素除去プラットフォームの崇高な映像を脳裏に焼き付けたまま、現実のスタートアップ企業が手がけた、はるかにささやかな装置と対面することになる。現実の装置が、フィクションの側から遡行的に「巨大な未来の萌芽」として見えるように再構成され、Climeworksが惑星修復という物語の第一章に書き換えられるのだ。 ギャラリーの問いかけは現実を変えない、というSCDのアポリアに対して、ヤングは現実の技術開発の現場を物語に組み込み、その仕事に「より大きな未来の一部」という意味を遡及的に付与してみせる。ロビンソンが小説『The Ministry for the Future』（2020）で試みた「現存する技術と制度だけで組み立てられた未来史」の展示空間版ともいえるし、『After Geoengineering』（2019）の著者バックの参加は、《The Great Endeavour》の世界設定が炭素除去をめぐる統治や正義の議論を踏まえて構築されていることを裏付けている。 他方で、この構成は現実の側の摩擦を取り除くことによって成立している。Climeworksは2025年5月、従業員の約2割を削減した。アイスランドのプラント「Orca（オルカ）」は設計容量が年間4,000トンに対し捕集量は最高でも約1,700トン、後継の「Mammoth（マンモス）」（設計容量36,000トン／年）は稼働開始からの捕集量が805トン、自社排出を差し引けば正味121トンに留まると報じられている（CNN、2025年5月）。つまり現実のClimeworksは、《The Great Endeavour》の第一章であるどころか、その物語に到達できるかどうか自体が未決の、脆弱な実験である。 ヤングの構成は、この脆弱性を「まだ小さいだけの萌芽」として物語化する。だが「まだ小さい」と「原理的にスケールしないかもしれない」の間には深淵がある。崇高なイメージに接続された瞬間、個別企業の未決性は物語の推進力の中に溶けて見えなくなる。未来の炭素除去への期待が、現在の排出削減の切迫性を弱める──気候政策で長く議論されてきたこの逆説の、美学版と言うべき事態だ。しかも本展のリードスポンサーが不動産開発（Panorama St Paul’s）であることまで含めて考えれば、「想像力はインフラである」というテーゼは、想像力がインフラ資本を駆動する物語になるという事態と、常に紙一重である。 「In Other Worlds」より。Car Park 5に展開する《Future Present》の展示風景。床の矢印や柱の「5」の表示が残る現役の駐車場に複数のスクリーンが並び、集光型太陽熱発電のタワー、風力発電群、エンジニアへのインタビューといった、実在するエネルギーテクノロジーの取材映像が同時に流れる［筆者撮影］   スペキュレーションからインプリメンテーションへ この危うさを、筆者は展覧会の失点として書いているのではない。安全圏から問いを発する2010年代的な身振りを捨て、共犯関係のリスクごと未来像を建設する賭けの大きさこそが、本展を同時代の類似企画から隔てている。 ヤングの方法を映画の工程になぞらえれば、それはプリプロダクションに相当する。世界設定を固め、美術と衣装とミニチュアを作り、絵コンテを切る。本展に並ぶ模型、衣装、グラフィックノベルは、文字どおりその工程の産物だ。ヤングが率いる修士プログラムの名が「Fiction and Entertainment」であることも含めて、この実践は映画産業のワールドビルディングの技法を、未来の設計思想を提示するための道具として転用している。技術の設計思想を、論文やロードマップではなく、プリプロダクションの形式で世に出す。それ自体は、2010年代のSCDが到達できなかった射程だ。 だが、プリプロダクションの次の工程が、ここには用意されていないようにも見える。プリプロダクションは本来、撮影という現実の工程に接続されるからこそ意味をもつ。ヤングの世界設定は、特定のナラティブを経て、現実の技術開発や制度設計の現場に手渡されるべきものではないのか。だが筆者の見るところ、ヤングの元でこの方法を学んだ者の多くが向かう先は、映画やゲームの制作現場である。未来を実際に形づくる側の技術開発──エネルギー、素材、製造、計算基盤──に進む人材は少ない。プリプロダクションが、プリプロダクションのまま消費されている。 思索と実装の間に横たわる距離の大部分は、イメージでは表現できない種類の困難である。既存の生産設備との互換性、データ形式の断絶、現場の熟練、資金調達の速度、規格と規制。ヤングがClimeworksを《The Great Endeavour》の第一章として編み込んだとき、削ぎ落とされたのは、まさにこの種の困難である。フィクションの重力によって実装の困難が見えなくなること──実装の側にいる者から見れば、それは実装の困難そのものがナラティブによって洗浄されている、と映る。 2010年代のスペキュラティヴデザインは、プリプロダクションのままでよかったのかもしれない。だが2020年代は違う。ハイパースケーラーが惑星規模の現実改変を進め、AIエージェントがその速度をさらに引き上げている時代に、思索が思索のまま留まる余地は狭まっている。いま求められているのは、より精緻なプリプロダクションではなく、それを本撮影、つまり構想を現実の実践に接続する工程そのものの設計だ。スペキュレーションからインプリメンテーションへ。 「In Other Worlds」より。《Planet City》セクションに展示されたムービーミニチュア《Recycled Residential Tower》［筆者撮影］   ブルータリズムの遺構を通り抜けて 最後に、本展がバービカン・センターで開催されたことの意味に触れておきたい。バービカン・センターは、第二次大戦の空襲で焦土となったロンドンの一角に、シティ・オブ・ロンドン自治体が戦後復興期の総合計画として建設したブルータリズムのユートピア建築である。集合住宅と芸術センター、温室、人工湖を一体化したこの巨大コンクリート構造体は、「都市の未来はこう建設できる」という20世紀的な確信の遺構だ。本展で、観客はThe Curveの湾曲したギャラリーで6つの世界のフィクションに浸り、化石時代のインフラである駐車場で現実のスタートアップと向き合い、コンクリートの回廊を抜けて、最後に緑の庭園へと放り出される。過去の世代が実際に建設した未来のただなかで、次の世代が建設すべき未来を観るこの身体的なシークエンスそのものが、「想像された未来はやがて政策に定着し、コンクリートに固まり、化石記録に沈む」★7という最後のステートメントの、空間による上演になっている。バービカンは、想像力がインフラになった後の姿そのものなのだ。 「私たちは、何かが変わってしまったことを知りながらここに到着する。世界が突然単純になったからではなく、世界が見えるようになったからだ」と始まるこのテキストは、今日見てきた機械はもはやSFではなく、未解決なのは技術ではなく想像力だと告げ、こう結ばれる。「もしここに希望があるとすれば、それは確実性のなかにではなく、勇気のなかにある」★8。SCDが「問いを持ち帰ってもらう」ことで展覧会を閉じたのに対し、本展は「建設への勇気」で閉じる。 展覧会の出口、真っ暗な駐車場を抜けると、突如としてバービカン・センターのひらけた明るい中庭に放り出される ［筆者撮影］ おわりに──リハーサルの先へ ヤングは本展を「ファンタジーでも予測でもなく、私たちが望むなら建設できる世界を練習する場所」だと言い、「世界を建設することで、私たちは未来をリハーサルする」★9と続ける。思索的デザイン（speculative design）と投機的資本（speculative capital）が「未来を先取りして見る」という同じ動詞を共有する以上、その両面性から目を逸らさないことが、リハーサルに参加する側の最低条件になる。そしてリハーサルは、本番があってはじめてリハーサルと呼べる。この展覧会が観客に要求しているのは、勇気というより、その先の工程を引き受ける覚悟なのだ。   ★1──原文：“This is not a rocket built to flee a wounded planet; it is a vessel built to reckon with it.”（《Emissary》セクション パネル） ★2──原文：“At this scale, imagination is not decoration. It is infrastructure.”（最終セクション掲出ステートメント） ★3──ハイパースケーラー：Amazon、Microsoft、Googleなど、世界規模のクラウド／データセンター基盤を自社で建設・運営する巨大IT企業の総称。 ★4──原文：“In this world, to dream of Artificial Intelligence at a planetary scale is to reimagine the Earth itself becoming a machine.”（《World Machine》セクション パネル） ★5──原文：“The future doesn’t rush over us like water. It’s not something that happens to us. It’s an act of creation. It’s something we make, moment by moment, together.”（導入パネル、リアム・ヤングの言葉。本文訳では第2文を省略） ★6──原文：“In this world, our greatest construction is the land we choose not to build on.”（《Planet City》セクション パネル） ★7──原文：“The futures we imagine do not remain imaginary for long; they settle into policy, they harden into concrete, and they sink into the fossil record.”（最終セクション掲出ステートメント） ★8──原文：冒頭 “We arrive here knowing something has shifted. Not because the world has suddenly become simpler, but because it has become visible.” ／ 結語 “If there is hope to be found here, it is not in certainty, but in courage.”（最終セクション掲出ステートメント） ★9──原文：“These are not worlds of fantasy or prediction, they are places to practice the worlds we could build, if we want to.” ／ “By building worlds, we rehearse the future and by sharing stories we create the narratives we need the most.”（導入パネル）   参考文献 ・Barbican Centre. “Liam Young: In Other Worlds.” Exhibition website. https://www.barbican.org.uk/whats-on/2026/event/in-other-worlds（プレスリリース：Barbican Centre. “Barbican Opens 2026 Immersive Exhibition: In Other Worlds by Liam Young.” Press release, 2026. https://www.barbican.org.uk/our-story/press-room/barbican-opens-2026-immersive-exhibition-in-other-worlds-by-liam-young） ・Dunne, Anthony. Hertzian Tales: Electronic Products, Aesthetic Experience, and Critical Design. London: RCA CRD Research Publications, 1999. Repr., Cambridge, MA: MIT Press, 2005. ・Dunne, Anthony, and Fiona Raby. Speculative Everything: Design, Fiction, and Social Dreaming. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press, 2013.（邦訳『スペキュラティヴ・デザイン』東京：BNN、2015年） ・Strelka Institute. The New Normal Programme. https://www.e-flux.com/announcements/69635/the-new-normal ・Young, Liam, ed. Machine Landscapes: Architectures of the Post-Anthropocene. Hoboken, NJ: Wiley, 2019. ・Robinson, Kim Stanley. The Ministry for the Future. New York: Orbit, 2020. ・Buck, Holly Jean. After Geoengineering: Climate Tragedy, Repair, and Restoration. London: Verso, 2019. ・Paddison, Laura. “This Company Says Its Technology Can Help Save the World. It’s Now Cutting 20% of Its Staff as Trump Slashes Climate Funding.” CNN, May 30, 2025. https://edition.cnn.com/2025/05/30/climate/climeworks-pollution-carbon-capture-layoffs ・Lukowski, Andrzej. “Review Liam Young: In Other Worlds.” Time Out London, June 1, 2026. https://www.timeout.com/london/things-to-do/liam-young-in-other-worlds-review ・Paghdar, Bansari, and Anmol Ahuja. “On Planetary Speculation as Shared Cultural Infrastructure: Liam Young’s In Other Worlds.” STIRworld, May 28, 2026. https://www.stirworld.com/think-books-and-movies-on-planetary-speculation-as-shared-cultural-infrastructure-liam-youngs-in-other-worlds ・Tesler, Francesca. “Liam Young Imagines AI-Powered Mega Cities and Planetary Supercomputers in Barbican Exhibition.” Dezeen, June 5, 2026. https://www.dezeen.com/2026/06/05/barbican-in-other-worlds-liam-young/   リアム・ヤング「In Other Worlds」 会期：2026年5月21日（木）〜9月6日（日） 会場：バービカン・センター （Silk Street, Barbican, London EC2Y 8DS） https://www.barbican.org.uk/whats-on/2026/event/in-other-worlds

items.excerpt: 会期：2026/08/15～2026/10/12 会場：根津美術館［東京都］ 公式サイト：https://www.nezu-muse.or.jp/jp/exhibitions/current/ 日本の陶磁器は、中国、朝鮮半島から多大なる影響を受けて発展してきた。こと磁器に至っては、朝鮮陶工の尽力によって誕生した経緯があり、大陸とは切っても切り離せない関係にある。とはいえ、東アジア一帯の中国、朝鮮半島、日本で生まれた陶磁器を「東洋陶磁」と一括りにして語るには大雑把過ぎるところがあり、互いに有機的なつながりを持ちながらも、それぞれの土地に根ざした個性が育まれてきたと解釈するのが良いのである。そうした陶磁史の大きな流れを捉えるのに、本展はまさにうってつけだった。 重要文化財 五彩宝相華文瓶 景徳鎮窯 中国・明時代 16世紀 根津美術館蔵 根津美術館1階の展示室1で中国、展示室2で日本、そして2階に上がり、展示室5で朝鮮半島のやきものが展示されていたのだが、同館が所蔵する2300件に及ぶやきものの中から名品を選りすぐったというだけあり、作品数は絞られていたものの、かなり凝縮された内容となってい
items.body: 会期：2026/08/15～2026/10/12 会場：根津美術館［東京都］ 公式サイト：https://www.nezu-muse.or.jp/jp/exhibitions/current/ 日本の陶磁器は、中国、朝鮮半島から多大なる影響を受けて発展してきた。こと磁器に至っては、朝鮮陶工の尽力によって誕生した経緯があり、大陸とは切っても切り離せない関係にある。とはいえ、東アジア一帯の中国、朝鮮半島、日本で生まれた陶磁器を「東洋陶磁」と一括りにして語るには大雑把過ぎるところがあり、互いに有機的なつながりを持ちながらも、それぞれの土地に根ざした個性が育まれてきたと解釈するのが良いのである。そうした陶磁史の大きな流れを捉えるのに、本展はまさにうってつけだった。 重要文化財 五彩宝相華文瓶 景徳鎮窯 中国・明時代 16世紀 根津美術館蔵 根津美術館1階の展示室1で中国、展示室2で日本、そして2階に上がり、展示室5で朝鮮半島のやきものが展示されていたのだが、同館が所蔵する2300件に及ぶやきものの中から名品を選りすぐったというだけあり、作品数は絞られていたものの、かなり凝縮された内容となっていた。つまり中国、朝鮮半島、日本に点在していた窯の歴史や風土、特徴などをかいつまんで捉えられる構成となっていたのだ。例えば中国では紀元前のやきものの創成期に始まり、唐時代、北宋時代、南宋時代と時代を追って青磁などのやきものが紹介されており、近世からはいよいよ景徳鎮窯が登場する。青花（染付）や絢爛豪華な五彩（赤や緑、金彩などの上絵具で絵付けした表現手法）など、中国陶磁らしい作品に目を奪われる。そして日本では備前や信楽といった六古窯、美濃をはじめとする桃山陶、野々村仁清や尾形乾山らによる華麗な京焼などが紹介され、さらに江戸時代に肥前で盛んに作られた染付磁器や色絵磁器が続く。朝鮮半島では高麗時代と朝鮮時代に分かれ、青磁や白磁、また清楚な青花や白土を使った象嵌などが紹介されていた。 重要文化財 銹絵染付金彩絵替土器皿 京都 尾形乾山作 日本・江戸時代 18世紀 根津美術館蔵 このように一望すると、青磁ひとつ取ってみても、時代や窯によって水色から青、緑、褐色とずいぶん色合いや質感が異なり、その解釈の幅広さに驚く。白磁すら真っ白というのは少なく、青みがかっていたり黄みがかっていたりするのである。現代のように方々から材料を調達していたわけでなく、かつてはその土地で採れる土だけで作られていたのだから、当然といえば当然なのだ。本展を通して、東洋陶磁の奥深さと豊かさを改めて知ることができるだろう。 色絵三果文稜花皿 肥前 日本・江戸時代 17～18世紀 根津美術館蔵 山本正之氏寄贈 粉青象嵌牡丹文厨子 朝鮮半島・朝鮮時代 15世紀 根津美術館蔵 鑑賞日：2026/08/29（土）

items.body: The Red Garland Quintet Featuring John Coltrane and Donald Byrd - Soul Junction (Prestige, 1960) Culinary writers frequently refer to comfort food. Soul Junction is my comfort music. I go to this album when I’m not in the mood to be blown away by wild flights of improvised fury or complex compositions or arrangements. This is an “end of an exhausting day” or a “reminder that maybe all will be well” kind of an album. I love the relaxed, bluesy feel of it. Listen to Garland’s piano on the opening title track. It’s pure bliss. George Joyner’s bass is understated perfection. The piano trio portion of the track goes on so long and is so hypnotic that you’re to be forgiven if you forget there’s a sax and trumpet still to come. Hey, there’s the saxophone. It feels like Trane was digging Garland’s playing and was dying to join in. Recorded in 1957, Trane hadn’t perfected his style yet. But his genius is right there to hear. He’s fantastic on Dizzy’s classic Birk’s Works . Donald Byrd doesn’t get much mention on this website, but I love a lot of his Blue Note music. He’s the perfect trumpeter for this session. Garland wisely gives the two of them lots of space to play, and they take every advantage of it. John Coltrane- First Meditations (For Quartet) ( Impulse!, 1977) As far as I’m concerned, A Love Supreme is the greatest jazz album of all time and Coltrane’s classic quartet the greatest group. First Meditations (For Quartet) is a beautiful piece of music and a fascinating document of a band just on the verge of transforming, both in terms of its personnel and its approach to music. (I prefer to say “transforming” to “ending”.) The first track, Love, clearly recalls A Love Supreme, as if that classic album is the starting point of this new music. Trane is stunning as always and McCoy is the perfect accompanist. The best track, Joy, is relatively calm and peaceful, until it isn’t. It begins as any number of other tracks from this quartet and then Trane sits out. He’s let the remaining trio play some (for this group) fairly straightforward piano trio music. But then he returns with an absolute roar, as if he wants to break constraints the rest of us can’t see. This is one of several places you can see the seams of the band starting to tear. It’s fascinating to hear. Much of this music was reconsidered on the subsequent album Meditations with Trane’s new group. A comparison of the two albums and the approach of two different groups to the material is fascinating, the second album justifiably being the more renowned of the two. But I find the first to be the one I keep returning to, as if I don’t want to say goodbye to this quartet. I genuinely love this album, but I had an ulterior motive for writing about it here. It gives me the opportunity to tell the story of the time I met Elvin Jones. He had been doing a drum demonstration and a line formed afterwards for autograph seekers. When I arrived at the front of the line, I barely refrained from doing “We’re not worthy”, but I did tell him how much his music meant to me and said I’d be honored if he’d sign this album. He took the CD booklet from me, looked at it and asked “Did I play on this?”. (I assume that since the album wasn’t released until 10 years after it was recorded, he never saw the album cover.) I showed him his name in the booklet, he laughed and signed it, making this album all the more special to me. Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items.body: Label: Edition Records, 2026 Personnel - Mark Guiliana: drums, percussion, electronics, keyboards, guitar, vocals; Nicholas Semrad: keyboards; Stu Brooks: electric bass (#3), electronics (#2,4,7,8); Tim Lefebvre: electric bass (#2,4,6); Gretchen Parlato: vocals (#4,5); Marley Guiliana: vocals (#5). Mixed feelings arose from listening to Beat Music 2.0 , the synth-infused follow-up to Mark Guiliana’s Grammy-nominated album Beat Music! Beat Music! Beat Music! (Motéma, 2019). Retro and futuristic waves emerge from Guiliana’s compositions, which draw inspiration from early gaming culture and electronic music. Still, the focus here is on human connection and collaboration, as he enlists keyboardist Nicholas Semrad, bassist Tim Lefebvre, vocalist Gretchen Parlato, and Stu Brooks on electronics. The opener, “ B.ANG ”, excavates retro electronic music through glitchy synth ostinatos that march alongside the harmonic progression, along with a mix of ambient undercurrents and Gary Numan-style electro-rock energy. Although it tests the elasticity of the song’s edges, this piece failed to leave a strong impression on me. “ B.ORN ” and “ W.EST ” are also nothing special, while “ D.RUM ”, with its industrial stomp generating controlled trepidation and Parlato’s vocals highlighting the contrasting ambient-leaning passages, has a little more flair. I did feel a spark on numbers like “ P.LAY ”, whose actively propulsive drumming, together with Lefebvre’s brawny bass fluxes and pedals, is nothing short of gravity-defying, and “ B.EAT ”, whose grooving dub atmosphere morphs into club-dance territory for a while. Brooks, who infuses relevant, to-the-point electronics into the former, switches to electric bass on the latter. Also worth mentioning is “ M.OVE ”, whose danceable techno patterns reminded me of 808 State. Cross-rhythmic tides and dramatic shifts make this one a standout. Guiliana’s passion for what he does is undeniable, yet the prevailing virtues of Beat Music 2.0 come to the fore when the layers adopt a less explicit old-school electronic vibe in favor of more modernistic experimentation. Favorite Tracks: 02 - P.LAY ► 03 - B.EAT ► 07 - M.OVE

items.body:
Thailand has a new rock star to celebrate.

Nene Royal, the 16-year-old guitarist and singer from Phuket, has been crowned the winner of America’s Got Talent Season 21, becoming the first Thai contestant to win the long-running competition.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by America's Got Talent - AGT (@agt)

Ahead of the results announcement, Nene joined Linkin Park onstage for 'The Emptiness Machine', playing guitar and trading vocals with the band’s Emily Armstrong.

The performance capped off a breakout run on the show for Nene, whose real name is Rattikarn Amloy. For the finals, she delivered a heavy rendition of The White Stripes’ 'Seven Nation Army'. Throughout the competition, she also performed Soundgarden’s 'Black Hole Sun' and The Cranberries’ 'Zombie', with the latter earning her widespread attention after her audition went viral.

Nene also jammed with Mexican rock trio The Warning during the finale.

Before making it onto America’s Got Talent, Nene started playing guitar at seven and performed as a street musician in her hometown of Phuket, including busking at the city’s Naka Weekend Market. She has since built an online following through her performances on YouTube.

Following her victory, Nene thanked everyone who supported her, saying: “I’m very happy and emotional right now.”

As the season’s champion, Nene takes home US$1 million and earns a showcase on the Las Vegas Strip.

items.body:
All That Matters 2026 has unveiled its full programme and expanded speaker line-up ahead of its return to Singapore this October.

Happening from 2 to 7 October, the 21st edition of the cross-industry event will bring together music, sport, gaming, marketing, and entertainment under the theme Where Culture Is Currency. More than 100 global speakers and over 2,000 senior decision-makers are expected to take part.

The six-day programme kicks off with Music Matters Live from 2 to 4 October at CQ @ Clarke Quay, before the All That Matters Conference takes over Hilton Singapore Orchard from 5 to 7 October. Music Matters Live will also return for its closing-night programme on 7 October.

This year's conference will explore the growing intersections between fandom, technology, live entertainment, AI, the creator economy, cultural investment, and brand building.

Among the organisations represented across the speaker line-up are Universal Music Group, Warner Music, Warner Chappell Music, HYBE America, YouTube, YouTube Music, SoundCloud, IFPI, Live Nation Singapore, Virgin Music Group, Meta, Microsoft Xbox, Billboard, Luminate, Avex Music Creative, Believe Music, Singapore Tourism Board, National Arts Council, NBA, and Singapore GP.

On 5 October, the conference will open with Jasper Donat, Co-Founder and CEO of BRANDED, before turning to Singapore's role as a hub for culture, creativity, and innovation. The first day will also feature conversations around Asia's music industry, YouTube's entertainment ecosystem, fandom, live touring, J-pop, and visual storytelling, alongside the Music Matters Academy and Virgin Music Industry Mixer.

The second day will spotlight Asia's growing role in global live entertainment, with Adam Firth, Executive Director of Singapore GP, and Brett Murrihy of William Morris Endeavor discussing the convergence of sport, music, tourism, and culture. Sessions will also tackle AI in music, Asian music's global growth, songwriting camps, esports, gaming, cultural investment, and Singapore's ambitions as a global music hub.

Marketing and culture will take centre stage on 7 October, with discussions on the relationship between sport and music, cultural investment, brand relevance, creators, esports, and the arts. The conference will conclude with Fame + Fandom = Fortune for the New Power Players, followed by the Girls' Night Out showcase at CQ @ Clarke Quay.

Music Matters Live brings 44 artists from 15 countries to Singapore

Beyond the conference rooms, Music Matters Live will celebrate its 21st edition with four nights of live music on 2, 3, 4, and 7 October.

The free festival — except where otherwise stated — will feature 44 artists from 15 countries, including Lola Amour, DOLLA, KAIA, PIX!E, LIL LEAGUE from EXILE TRIBE, KID PHENOMENON from EXILE TRIBE, Supercatkei, Maisha Kanna, Bratty, Borderline, Reuben De Melo, Pierce Brothers, and more.

View this post on Instagram

Fans can also catch several dedicated showcases, including MadeIN Japan presented by EXILE TRIBE, MadeIN Philippines presented by NCCA, the debut MadeIN Nagaland showcase presented by the Government of Nagaland and TaFMA, two Sounds Australia showcases, and Music Is Universal by Universal Music.

KATSEYE are bringing EYEKONS closer to their journey with a new documentary film. KATSEYE: WILD HEARTS will begin streaming on 16 October on Disney+ internationally, as well as Disney+ and Hulu in the U.S.

The documentary takes fans behind the scenes of the global girl group's rise while exploring their relationship with EYEKONS around the world. It features never-before-seen footage, fan videos, and intimate interviews with the members.

KATSEYE: WILD HEARTS will trace the group's journey from the pressures and challenges of Dream Academy to their viral breakthroughs and global pop success, highlighting the sacrifices, setbacks, and milestones along the way.

Directed by Nadia Hallgren, the film is produced by Interscope Films and Boardwalk Pictures in partnership with HYBE x Geffen.

The streaming release follows the documentary's limited theatrical run and the kickoff of KATSEYE: THE WILDWORLD TOUR earlier this month. It also arrives following the release of KATSEYE's third EP, WILD, which debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard 200.

items.body:
Curating a retrospective of 40 years of recorded music is a daunting task, particularly when it is your own. Accurately representing the arc of the work and the life that created it requires frankness and acceptance. It is a process punctuated with winces and sighs and the occasional grin. Composer and improviser Jin Hi Kim experienced it all when compiling The Jin Hi Kim Collection, recently issued by Neuma. If the use of “odyssey” requires a great voyage, discovering new lands, and encountering titans, then Kim’s journey easily qualifies. Not only did she leave Korea at 23 for the US in 1980, Kim traversed an arguably greater gulf by leaving her elite training in traditional Korean music to study electronic music and composition with Lou Harrison, Terry Riley, and others. In the intervening decades, she worked with leading exponents of contemporary composition and improvisation like Kronos Quartet and Derek Bailey, and transformed the komungo, the traditional five-foot-long lute dating from the 4th Century CE, exponentially extending its sonic range through computer interfaces and signal processing.

Rediscovery accompanied the selection process for the 9-CD Collection. She was especially surprised when reviewing early works transliterating Korean music through Western instruments, or employing graphic notation. “It was created by a young mind,” Kim recently recalled with a laugh. “Sometimes it was hard to hear that’s what I did. But it was also good evidence for an archival collection. It was a wonderful feeling to look at everything I did – well, almost everything – but one thing that I was really proud about it is that there is not just one kind of music. Each piece has its Korean roots but, like I’ve said, I came to America to make new music, so I look at my 40 years of work and, yeah, I achieved that. So, it was a very satisfying process.

“When I listen to some of the improvisations, I realized how young and unafraid I was. Komungo has a limited sound compared to other instruments. When you work with virtuoso improvisers, they have vocabularies that are so rich. They are creating so many different colors and textures, but komungo has limits. It doesn’t allow you to express so much of the story. It has a meditative energy, of nothingness, of slowness. I was so brave to use this instrument with such incredible masters and to communicate with them and create music with them. I did it somehow with my inner energy. I was able to present this inner energy.”

The Collection almost equally divides Kim’s work in composition and improvisation, with five discs devoted to works for orchestra and chamber music ensembles, and four documenting improvisations with, among others, an impressive diversity of percussionists, including Gerry Hemingway, Susie Ibarra, and Tony Oxley, and string players like Bill Frisell, Min Xiao-Fen, and Hans Reichel. If anything can be read into it, the slight tilt reflects her ardent pursuit to articulate the concept of Living Tones Compositions, and how central it is to her work.

“The most important thing about the Living Tones Compositions is to convey the Korean element and philosophy through Western contemporary music,” she explained. “When I came to the United States after training in traditional Korean music, European classical music was more respected in Korea than the traditional music. They didn’t know much about American avant-garde music then, in the 1970s. I was a young musician who trained with the very best teachers and saw that I was not respected because I was not doing Western music.

“That created within me a great desire to fix that problem. You can’t fix anything, but I was young, I had a passion and a mission. I was living in the United States; I was composing for Western musicians; so how could I make this Korean idea, this Korean state of mind in making music, how could I put this together with Western music with equal respect? That was my thing. All my Living Tones Compositions come from the idea of putting together the Korean context and philosophy and Western instruments and musical context, to see how Western musicians took to the Korean attitude – not necessarily techniques, scales, anything like that – but this attitude, this state of mind. That’s what I’m doing with Living Tones music.

“Korean traditional music was once influenced by Chinese music,” Kim prefaced to explain the context and philosophy of Korean music, which she also detailed extensively in her book, Duality of Ancient Korean Roots and Western New Music. “Korean music can be divided into folk music and court music. Court music was quite different from music of ordinary people. The court was deeply influenced by ancient Chinese philosophy – yin and yang; the five elements, and ancient ancestors worship. The music wasn’t entertainment; it was ritual – that was part of both court and folk music. For ordinary people, they associated music with the shaman. For court music, there were virtuoso musicians who created an austere music, based on a philosophy of cosmic sound and abstract thinking; but for ordinary people, the shaman always took care of pain, community pain. Music was performed for celebrations of harvests and other things, but more for problems like drought, someone who is sick, some kind of problem. The shaman is always dealing with the problem of pain in their lives. They always had to sing something very sad. Her song has nothing to do with joyous things – always grief and pain. Ordinary people related to that.

“Both court and folk music had an emphasis on energy – they never thought of music as just sound. It had healing energy. In the folk community, they tried to imitate the shaman, the way she sang, shaking the notes, trying to reach out to another spirit, trying to connect heaven and earth. If you listen to a shaman’s song, there’s a very strong vibrato. The instrumentalists who don’t sing listen to this type of music; it’s very touching, very soulful, and it reflects the problems in their lives. Korean instrumentalists are all shaking, shaking their hands, shaking their instruments, shaking their notes. I play komungo, where the strings can move a lot, up and down, so you can really shake the notes and express the music in the same way as the shaman. I translate that process, that context, that spirit, into Living Tones. Each tone has its own light, and because it has its own light, its time is elastic. It is not like abstract Western time, where you count the time of each note perfectly, and you don’t have the space for microtones. There’s no time to do that in Western music. Time becomes much more open and that’s why in Korean music they don’t talk about abstract time but time in a cycle. Within that cycle, you have a lot of freedom of how to use that space with deep vibratos or any other articulation to create that intense feeling.”

The qualities Kim ascribes to Korean music are manifest in the komungo. It has a palpably plangent sound, with a bass register lower and more resonant than the guembri’s and the sting of ancient harps in its highest notes. It has a timbral luster comparable to the dark, iridescent glazes of pit-fired ceramics or the blocks of deep color that hover over the black basecoats of a Mark Rothko painting. Its dredge-like twang and the skeletal figures central to the music stop the racing, associative Western mind dead in its tracks. Even before Kim augmented the instrument with signal processing, Western improvisers had a strong attraction to the komungo. Conversely, improvisation has, over the decades, impacted Kim’s outlook.

However, Kim has a nuanced view on how improvisation has influenced her. “Influence is the result over a long period,” she elaborated, “because I played with a person one time or two times. That long period is a really deep space. It’s not that a particular musician gave me something. It is that the experience of playing with someone becomes part of my life experience. Now I look at something differently than when I was young. I understand how the universe works because of scientists and I understand how improvisation works because of improvisers. When you travel all around the world – I’ve performed in over 60 countries and have lived in some of these countries for a long time, six months or even a year – then you have an incredibly different life perspective. All of those things interest me. So, I have been influenced by many things over the decades, so that when I play with someone, it is not just that moment I am responding to; it’s everything about the other musicians: their instruments; their traditions; their culture. That gives me a very clear idea what to do.

“When I was young, I was so desperate to communicate successfully with each improviser I played with. I was trying to understand their personality; I was trying to understand their vocabulary. There have been very few times that I played on the spot without any information about the people I was playing with. I had heard them before I had the opportunity to play with them, playing with other musicians or solo. In my own way, I understood who they are. If I don’t understand them and their musical elements, I have no way to contribute anything on komungo. I have to understand their personality, their energy, how they process the music. Not all people process the same way; some people are poetic; some people are very emotional; some people are very funny. Everybody has those things happening. Understanding that was very important to me. It helped me to communicate, to hear what they were giving me, so I could give back. I listened a lot to what they were doing at a particular moment.”

Given that improvisers spanning James Newton and Elliott Sharp, and Rüdiger Carl and Oliver Lake, are heard throughout the box set, it is noteworthy that Kim singles one out to illustrate her approach to improvisation. “When I work with William Parker, he has a very deep energy in his soul,” she said of the bassist. “When I played with him, he influenced me with his deep energy. It’s really big. That influenced me to be really big. That bigness, that abundance, that tireless energy; that lets us play a really long time. He has the qualities to do something that a Korean shaman could do, playing the same idea over and over and over for a long time – trance like – but the energy becomes more powerful. William Parker has that type of energy. The bass is like the komungo; it has a deep energy and incredible power. I’m really influenced by that.”

Retrospectives like the Collection are generally considered to be merely summations, but in Kim’s case, it is more a marker of distance travelled and journeys ahead. “It reflects my continuous evolution as an artist. Throughout my musical journey, I have always searched for new ways to express myself creatively while remaining deeply rooted in my Korean musical identity.

“In essence, every work in this collection is the result of my enduring desire to elevate often-neglected Korean aesthetics, shaped alongside the freedom I found in America – a place that allowed me to pursue my artistic passions and ideas without limitation.

“Today, my perspective extends beyond national boundaries to the increasingly interconnected global community. I have aspired to use music as a spiritual and transformative force to confront social challenges. I believe this has become the new direction of my artistic journey.”

Kim’s new direction has steered her towards to uplifting marginalized subalterns and breaking through the fourth wall of the concert hall separating musicians from listeners. “Right now, because the world has changed so much, and America is now so blue, and so many people are mentally ill – I know because I recently gave a music meditation workshop at the Yale mental health center – I want to do something about community pain. I always go back to what the shaman does. I think I have sort of achieved my goal of blending Korean and Western ways of thinking with Living Tones, so right now I want to make music that the community participates in. Not necessarily well-trained musicians, but anybody who is interested. I already started on this in 2023 with a piece called ‘Ritual for Earth.’ I would like to do these things for now. I’m not anxious about my career or my next commission. I’m thinking about community pain, environmental issues like wildfires and floods, the world we are living in. So, if I have the opportunity, working with communities is what I want to do.”
